items.title: Mahama describes AfCFTA as Africa’s ‘greatest architecture for conflict prevention’
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called for deeper economic integration among African countries, describing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a major instrument for preventing conflict and strengthening peaceful relations across the continent. Speaking at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Peace in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, President Mahama presented the 2026 State of Peace and Security in Africa Report, covering developments from January 2025 to June 2026. He argued that the AfCFTA should not be viewed solely as a commercial initiative, but also as a framework for reducing tensions by making African countries more economically interdependent. “We often view the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) purely as a commercial project. That is a mistake. The AfCFTA is perhaps our greatest architecture for conflict prevention,” he said. President Mahama explained that stronger trade links could increase the economic cost of conflict and encourage countries to see their neighbours as valuable trading partners and suppliers rather than adversaries. He also said integrated and traceable value chains could help dismantle illicit economies associated with smuggled minerals, illegal taxation at roadblocks and the activities of warlords. The President further highlighted the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which facilitates cross-border payments in African currencies, as another mechanism for strengthening regional economic ties and reducing Africa’s exposure to external economic shocks. However, he cautioned that economic integration alone could not resolve conflicts, stressing that political agreements and settlements remained necessary for lasting peace. “Trade cannot replace political settlement, but poverty and border friction will always guarantee war,” he said. President Mahama urged African countries to strengthen regional cooperation and address the economic conditions that fuel instability, arguing that sustainable peace must be supported by both security measures and economic justice.

items.title: Africa needs stronger digital payment links to unlock regional trade – Femi Osinbajo
items.description: Professor Yemi Osinbajo, a former Vice-President of Nigeria, has called for stronger cooperation among African countries to improve cross-border payments, strengthen digital integration and support trade and investment across the continent. He said although African countries had made progress in developing domestic payment systems, transferring money across borders remained difficult and costly for traders, businesses and individuals. Prof. Osinbajo was speaking at the opening of the Mobex Africa Conference 2026 on the theme: ” Resetting Africa’s Digital Identity and Sovereignty from Promise to Practice.” He said some transactions still depended on correspondent banking arrangements outside the countries involved, often introducing additional intermediaries and costs. The former Vice-President said the challenges could undermine efforts to deepen regional economic integration and expand opportunities for businesses operating across national borders. He said initiatives such as the African Continental Free Trade Area and digital transformation programmes demonstrated the continent’s commitment to integration, but their success depended partly on efficient, secure and accessible payment systems. He called for stronger collaboration among central banks, financial institutions, governments, and other relevant authorities to improve connections between national payment systems. He said integration required more than technical partnerships, stressing the importance of trust, common standards and effective regulatory cooperation among African countries. The former Vice-President said digital integration must also protect financial stability and ensure that improved connectivity did not introduce risks into national financial systems. He urged governments to establish supportive policy environments, while central banks strengthened the resilience of financial infrastructure and financial institutions developed services that responded to the needs of households and businesses. He said digital financial services could create opportunities for traders and small businesses by improving access to financial information and enabling lenders to make better-informed decisions. He, however, stressed the need to protect customers, ensure fair lending terms and provide safeguards when technology failed or payment transactions encountered problems. The former Vice-President said accessible digital identification and straightforward verification processes were also important to making financial services available to more people. He noted that concerns about data exposure and increased visibility to authorities could discourage some traders from participating in formal digital financial systems. He called for safeguards to protect personal and business information and ensure that users could benefit from digital services without compromising their privacy or rights. Mr Owureku Asare, Director of the Fintech and Innovation Office at the Bank of Ghana, highlighted Ghana’s experience in developing payment infrastructure to improve connectivity among banks, microfinance institutions and other service providers. He said Ghana’s experience demonstrated that public investment, strong institutional leadership and enabling regulation could support secure and accessible payment systems while allowing financial institutions to innovate and compete. Mr Asare said Ghana remained committed to working with other central banks, regional institutions and industry partners to improve the efficiency and connectivity of payment systems across Africa.

items.title: Africa must prove climate adaptation is saving lives, not just spending money
items.description: When floods leave roads impassable, water supplies become contaminated and children fall ill, the consequences of climate change are measured in more than damaged infrastructure or financial losses. They are measured in lives disrupted, household incomes lost and families struggling to cope. For Dr Richard Munang, Director of the United Nations University Institute for Natural Resources in Africa (UNU-INRA), these are the realities that must shape how Africa measures progress on climate adaptation. “Adaptation is not what we spend. Adaptation is who we protect,” he told participants at the African Technical Workshop on the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) Indicators in Accra. The three-day workshop, held from 22 to 24 October 2026 at the West African Genetic Medicine Centre, brought together African climate negotiators, government officials, technical experts and representatives of the United Nations University and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Its central task was to test whether the global adaptation indicators can adequately reflect Ghana’s national priorities, what existing data systems can measure and where gaps must be addressed. The exercise comes as countries begin working with the 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators adopted under the Global Goal on Adaptation process. For African countries, the challenge is no longer simply to agree on a framework for measuring adaptation, but to determine whether it captures the results that matter to people and communities. Measuring what matters to people Dr Munang argued that climate adaptation must be judged by its impact on people’s lives, rather than by the amount of money allocated or spent. Drawing on his childhood in north-western Cameroon, where failed maize harvests left his family struggling to find food, he recalled how climate pressures can deepen the vulnerability of households already facing economic hardship. That experience, he said, reinforced the need to connect adaptation policies and investments to tangible improvements in people’s lives. “Because if you don’t count what is failing, you cannot fix it,” he said, calling for evidence that identifies both successful interventions and those that fall short. He pointed to the links between disaster risks and public health, arguing that poorly maintained drainage systems, flooded roads and delayed early-warning messages can have consequences that extend well beyond the immediate disaster. A flooded road can prevent an ambulance from reaching someone in need. Contaminated water can expose children to waterborne diseases. When early warnings fail to reach communities in time, the consequences can be devastating. These connections underpin the workshop’s decision to focus on disaster risk reduction and health, two areas where the effectiveness of adaptation measures can have direct consequences for human wellbeing. For UNU-INRA, working with the United Nations University International Institute for Global Health offers an opportunity to examine these connections more closely and strengthen the evidence used to assess adaptation outcomes. Ghana’s national priorities take centre stage Ghana is serving as the pilot country for the exercise, providing an opportunity to compare its National Adaptation Plan and sector priorities with the global indicators. The assessment is intended to establish where national priorities align with the indicators, where important outcomes may be missing and whether the data and institutional arrangements needed for reporting are already in place. Director of the United Nations University International Institute for Global Health, Dr Revathi Phalkey, said the exercise should help countries determine whether their existing systems can adequately measure progress towards their adaptation ambitions. “What we really need to measure is where do we need to go and how fast we can get there,” she said. Her remarks underscored the importance of looking beyond historical performance to assess the pace and scale of action needed to meet future adaptation goals. Representing the Chair of the Africa Group of Negotiators, Stella Okoh of Ghana’s Environmental Protection Authority said the workshop would help institutions identify how existing national reporting systems could be used to track the indicators. “The conversation is not to create different reporting formats,” she said, explaining that the priority was to build on existing national systems, identify gaps and determine what needed to improve. She also highlighted the importance of monitoring whether adaptation interventions were actually building resilience in Ghana. The approach is expected to bring together institutions responsible for climate adaptation, health, disaster management and reporting, helping them assess what information is available and where additional work is required. From global indicators to national action For the UNFCCC Secretariat, the exercise forms part of the wider effort to establish how the global indicators can be applied across different national contexts. Motsomi Maletjane of the Secretariat’s Adaptation Division said countries had agreed to test the indicators voluntarily following their adoption at COP30. The resulting experience will help inform the development of indicator metadata and methodologies, as well as assessments of their applicability to national circumstances. “These exercises by Ghana, many other countries that are doing similar exercises are very key to being able to tell how countries can start to work with the indicators,” he said. The findings are also expected to contribute to countries’ reporting on adaptation progress and inform their own planning processes. For Ghana, the workshop’s practical work centres on mapping national adaptation priorities against the relevant indicators, examining data availability and identifying methodological, institutional, technical and financial gaps. Participants are also expected to develop recommendations for addressing those gaps and identify lessons that could be adapted by other African countries. Building an evidence-based African position Beyond the technical assessment, the exercise carries implications for Africa’s engagement in international climate negotiations. Dr Munang said the continent needed evidence to demonstrate whether adaptation investments were delivering results and whether the global indicators adequately reflected African priorities. He argued that indicators should not be accepted simply because they form part of an international framework. Where they fail to capture national ambitions or outcomes, countries should be able to demonstrate the shortcomings and make the case for improvement. “Africa is not poor. Africa is uncounted,” he said, stressing the importance of strengthening the evidence available to African policymakers and negotiators. The workshop is expected to produce an assessment of Ghana’s alignment with the indicators, a review of implementation gaps, practical guidance for future country-level exercises and policy messages to support African engagement ahead of COP31 and COP32. The wider ambition is to develop an approach that other African countries can use to assess the indicators against their own adaptation plans, priorities and reporting systems. For Dr Munang, however, the ultimate test remains whether adaptation makes a measurable difference to ordinary people. “We can only say we have adapted if that child who is playing aside today will not end up in a clinic tomorrow,” he said. That challenge places the focus firmly on outcomes of whether communities are better protected from disasters, whether health risks are reduced and whether public investments are building resilience where it is needed most. As Ghana undertakes the pilot assessment, its findings could help shape a more practical approach to measuring adaptation across Africa, one that connects international commitments to national priorities and, ultimately, to the lives those commitments are intended to protect.

items.title: PIAC seeks details of petroleum funds allocated to Big Push projects
items.description: The Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) released its 2026 semi-annual report on Ghana’s petroleum revenue management, noting that additional information on how the government uses petroleum revenues allocated to the national budget would strengthen its assessment of government expenditure. Mr Richard Ellimah, Chairman of PIAC, said the Committee had yet to receive information from the Ministry of Finance on the utilisation of the Annual Budget Funding Amount (ABFA), which limited its ability to fully assess expenditure under the programme. He made this known at the launch of PIAC’s 2026 semi-annual report in Accra, explaining that the Committee had requested the data from the Ministry but was still awaiting a response. Mr Ellimah said the information was particularly important for monitoring expenditure on infrastructure projects, including the government’s Big Push Agenda, which includes the construction of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway. He said the concentration of a significant proportion of the ABFA in the Big Push programme could also influence how PIAC conducted its project inspections. “We are hoping very much that the Ministry of Finance will give us the data so we can understand what is going on,” he said. “It is something new for us because it is going to change the way we also do our project inspections.” Mr Ellimah also called for greater attention to compliance with the legal provisions governing the provision of information to PIAC. He said in the Committee’s 15 years of operation, he was not aware of any prosecution for failure to comply with the Petroleum Revenue Management Act (PRMA). PIAC intended to engage the Attorney-General for guidance on addressing recurring compliance concerns, he said, noting that the Committee could not independently initiate legal action to enforce its recommendations or compliance with the Act. “These are clearly legal infractions,” he said, adding that the Attorney-General’s advice would help determine the appropriate course of action. PIAC was established under Section 51 of the PRMA to promote transparency and accountability in the management and use of petroleum revenues. Its mandate includes monitoring compliance with the Act and providing independent information to the public to support informed debate and Parliament’s oversight responsibilities. Mr Isaac Dwamena, PIAC’s Executive Secretary, said the Petroleum Revenue Management Regulations specified the timeframe within which institutions were expected to respond to the Committee’s requests for information. Regulation 25 requires institutions requested to provide information for PIAC’s annual and semi-annual reports to do so within 15 days of receiving the request. Despite the outstanding information, the report assessed developments in petroleum revenue collection, production, expenditure and the management of the country’s petroleum funds during the first half of 2026. It said petroleum revenue receipts increased to US$561.4 million in the first half of 2026, from US$370.3 million in the corresponding period of 2025. The increase was attributed largely to higher crude oil prices and a rise in corporate income tax receipts. The average achieved crude oil price was US$92.80 per barrel, above the benchmark price of US$76 per barrel. PIAC, however, cautioned that the increase in revenue was driven substantially by higher prices rather than a corresponding rise in production. It highlighted the vulnerability of petroleum receipts to fluctuations in the international oil market.

items.description: The National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) in the Bono Region has lauded the quality of work on the Sunyani-Inner Ring Road Project, being funded by the government’s “Big Push” Road Infrastructure programme. Mr Gabriel Kwame Okyere, the Public Relations Officer at the Bono Regional Office of the NRSA, however, cautioned tricycle riders in particular against reckless riding. Kofi Job Constructions Limited, contractors executing the 9.2-kilometre Road Project from Fiapre Roundabout, connecting the Sunyani Technical University, has asphalted the road. In an interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA) in Sunyani, Mr Okyere said: “Our major concern now is how tricycle riders are speeding on the road since it was asphalted”. “In fact, the office continues to receive complaints of recklessness by the tricycle riders, using portions of the asphalted road project”, he stated. He commended the government for the ‘Big Push’ programme, saying that the inner ring road project had opened the Sunyani Municipality for economic growth. Mr Okyere said small-scale businesses had started springing up along the road project, since it was asphalted, thereby creating economic opportunities for the locals. In a separate interview, Mr Kofi Kamkam, the site engineer of Kofi Job Construction Limited, said 2.5 kilometres of the road project had been asphalted for use, assuring that the project would be completed within the two-year stipulated period.

items.title: My wife died two years ago, then grief opened door for madness
items.description: My Peju Akande Mywife died two years ago. Before then, she had been sick for a long time; the kind of sickness that drains everybody in the house. You know that saying: “The person caring for the sick is sometimes sicker than the sick person.” It’s true. It’s painfully true. I won’t stand here and claim I did all the caring. Her children, our children, carried that burden with full chest. They were her hands, her legs and her nurses. But she was still mywife. I did what I could, in my own small way. I put all my manhood on hold and accepted it as destiny. You know what I mean. When she died, the house became quiet in a way that frightens even an old man. There used to be noise, you know, the good kind. People trooping in and out. Neighbours, people from our mosque, alfas, children she helped, women she advised, men she encouraged. Big tree Mywife was a big tree. When she fell, the shade disappeared. People came for the burial, stayed for a while, then left one by one like leaves falling off a branch. And I was alone. My children begged me to come and stay with them, but grief is a stubborn companion. I said I wanted to be alone. I didn’t realise loneliness has teeth. Not that I feared ghosts, if mywife appeared, even as a ghost, she wouldn’t harm me. She would probably scold me for misplacing my glasses, or my phone or even money. Eventually, my children arranged someone to cook and clean. I was turning 80; I needed help. Even if it was someone to quarrel with. That’s how I met this woman at the mosque. The ‘eleha’ who hid her evil under a burqa. She was an eleha, fully covered, soft‑spoken, eyes lowered. But I was fooled in my old age! I’m not saying women who wear hijab or burqa are evil. No. But this particular one used that covering to hide her wickedness like a snake hiding under dry leaves. She was 45 when we met. She said her husband left her with three children. At my age, I wasn’t looking for romance. I have 11 grandchildren. My prostate is enlarged — so that department is closed for renovation. Companionship All I wanted was companionship, you know, someone to talk to. Someone to sit with, someone to keep me warm in the evenings. I told her clearly: “I will help you financially. But I cannot father your children. They cannot live with me.” She agreed, or she pretended to. We started “seeing” each other quietly. I didn’t introduce her to my children, they would never accept it. But I’m sure they suspected. That woman entered my life like a thief in the night and she has been stealing me blind. She stole more than Shina Rambo! Do you know Shina Rambo? Ah, you are young. Shina Rambo was the most notorious armed robber in Nigeria in the 80s and 90s. This woman? She stole more than him, without gun, without knife, without breaking the door. She would take my money and claim I gave her myself. She lies like someone who practices lying as a profession. I would put money on top of the fridge, she would take it and swear I took it myself. I don’t have an ATM card, so I withdraw large sums at once. Before I know what is happening, fiam! All the money is gone. I told her I would help her financially. I didn’t tell her to help herself to my money like a rat eating ‘breadi agege’. She turned me into an ATM machine, and that is what I will not accept. So I told her not to come to my house again. And I will stand by it. Because as old as I am, I have learned one bitter truth: loneliness is not enough reason to invite madness into your home! •Series, first published in thisislagos.ng, was written and edited by Peju Akande and based on true stories The post My wife died two years ago, then grief opened door for madness appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama warns foreign powers against treating Africa as a ‘chessboard’
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has urged African leaders to unite against foreign interference and protect the continent’s sovereignty, warning that external powers are seeking strategic influence and access to Africa’s resources. Speaking at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, he said African countries must take greater control of their political, economic, and security priorities instead of allowing foreign interests to determine their future. “External powers, from the East, the West, and the Gulf, are actively seeking leverage, access, and client states on our soil,” President Mahama said. He warned that Africa risked becoming a battleground for competing foreign interests if its leaders failed to act collectively and establish a common vision for the continent. “Africa is not an empty chessboard for foreign powers to play their games. We are not spectators,” he added. President Mahama stressed that African countries must take the initiative in shaping their own future, cautioning that failure to do so could leave the continent at the mercy of decisions made by others. “But unless we consciously decide to take up the pen and write our own script, someone else will write it for us, and we will not like how the story ends,” he said. The President called for stronger continental unity and greater African ownership of political, economic and security decisions, arguing that the continent must define its priorities and safeguard its sovereignty amid growing competition for influence.

items.title: GoldBod will not compromise LBMA certification for galamsey – Minkah
items.description: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) has rejected suggestions that it would support illegal mining, insisting that doing so would undermine its efforts to secure certification from the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA). The Board’s Head of Communications, Prince Kwame Minkah, said responsible sourcing was a key requirement for the certification, which demands that gold entering the market comes from legitimate sources and is produced without causing environmental destruction. He explained that GoldBod’s ambition to meet international standards meant it could not endorse mining activities that violate the law or damage the environment. “Nobody should fall under any delusion that the CEO of GoldBod, whose institution is aspiring for LBMA Certification, would endorse illegal mining, especially when the prerequisite for LBMA Certification is responsible sourcing,” he said. Mr Minkah’s comments follow public criticism of GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi over remarks concerning efforts to formalise unlicensed small-scale miners. Mr Gyamfi subsequently clarified that his position was to bring eligible operators into a regulated system, rather than endorse illegal mining. Speaking on Channel One TV on Saturday, October 24, Mr Minkah said his intervention was intended to reinforce Mr Gyamfi’s position on transitioning eligible miners into lawful operations. The LBMA is a global authority in the precious metals market, with standards covering the quality of gold and silver as well as responsible sourcing.

items.title: GES, stakeholders call for stronger action against child marriage in Eastern Region
items.description: The Eastern Regional Directorate of the Ghana Education Service (GES) has marked the International Day of the Girl with a call for increased investment in girls’ rights and efforts to end child marriage. The celebration was held at Oyoko Methodist Senior High School on the theme: “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights.” It brought together students and stakeholders to promote girls’ education, protection and empowerment, while encouraging boys to play an active role in addressing teenage pregnancy and gender-based violence. Madam Patricia Birago Gyamfi, Eastern Regional Girls’ Education Officer, said the participation of boys was essential to efforts to protect and empower girls. She stressed that no girl under 18 years should be forced into marriage, adding that every child deserved the opportunity to learn, develop and make informed decisions about her future. She called on parents to keep their daughters in school and urged teachers, community leaders and other stakeholders to create safe learning environments and support programmes that promoted girls’ education, health, safety and leadership. Mr Kwasi Owusu Obeng, Eastern Regional Population Officer of the National Population Council (NPC), said teenage pregnancy and early sexual activity posed serious threats to girls’ education and prospects. He said the Eastern Region had a teenage pregnancy rate of about 14 per cent, describing it as a concern that required stronger interventions. Mr Obeng said reproductive health education often focused on girls, despite the role boys played in teenage pregnancies, and called for greater attention to educating boys on abstinence and responsible sexual behaviour. He said involving boys in reproductive health programmes would help reduce teenage pregnancies and promote shared responsibility among young people. Dr Moses Barima Djimatey, Eastern Regional Deputy Director of Public Health, said addressing teenage pregnancy required the active involvement of both boys and girls. He disclosed that more than 4,000 girls aged between 10 and 19 became pregnant between January and June, describing the situation as a concern with health, social and economic implications. Dr Djimatey called for stronger collaboration among district assemblies, religious and traditional leaders, schools, the police and health workers to guide young people and protect their future. Assistant Superintendent of Police Lydia Wemegah, Eastern Regional Coordinator of the Domestic Violence and Victim Support Unit (DOVVSU), highlighted the need to intensify efforts to end child marriage and protect girls from abuse. She called for stronger enforcement of laws against child marriage, community sensitisation and support for victims, noting that poverty, cultural practices and limited education contributed to the persistence of the practice. As part of the celebration, students were divided into nine groups and assigned mentors to share their life experiences and discuss decisions that could shape their future. Madam Diana Mintah, Headmistress of Ghana Senior High School (GHANASS), called for regular mentorship programmes for students, saying they would equip them with the knowledge and values needed to become responsible leaders and positive role models for future generations.

items.title: NDC to investigate vote-buying allegations in constituency elections if evidence is provided
items.description: The National Democratic Congress (NDC) says it is prepared to investigate allegations of vote-buying in its ongoing constituency elections if credible evidence is brought before the party’s national executives. The party’s Deputy Director of Elections, Rashid Tanko-Computer, said the NDC would not condone conduct that compromises the integrity of its internal electoral processes. He cited the party’s response to a previous incident involving Ayawaso as an indication that it was willing to act when concerns about electoral conduct were brought to its attention. Mr Tanko-Computer, however, said the party had not recorded any incidents of vote-buying in the constituencies where voting had taken place, describing the elections overall as largely peaceful and successful. He acknowledged that the exercise had encountered difficulties in some areas, including Odododiodioo, where counting was suspended following violence but resumed after party officials intervened. He also disclosed that voting in some constituencies in the Ashanti and Eastern regions had been postponed until the following day to allow outstanding issues to be resolved. Speaking on Channel One TV, Mr Tanko-Computer said: “If somebody has any evidence of that and it’s brought to the notice of the national executives, why not? We’ll take notice of it.”

items.title: Transport Minister calls for efficient, competitive ports to boost regional trade
items.description: c Mr Nikpe said achieving the ambition required sustained collaboration among the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA), the government, private-sector operators, regulatory agencies, and other stakeholders across the transport and logistics value chain. He made the call in a keynote address at the GPHA’s 40th Anniversary Dinner and Industry Awards, where he highlighted six priorities for building a more efficient, competitive, and sustainable port system. The priorities include improving cargo handling and evacuation, reducing avoidable delays, strengthening coordination among port operators and regulatory agencies, and making port services faster, more reliable and cost-effective. The Minister said port competitiveness depended not only on infrastructure but also on the quality and efficiency of services delivered to businesses and customers. He also called for the adoption of integrated digital systems, automation, and data-driven operations to improve transparency, simplify procedures, and enhance customer experience. On transport connectivity, he said stronger links among ports, roads, railways, inland terminals and logistics centres were essential to easing congestion, facilitating cargo movement, and improving access to regional markets. Mr Nikpe urged stakeholders to prioritise environmental sustainability, energy efficiency, workplace safety and operational resilience as the country modernised its port infrastructure and services. He said workforce development was equally important, calling for investment in professional training, digital skills, technical expertise and leadership development to prepare workers for the changing demands of the maritime and logistics industry. On regional trade, the Minister said Ghana had an opportunity to strengthen its position as a preferred gateway for landlocked neighbouring countries and a leading logistics hub for West Africa. He said realising that potential required reliable services, competitive costs, efficient transit procedures and deeper collaboration with regional partners. The Minister said the six priorities reinforced the anniversary theme of service, partnership and progress, stressing that no single institution could achieve the objectives independently. He encouraged stakeholders to sustain cooperation to improve the competitiveness and efficiency of Ghana’s transport sector. The event also recognised individuals and organisations whose dedication, professionalism and contributions had advanced GPHA and the country’s maritime industry. The Minister congratulated the award recipients and urged stakeholders to uphold high standards of service, integrity, and innovation. As GPHA looked towards its next 40 years, he called for continued investment in digital transformation, transport connectivity and workforce development to expand Ghana’s contribution to regional trade. He said the ambition to build West Africa’s premier trade and logistics hub must be reflected in service quality, strong partnerships and tangible results for businesses, communities and the country.

items.title: Soludo in Tinubu’s Campaign: ‘Bitter truth’ is South-East must align with centre — Sly Ezeokenwa, APGA National Chair
items.description: •Dismisses anti-party claim against Anambra gov By Dickson Omobola National Chairman of the All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA, Sly Ezeokenwa, in this interview first aired on Arise News, speaks on the reasons Anambra State governor and national leader of APGA, Professor Charles Soludo, has pitched tent with President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, APC, ahead of the 2027 elections, despite concerns over alleged anti-party activities. Excerpts: Your party, APGA, has adopted President Bola Tinubu, and your governor, Professor Charles Soludo, has now been named on APC list. What should this tell the average voter? Is this merely a symbolic show of strength and dominance by the APC? Would the allegation of anti-party activity apply to Professor Soludo? I think it would be good to state that the decision of Professor Charles Soludo, who, by the way, is the national leader of our party, to support the President transcends their personal relationship. Once you become the leader of a party, the Constitution imposes certain obligations and responsibilities on you. In a multi-party democracy such as ours, coalitions are inevitable. When you have about 22 political parties, as we currently do, with people from diverse ethnic groups and different religious backgrounds, you can be certain that any presidential candidate seeking to meet the constitutional threshold faces a considerable task. You must recall that to be elected president of Nigeria, the Constitution requires you to secure a simple majority and at least 25 per cent of the votes cast in at least two-thirds of the states in the country. You will agree with me that this is not an easy task for any presidential candidate in a multi-party democracy. That, therefore, calls for broader coalitions. Those who are well versed in our politics will know that such coalitions have historical precedents. There have been instances of alliances and coalitions before independence, after independence, during the 1979 elections and beyond. For me, this is nothing new. However, our decision as a party to support the President stems from three perspectives, and I must make that emphatically clear. First, it draws from history. APGA has a standing policy under which the party considers a cordial relationship with the ruling party part of its strategic alliances and survival. You know very well that this policy was adopted around 2011. Incidentally, the only governor on the platform of APGA at the time was the current presidential candidate of the NDC. That was when APGA adopted the presidential candidacy of the then President Goodluck Jonathan, a decision it repeated in 2015. Even in 2019 and 2023, when the party nominated its own presidential candidates, it did not derogate from that tradition of supporting the incumbent. Beyond the policy and historical perspectives, we come to the more germane issue. Our leader popularised an aphorism that, in a multi-party democracy, it does not make sense for every political party in the country to field a presidential candidate when some of those candidates are unlikely to secure even 50,000 votes. If our affiliations and alliances in a multi-party democracy should be ideologically driven, then there is nothing wrong with political parties that profess similar ideologies coming together to support a common presidential candidate. That was how our leader popularised the phrase that progressives are working together, which stemmed from his charge or call during the President’s visit to Anambra. For our party specifically, there is a strong, longstanding alliance with the administration of President Bola Tinubu. That alliance led to the appointment of a serving member of APGA’s Board of Trustees, BoT, Bianca Ojukwu, as a minister in President Tinubu’s cabinet, as well as the appointment of another APGA member. If you look at the 2023 elections, despite having much of the influence in the South-East, Peter Obi of the Labour Party secured over 90 per cent of the votes in the region. How will APGA’s influence change that result in favour of the APC, bearing in mind that Obi was once a member of APGA and would still have some supporters in your party? Obi is from Anambra and still wields that level of influence in the South-East. How would you turn the region in favour of President Bola Tinubu now that APGA has aligned with his candidacy? As a party, we have our position, which is that we have endorsed and adopted the candidacy of President Bola Tinubu. That is a fact. Now, we have a critical issue involving a proud son of Anambra, the first governor elected on the platform of APGA, who is also running in this election. However, in this context, it is better for us to be politically correct as we approach the 2027 presidential election. It is a question of whether to be politically correct or join the bandwagon of sensationalism surrounding a particular candidate. We believe that, before the advent of the current Fourth Republic in 1999, the promoters and founders of the ruling party, the PDP, came together and crafted an agreement. It was more or less an unwritten agreement on power rotation or power sharing between the North and the South. We believe that, whatever the circumstances, it is now the South’s turn. Someone from Southern Nigeria, President Bola Tinubu, is currently in office. So, the South has another four years, and it only makes sense to allow the South, through President Tinubu, to complete its tenure. That is one fact. For us as a party, we believe it is our responsibility to tell the people the bitter truth, regardless of whose ox is gored or how people feel about it. That bitter truth is that we believe it has not served the interests of the South-East to continue on this trajectory of political alienation. If you look at the data or statistics recently released by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, showing the percentage of registered voters across the country, the South-East accounts for, I think, about 11 per cent of registered voters. The question is whether the South-East, on its own, can produce a President without building a broader coalition with other regions. We believe that the roadmap to the presidency, for the foreseeable future, requires the South-East to find a way to align with the centre. If we align with the centre and other regions, we can return to the question at the appropriate time. For now, it is the South’s turn to complete its remaining four years through the incumbent President. We believe it serves the interests of the South-East better to align with other regions by supporting President Tinubu’s bid for re-election. We see this as a means of bringing the South-East back into the equation. Since 2015, it has been our belief that the South-East has been left out of the scheme of things in the country. No matter how anybody feels about it, that is the bitter truth. It ought not to be so, but that is the reality on the ground. You called Obi your precious son from Anambra and the first person to win the governorship on APGA’s platform. Why denigrate him openly for political reasons? Win or lose, the 2027 elections will be over by January 15, but the impact of the damage you people would do to your fellow Igbo man would never be forgotten. How do you react to that? Emotions will get us nowhere. I head a political party; I do not run a charity organisation. As a political party, we make decisions based on what our leaders believe serves our strategic interests at a particular time. At this point, that means supporting President Bola Tinubu’s candidacy. It is the party’s decision, and, as I said, it is driven by historical alliances, policy and other factors. I have not seen any former governor who was given the kind of pre-eminence Peter Obi enjoyed under APGA. When he joined the party, APGA gave him its platform on a platter of gold, and he contested the election. Barely six months after completing his tenure, he left the party. Since then, he has continuously worked against APGA. His only mission, in our view, is to annihilate the party. APGA has survived various attempts by Peter Obi to undermine it. Let us start from 2015. Barely a year after leaving the party, he joined the PDP and became part of the coalition forces working against APGA’s National Assembly candidates. This was despite the fact that APGA had adopted the candidacy of President Goodluck Jonathan at the time. In 2017, Peter Obi was instrumental in the emergence of Chief Willie Obiano. However, that same year, he backed another candidate and took that candidate across the state. We have videos of him calling the then governor of the state a drunkard at a campaign rally. In 2021, he repeated the same thing, supporting another candidate. Despite all this, Professor Charles Soludo, who became governor in 2022, recognised that Obi was a son of the state and a former member of the party. He invited him back to APGA because we believed that building that brotherly alliance was necessary if we were to have a shot at the presidency. President Bola Tinubu, the brother you referred to, built alliances across the South-West before taking office. Even when the time came for him to run for President, he stepped aside from his ambition to support another presidential candidate because he believed it was not the right time for him to contest. That is what a true leader who has the interests of his people at heart does. A quick flaw in your argument: you said that when Peter Obi left, he still returned to work with the party to ensure Willie Obiano’s emergence. Did he not? No, no, no. That is wrong. Who worked for Obiano’s emergence? He was still in the party when he worked for Obiano’s emergence. The part of the story you have not mentioned is that all this started when they fell out. You are wrong. They did not fall out before he left the party. Immediately after Peter Obi handed over to Obiano on March 17, 2014, some Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, governors visited him at his residence somewhere in Onitsha and invited him to join the party. If you recall, he never said at the time that he had fallen out with Obiano. He called APGA a special purpose vehicle. But you have just made my point. He was elected, helped APGA win re-election and handed over an APGA government in the state when he left… We have never denied that Peter Obi helped us to get re-elected. But you are putting the cart before the horse. The fact is that APGA first did someone a favour by offering him its platform in 2003. When he was rigged out, APGA members went to the tribunal to defend his mandate. They testified, presented certified true copies of result sheets and tendered them as evidence, leading to the historic overturning of the declaration of then Governor Chris Ngige. So, you must give APGA credit. Now that your party is supporting President Tinubu, we have heard that in Edo State, the APC expects to deliver 2.5 million votes. In Osun, the Accord Party says it will deliver 1.8 million votes. How many votes will APGA deliver? For me, it is not about figures. It is about presenting our people with the facts, the truth and, as it were, the bitter truth: that, in this election, there is no pathway for our so-called brother. As painful as it is, that is our position. It is in the strategic interests of Ndi Igbo to align with President Bola Tinubu’s aspiration. That is what APGA stands for, and we will do everything possible to convince our people why they should vote for President Tinubu. Vanguard News The post Soludo in Tinubu’s Campaign: ‘Bitter truth’ is South-East must align with centre — Sly Ezeokenwa, APGA National Chair appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GoldBod begins stakeholder consultations ahead of 2027 small-scale mining support programme
items.description: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) has begun engaging industry stakeholders on a proposed programme to formalise artisanal and small-scale mining and provide financial support to eligible operators ahead of its planned launch in 2027. The initiative, known as the Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining (ASM) Formalisation and Financing Support Programme, is expected to bring eligible informal miners into a regulated system while improving their access to financing and strengthening oversight of their activities. GoldBod said the consultations involve relevant government agencies, small-scale miners’ associations, civil society organisations and other industry stakeholders. The engagements are intended to gather input to ensure the programme reflects industry needs and can be implemented sustainably. The Board is developing the programme in collaboration with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT) and the Mineral Income Investment Fund (MIIF), with technical support from South Africa’s Rand Refinery. According to GoldBod, the initiative is expected to increase gold production and mineral revenues, create jobs, reduce operational costs and limit environmental degradation associated with mining activities. The programme also forms part of efforts to tackle illegal mining by ensuring that eligible operators are licensed, monitored and held accountable for their environmental and operational practices. GoldBod has stressed that the objective is not to legitimise galamsey, but to help eligible informal miners transition into lawful operations and comply with the country’s mining regulations. In a statement issued by its Media Relations Unit, the Board said it had “commenced stakeholder engagements with key industry stakeholders, including relevant government agencies, small-scale miners’ associations, civil society organizations, among others, on the proposed ASM FFSP”. The consultations come amid public debate over comments by GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi on the formalisation of unlicensed small-scale miners. GoldBod has rejected allegations that he endorsed illegal mining, arguing that a video of his remarks was selectively edited and omitted important context.

items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: WHY POLITICAL RADICALISM EATS ITSELF
items.description: Political radicalism sits uneasily within the paradigm of mainstream politics. Interestingly, this phenomenon has increasingly manifested among the middle classes. The lineage of both left and right ideological extremes can be traced to two historical junctures. Left-wing radicalism finds its genesis in the 18th century French Revolution and right-wing extremism in the ascent of Nazism in 1930s Germany. In both instances, the working classes served primarily as foot soldiers. They were mobilised by middle class concepts and aspirations. The French Revolution was animated by the theories of ‘enlightened’ middle-class intellectuals and Nazism was built upon convoluted race theories conceived by middle-class thinkers. In 18th century France, radical philosophies emerged from an ascending and fledgling middle class that felt its economic and social progress impeded by the remnants of the ancien régime, such as decadent monarchs, landed nobility and an exploitative clergy. These were overthrown through bloody upheaval, driven largely by downtrodden mobs. However, when this triumph’s middle-class architects attempted to translate their radical philosophies into governance, they plunged the nation into further turmoil. This instability was checked by the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte, who established a dictatorship. The resultant political trajectory finally matured into the secular democratic system that endures in France till today. The maturation was a synthesis of clashing ideas, crystallised by an overwhelming need for moderation and stability in a country that had been turned on its head. From revolutionary France to contemporary Pakistan, radical movements have repeatedly demonstrated how the pursuit of political absolutism can become an instrument of self-destruction By the 1930s, Europe’s middle class was expanding its influence within this evolving arrangement. But the arrangement was suddenly unsettled by the expansion of socialist movements following the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution in Russia. As socialist ideologies gained political traction among the growing working classes, the middle class began to experience severe insecurity. They felt they were being squeezed between entrenched elites and increasingly active working class constituencies. In Germany, this middle class anxiety manifested as hostility toward democracy. It began being blamed for Germany’s economic ruin, military humiliation and the perceived infiltration of communism. To the middle classes, communism threatened the socio-economic hierarchy through which their own aspirations were sustained. As a result, in 1933, a significant portion of the German middle class cast its ballots for Adolf Hitler’s radical far-right Nazi party, viewing it as a bulwark against communism. Many middle class intellectuals, professionals and jurists aligned themselves with traditional economic and religious elites to elevate a fanatic to power. But Hitler’s ensuing radical agenda plunged Germany into catastrophic warfare and widespread devastation, underscoring the destructive capacity of radicalism when integrated into mainstream statecraft. Political radicalism in mainstream politics often operates through a self-consuming dynamic, ultimately destroying the very leaders and movements that champion it. According to American political scientists Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, when radical movements enter the political mainstream, their rejection of political norms invites counter-mobilisation and their own downfall. Radical actors trigger a chain reaction that eventually dismantles their power, fractures their movements, and leaves them vulnerable to judicial and political prosecution. Levitsky and Ziblatt suggest that the main problem with bringing radical ideas into mainstream politics is that they simply do not work with normal governance or the art of working together. Governing effectively requires making deals and knowing when to compromise. Radical political figures who refuse to compromise or work within institutional rules eventually undermine their own ability to govern. They view political rules and traditions not as guidelines, but as traps set by their ‘corrupt’ rivals. Their strict ‘no-compromise’ attitude makes it nearly impossible to build stable alliances. Moderate voices inside the party are slowly pushed out or silenced. This leaves the leader surrounded only by yes-men and extreme loyalists, destroying the party’s ability to think pragmatically or adapt when a major political crisis hits. On a social level, political radicalism creates deep divisions in society and leaves the public exhausted. Indeed, tapping into anti-establishment anger can be an effective way to turn economic frustration into massive street rallies, but keeping that radical momentum alive requires the constant sustaining of the outrage. This leads to protest fatigue. According to the Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde, radical populism splits society into hostile camps, turning normal debates over policy into dramatic ‘us versus them’ battles. Over time, average citizens, the more thoughtful voters, and the business community grow weary of the continuous turmoil. The country becomes politically exhausted and economically fragile. The researchers Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan concluded that when society begins to crave stability, radical politics rapidly loses its broad electoral appeal. Its practitioners become isolated. When radical leaders urge their followers to confront state authorities directly, public sentiment gradually begins to move toward the desire for order and security, legitimising the state’s countermeasures. In 1972, the British psychologist Irving Janis demonstrated that radical movements are driven by collective arrogance and a charismatic leader’s illusion of invincibility. Such leaders often develop “hubris syndrome”, mistaking mass rallies for absolute mandates. They believe they are immune to legal or institutional limits and begin to couple their personal political survival with the destiny of the nation itself. This prompts them to make constant strategic blunders. A modern illustration of all this is Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI). PTI entered mainstream Pakistani politics by mobilising public discontent against established political parties. Khan put forward a radical agenda that mostly attracted the middle classes. However, after bumbling across his three-year government, and losing parliamentary support in 2022, he and his party escalated their anti-establishment rhetoric to unprecedented levels, framing the struggle for Khan’s political survival as a ‘national liberation’ movement. This radical route culminated in the violent events of May 2023, and November 2024, where party supporters targeted state and military installations. The state responded with crackdowns, mass arrests and judicial trials. Khan’s strategic reliance on populist radicalism and uncompromising confrontation resulted in his imprisonment, and then his party’s gradual organisational paralysis, demonstrating how mainstream radicalism provokes its own undoing. PTI’s undoing now seems complete with the sidelining of its one remaining provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. What’s more, the party’s core middle class constituency followed it all the way till it crumbled into a political black hole. Radical populists destroy their own political longevity by rejecting formal and informal political norms, and confusing their irrational bullheadedness as an uncompromising commitment. The German sociologist Max Weber warned of a mindset where leaders prioritise absolute moral purity over pragmatic political outcomes. Weber argued that political figures driven by radical moral conviction inevitably produce catastrophic results and trigger their own downfall, whereas enduring statesmanship requires an “ethic of responsibility”, grounded in compromise, foresight and restraint. Published in Dawn, EOS, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Food, Floods, Erosion: 16,140 households targeted with 5,380 tubewells, dams, irrigation projects in Kano
items.description: •Inside the Ecological Project Office interventions in dry-season farming By Nnamdi Ojiego For farmers in Kano State, the end of the rainy season often marks a difficult transition. As rainfall declines, access to water becomes a major concern, particularly for smallholder farmers who depend on seasonal rains to cultivate their land. In communities exposed to flooding and erosion, the challenges are even greater, with damaged roads, threatened homes and disrupted economic activities adding to the difficulties of rural life. In Sumaila Town, Sumaila Local Government, for instance, residents faced serious challenges due to a lack of accessible roads and the threat of gully erosion. Vehicles could not enter parts of the neighbourhood, forcing car owners to park outside. Against this backdrop, the Federal Government has embarked on a series of ecological and agricultural interventions across Kano State, combining flood control, erosion remediation, road improvement and irrigation infrastructure in a programme intended to support farming throughout the year. The projects, implemented by the Ecological Project Office under the leadership of Permanent Secretary, Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Dr. Aishetu Gogo Ndayako, include interventions in communities spread across several local government areas, as well as irrigation schemes linked to Tiga, Challawa-Gorge and Kafin Chiri dams. Project documents obtained by Sunday Vanguard indicate that the programme covers erosion control, flood mitigation, the construction of bridges and culverts, improvements to rural roads, the provision of tubewells and pumping machines, and the development of canal networks to supply water to farmland. A separate watershed management programme lists 18 projects involving the provision of 5,380 tubewells and an equal number of pumping machines, with 16,140 households identified as intended beneficiaries. The programme is reported to have achieved an average completion rate of 99.7 per cent, according to a brochure published by the Ecological Project Office. The interventions form part of the Federal Government’s special ecological programme for the Kano River Irrigation Project under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda. Beyond the number of projects and facilities listed, the programme raises important questions about the relationship between water management, agricultural productivity, rural infrastructure and the ability of farmers to sustain production beyond the rainy season. Ecological interventions The erosion and flood-control component of the programme covers a range of communities where the government has listed projects intended to address erosion, flooding and deteriorating road infrastructure. The project schedule contains 32 entries, including the construction of bridges and culverts for flood control, erosion-control works, remediation of affected areas and road improvement along selected routes. Among the locations listed are Zambur, Unguwar Gai in Kibiya Local Government Area, Rimmin Yamma and Sumaila, Rurum-Bunkini-Kazaurawa, Furuwa, Kibiya town bypass, Zango and Hanyar Kogo in Takai, Kachako, Karaye, Kukar Bashari and Kwanar Dan Goro. Other locations include Fulatan in Rogo Local Government Area, Kadabo Road, Darki bypass in Wudil, Kiru, Tiga-Runum Road, Gala, Wudil town, Daki community, Bebejii, Kadauji village and Magami. The programme also lists road improvement and erosion-control works along Sabon Gwandu, Kazaurewa-Gana Road in Rano, Unguwar Gora, Rano-Bunkure Road and Falali in Sumaila, among other locations. The projects vary in their stated purposes. Some are primarily concerned with erosion control, while others combine erosion remediation with road improvement. Several involve the construction of bridges or culverts intended to help manage flooding and improve movement within affected communities. Such infrastructure can be important in rural areas where roads provide links between farms, residential settlements, markets and other essential services. Where erosion damages roads or floodwaters cut off access, farmers may encounter additional difficulties moving produce to buyers, obtaining agricultural inputs or reaching their fields. The listed interventions therefore have potential implications beyond the physical structures being constructed. Their value to communities will depend on whether they address the problems for which they were designed and whether the infrastructure remains functional after construction. Challenge of flooding, erosion Flooding and erosion can place considerable pressure on communities whose livelihoods depend on agriculture and local trade. Heavy rainfall can wash away topsoil, damage roads, undermine structures and disrupt the movement of people and goods. Where water is poorly channelled, runoff can gradually erode the land, deepen gullies and threaten farmland and residential areas. Flooding can also make roads impassable, leaving some communities with limited access to markets and essential services. For farming households, the effects may extend beyond the immediate damage. The loss of productive land, interruption of cultivation and difficulty transporting harvested crops can affect household earnings and food availability. The Federal Government’s programme addresses some of these concerns through a combination of erosion-control structures, bridges, culverts and road improvement works. The inclusion of bridges and culverts in locations such as Zambur, Furuwa, Magami and Unguwar Gora suggests an effort to address specific points where water movement and access are important considerations. Other projects focus on erosion remediation or the improvement of roads in towns and rural settlements. However, without adequate maintenance, infrastructure intended to control erosion and flooding can deteriorate, reducing its effectiveness over time. The programme’s long-term value will therefore depend not only on construction but also on the quality of the works, their suitability for local conditions and the arrangements for monitoring and maintenance. Irrigation expansion While the erosion and flood-control projects address environmental and infrastructure challenges, the irrigation component seeks to improve access to water for agriculture. The EPO has listed interventions at Tiga, Challawa-Gorge and Kafin Chiri dams, with plans to open new sectors for irrigation and provide canal networks to serve designated areas of farmland. Together, the three schemes are designed to cover 1,279.91 hectares. The Tiga Dam intervention accounts for 875 hectares, Challawa-Gorge for 240 hectares and Kafin Chiri for 164.91 hectares. The proposed schemes combine main canals, distribution canals, field canals and pipe extensions, depending on the requirements of each location. The objective, according to the documents, was to make water available for cultivation beyond the main rainy season, giving farmers an opportunity to grow crops during periods when rainfall alone may not support production. Dry-season farming can provide an additional source of income for farmers and help maintain agricultural activity when rain-fed cultivation is no longer possible. Depending on local conditions, crops grown under irrigation can also supply markets at different times of the year. For the intervention to achieve these aims, however, the infrastructure must be completed, supplied with adequate water and operated in a way that allows farmers to use it reliably. Tiga Dam: 875 hectares earmarked for irrigation The Tiga Dam scheme is the largest of the three irrigation interventions listed in the project material. Completed in 1974, Tiga Dam is a major water-storage structure associated with the Kano River Irrigation Project. The supplied technical data describes it as a zoned earth-fill dam with a length of 6,000 metres and a maximum height of 48 metres from foundation level. Its reservoir capacity is listed at between 1,350 million and 1,450 million cubic metres, although the design capacity is given as two billion cubic metres. Under the current EPO intervention, 875 hectares have been earmarked for irrigation across three sectors identified as Renewed Hope Sector 1 at Yakasai, Sector 2 at Gawama and Sector 3 at Guriya. The project schedule assigns 46 hectares to Yakasai, 381 hectares to Gawama and 448 hectares to Guriya. The three sectors together account for the stated 875 hectares. To support irrigation across the designated area, the planned infrastructure includes 20.361 kilometres of distribution canals, 77.456 kilometres of field canals and a one-kilometre pipe extension. The proposed network is intended to convey water through the irrigation system and distribute it to the designated farming areas. The effectiveness of the scheme will depend on how the different components are connected, the availability of water and the arrangements for distributing it among farmers. The size of the area earmarked for irrigation gives the Tiga intervention particular significance within the programme. If the facilities become operational and farmers can use them consistently, the scheme could support additional cultivation during the dry season. Challawa-Gorge: another 240 hectares The second intervention is at Challawa-Gorge Dam, where the government plans to open an additional 240 hectares for irrigation. Completed in 1992, the dam is described in the supplied technical document as a rock-fill structure measuring 7,804 metres in length, with a maximum height of 42 metres from foundation level. Its total reservoir capacity is listed as 930 million cubic metres, comprising 904 million cubic metres of active storage and 26 million cubic metres of dead storage. The irrigation intervention involves an extensive network of canals, pipe extensions and access roads. According to the project schedule, the planned main canals measure 14 kilometres and 2.5 kilometres, while the distribution canals measure 13.5 kilometres and 3.5 kilometres. The listed canal works also include lengths of 25 kilometres and 4.5 kilometres under the description of additional canals, identified in the source material as “Reid Canals”. The project, marked as ongoing, includes a 1.37-kilometre pipe extension and 10.5 kilometres of access roads within the canal network. The inclusion of access roads alongside the canal network is significant because irrigation infrastructure must connect with the areas it is intended to serve. Roads can assist movement within the scheme, including access to farms and the transport of agricultural inputs and produce. The 240 hectares designated for irrigation could provide additional opportunities for cultivation if the scheme is completed and made operational. The actual benefits, however, will depend on the distribution of water, the number of participating farmers and the reliability of the infrastructure. Kafin Chiri: a smaller scheme with similar objectives At Kafin Chiri Dam, construction is listed as ongoing. The planned irrigation area is 164.91 hectares. The dam’s technical data lists a reservoir capacity of 31.12 million cubic metres and a reservoir area of 8.42 square kilometres at full capacity. The EPO intervention includes 9.474 kilometres of main canal, 7.106 kilometres of distribution canals and 2.748 kilometres of field canals. Although the area is smaller than those covered by the Tiga and Challawa-Gorge schemes, Kafin Chiri forms part of the same wider effort to expand irrigation infrastructure and support farming outside the rainy season. The proposed canals are intended to connect the water supply with designated agricultural areas. As with the other schemes, their usefulness will depend on the completion of the network and the availability of water when farmers need it. The three dam projects collectively account for almost 1,280 hectares of planned irrigation. That figure provides a measure of the scale of the government’s stated intervention, although the project documents do not establish how much of the land is already being irrigated. Tubewells, pumping machines for dry-season farming Beyond the dam-based schemes, the EPO’s watershed management programme is designed to provide water facilities for all-season farming across several local government areas. The brochure lists all the projects and states that the programme involves 5,380 tubewells, 5,380 pumping machines and 16,140 households. The listed locations include Garko, Sumaila, Gaya, Ajingi, Albasu, Karaye, Kiru, Rogo, Bunkure, Tudun Wada, Takai, Kibiya and Wudil. The project descriptions refer to drilling tubewells, providing water-harvesting facilities and installing watershed management systems to support dry-season cultivation and other agricultural activities. A tubewell can provide access to groundwater, while a pumping machine helps move water to a location where it can be used. When properly installed and managed, such facilities can give farmers a source of water that is less dependent on immediate rainfall. The provision of these facilities can be particularly relevant to smallholder farmers who cannot rely solely on rain-fed cultivation throughout the year. However, the usefulness of a tubewell depends on several factors, including the availability and quality of groundwater, the reliability of the pump, the cost of operation and the arrangements for repairs and maintenance. The distribution of the facilities among communities and households would also help clarify whether the programme is reaching its intended beneficiaries. Completion level One of the notable claims in the project material is the reported average completion rate of 99.7 per cent for the watershed management programme. If the figure reflects verified physical progress across all 18 projects, it would indicate that the programme is close to completion. However, the brochure does not explain whether the completion rate refers to construction, equipment installation, the delivery of facilities or the operational readiness of the schemes. What the programme could mean for farmers The potential benefits of the interventions extend beyond the construction of physical infrastructure. For farmers, reliable access to water can make it possible to cultivate land during periods when rain-fed agriculture is difficult. Additional cropping opportunities may help households spread their income across the year and reduce the gap between harvests. Irrigation can also support agricultural activity linked to produce handling, transportation, trading and the supply of inputs. Where production increases, the benefits may extend to other people who depend on farming for their livelihoods. The erosion-control and road improvement projects could complement these efforts by improving access to agricultural communities and reducing disruption caused by damaged roads and flooding. However, such outcomes are not automatic. They depend on whether the infrastructure is completed to the required standard, whether the water supply is sustainable and whether farmers can afford to use and maintain the facilities. Access to land, seeds, fertiliser, extension services, markets and suitable storage facilities can also influence the results. The project documents identify food security, employment, higher agricultural production and improved rural livelihoods among the expected benefits of the interventions. Beyond construction The programme’s wider significance will ultimately depend on the relationship between infrastructure delivery and the needs of the people it is intended to serve. For the flood-control component, this means determining whether the works have reduced the risk of flooding, protected affected settlements and improved access to roads. For the irrigation schemes, it means establishing whether farmers can obtain water when needed, whether the canals function as designed and whether the intended farming areas are being cultivated. For the tubewell programme, the key questions include how many facilities are working, how groundwater resources are being managed and whether communities have the means to keep the equipment in service. Maintenance is particularly important. Pumps require servicing, canals may need desilting and drainage structures can be damaged by heavy rainfall or the movement of debris. Without clear responsibility for maintenance, infrastructure may lose its usefulness before its expected lifespan. The government would also need to establish a system for monitoring the programme’s performance and publishing information on its results. The Ecological Project Office’s documents provide a broad outline of the intervention and the scale of the facilities planned. The programme represents a substantial stated effort to link ecological works with agricultural water supply across Kano State. Its lasting value will be measured by whether the infrastructure works, whether farmers can use it and whether communities experience a measurable improvement in their livelihoods. For now, the listed projects provide a framework for that effort. Their eventual impact will depend on implementation, accountability and sustained attention to the needs of the communities the programme is designed to serve.
