items.title: 13 remanded in NCCIA custody in animated child sexual abuse material cases
items.description: KARACHI: A court on Saturday remanded over a dozen suspects in the custody of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) in the cases pertaining to alleged online sale and production of animated child sexual abuse and pornographic material and deceptive social media activities. The NCCIA Karachi Zone claimed to have arrested the suspects on Oct 23 during a raid at Rabia City in Gulistan-i-Jauhar, targeting three firms allegedly involved in production, promotion, and online sale of sexually explicit animated cartoons, animated child sexual abuse material, pornographic digital content and other digital designing services to international customers. The NCCIA officials produced 13 suspects before a judicial magistrate (East) and sought their custody for further investigation and arrest of their alleged accomplices. They also submitted that mobile phones had been seized from the detained suspects and further time was required for technical examination and forensic analysis of these devices. The magistrate handed over the suspects to the NCCIA on four-day physical remand with direction to produce them at next hearing along with the progress report. Earlier, during the operation, 42 individuals, including company owners and employees, were arrested, while 45 mobile phones were seized. Regarding their method of operation, officials said as per preliminary findings, the companies were operating through organised teams of online agents who approached foreign customers using various social media platforms, particularly Instagram and X. The agents allegedly created and operated multiple social media accounts using fictitious identities, female names, and impersonated profiles to attract international clients. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: PLFR /Devant les députés, Mme la Ministre, Mariama Ciré Sylla défend un budget rectifié « à visage humain » : croissance forte, pouvoir d’achat protégé, des investissements pour impacter les populations.
items.description: Face à une représentation nationale fortement mobilisée, Mme la Ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, Mme Mariama Ciré Sylla, est montée au créneau , le samedi 24 octobre 2026, pour défendre le Projet de Loi de Finances Rectificative (PLFR) 2026 déposé pour examen et vote par les députés. Le message de Mme la Ministre a été clair : la Guinée croît fortement, et cette croissance doit désormais se traduire dans le quotidien des Guinéens. Une croissance soutenue et forte. Les chiffres présentés aux élus témoignent d’une dynamique soutenue : après 5,4 % en 2024 et 7,1 % en 2025, la croissance devrait atteindre 8,6 % en 2026 . Elle est portée par le secteur minier, le projet Simandou et les investissements structurants. Les perspectives de la notation souveraine s’améliorent et les investissements directs étrangers sont estimés à 7,8 milliards de dollars en 2025. Pour Mme la Ministre, l’enjeu est désormais de transformer cette croissance en emplois, en entreprises guinéennes plus fortes et en conditions de vie améliorées. 5 mille 489 milliards GNF d’efforts budgétaires pour contenir la flambée des prix Face aux tensions géopolitiques, aux perturbations des chaînes d’approvisionnement et à la volatilité des prix de l’énergie, le Gouvernement a choisi de protéger ménages et entreprises. L’État maintient le prix des produits pétroliers à 12 000 GNF le litre, grâce à un effort budgétaire global de 5. 489,7 milliards GNF. Cela comprend 4. 576,7 milliards de recettes auxquelles l’État renonce et 913 milliards de provisions pour le mécanisme de stabilisation des prix. Cet effort représente près de 10 % des recettes fiscales prévues. . Des ressources internes en hausse, un déficit contenu. Le PLFR 2026 mise sur la mobilisation des ressources propres : – Recettes fiscales en hausse de +8 %, avec une pression fiscale projetée à 14,2 % du PIB, contre 12,9 % prévu initialement ; – Recettes liquides : 44 225,37 milliards GNF mobilisés au 15 octobre 2026, soit 85 % des prévisions annuelles ; – Déficit budgétaire : ramené à 2,01 % du PIB, contre 2,07 % initialement. La santé, l’éducation et la proximité au cœur du budget Le PLFR traduit ces moyens en actions concrètes en continuation des appuis lancés dans la LFI : . Soutien au fonctionnement de 455 centres de santé et 2 514 postes de santé ; . Opérationnalisation des centres d’hémodialyse et équipement des hôpitaux régionaux ; . Meilleur approvisionnement en médicaments et vaccins, et prise en charge renforcée des fonctionnaires atteints de maladies graves ; . Amélioration des primes et indemnités du personnel éducatif ; . Financement de 1 600 points d’eau dans l’intérieur du pays ; . Hausse de près de 50 % des crédits de fonctionnement des sous-préfectures et de 110 % des transferts aux communes rurales ; . Poursuite de l’acquisition de bus pour les transports publics. FMI, Banque mondiale, BAD : Une confiance renouvelée et renforcée des partenaires au pays. Un accord au niveau des services du FMI a été conclu en août 2026 pour un programme économique et financier de 41 mois, soutenu par un financement envisagé d’environ 425 millions de dollars, sous réserve de l’approbation des instances du Fonds. Le Gouvernement prépare par ailleurs, avec la Banque mondiale et la BAD, des appuis budgétaires destinés à accompagner les réformes, la mobilisation des recettes et la gouvernance financière. Le Programme Simandou 2040 : mesurer le succès par ses retombées. Pour Mme la Ministre Mariama Ciré Sylla, le succès de Simandou « ne se mesurera pas uniquement à la quantité de minerai exportée », mais à ses effets concrets : infrastructures modernes, entreprises locales compétitives, emplois durables et développement équilibré des territoires . Le Gouvernement renforce en conséquence « la sélection des projets d’investissement, privilégiant les initiatives mâtures, financièrement soutenables et capables de produire rapidement des résultats impactant » Une nouvelle page avec le Parlement guinéen. Ce grand oral de présentation du PLFR marque aussi, « une première » avec l’Assemblée nationale de la Cinquième République. Mme la Ministre a félicité, à l’occasion, M le Président de l’Assemblée et les députés « pour la confiance placée en eux par les Guinéens « , et réaffirmé la disponibilité de son Département pour un dialogue « permanent, transparent et constructif », insistant sur le contrôle parlementaire et la reddition des comptes. « Sous l’impulsion du Président de la République, M. Mamadi Doumbouya, et la coordination du Premier Ministre, Amadou Oury Bah, le Gouvernement entend ainsi « protéger aujourd’hui, investir pour demain » et bâtir une prospérité partagée » soutiendra, en guise de conclusion, Mme la Ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget. Le Président de la Commission Finances, Hamidou Camara a décliné le projet du Chronogramme d’examen pour adoption du PLFR 2026 qui s’étendra du 24 octobre au 7 novembre 2026. Un chronogramme adopté sous réserves de prise en compte des amendements et observations des députés Intervenant à la cloture de cette plénière , Mr le Président de l’Assemblée Nationale a salué ‘’la présentation de qualité des argumentaires et hypothèses du Projet de Loi des Finances rectificative’’ par Mme la Ministre de l’Economie, des finances et du Budget. L’honorable Dansa Kourouma a exhorté les Députés à ‘’examiner avec rigueur, responsabilité et célérité ce Projet pour permettre à l’Etat guinéen de disposer dans les plus brefs délais d’un Budget rectifié pour faire face aux défis du développement conformément à la vision du Chef de l’Etat, Président Mamamdi Doumbouya matérialisée par le Programme Simandou 2040.’’ Dès lundis prochain, les études en commissions du volet recettes du PLFR commenceront à l’Hémicycle. La séance du jour a été levée par le Président Dansa Kourouma, dans une atmosphère de détente et de convivialité à l’Assemblée Nationale de Guinée. Service Communication, Relations Publiques MEFB.

items.title: INEC Figures: How North-West, South-West may hold key to Aso Rock
items.description: •Candidates’ performance in two regions has shaped presidential election since 1999 By Luminous Jannamike Behind the battle for the presidency lies a contest over voter numbers, party machinery and political alliances. Tinubu has a head start as incumbent, but Atiku, Obi and other challengers know that no region is anybody’s political inheritance. The road to Aso Rock in 2027 runs through two regions where elections can be won, lost or thrown wide open: the North-West and South-West. Their combined electoral strength gives them enormous influence over the calculations of President Bola Tinubu and the opposition figures seeking to unseat him. The Independent National Electoral Commission’s 2026 voter register puts the North-West at 25,083,411 registered voters and the South-West at 19,614,274. Together, they account for 44,697,685 registered voters, representing more than 43 per cent of Nigeria’s 103,428,715 registered voters ahead of the 2027 general elections. Those figures make the two zones central to the presidential contest. But the real battle is more complicated than regional arithmetic. Candidates must convert registered voters into ballots, hold their traditional strongholds, penetrate rival territories and build a coalition broad enough to survive the country’s political and geographical divisions. For Tinubu, the stakes are particularly high. His South-West political base helped launch his presidential ambition, while his 2023 victory also depended on support beyond the region. Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi must find ways to disrupt that balance if they hope to deny him a second term. The numbers that can make or break a candidate The North-West’s 25.08 million registered voters make it Nigeria’s largest geopolitical voting bloc. The South-West follows with 19.61 million, ahead of the North-Central, which has 16.97 million. The political significance is unmistakable. Kano, Kaduna and Katsina are among the country’s most populous electoral states, while Lagos leads the national register with 7,488,633 voters. A candidate who makes substantial gains across these states can dramatically improve his national tally. Yet neither zone is a political inheritance. The North-West contains competing party structures, influential local leaders and voters whose choices are shaped by security, economic conditions, personalities and the performance of elected officials. Kano’s political history, in particular, shows how a powerful state-level movement can disrupt calculations made in Abuja. The South-West presents a different challenge. Tinubu’s longstanding political network gives him an advantage, but it does not guarantee uniform support across the region. Lagos demonstrated this in 2023 when Obi defeated Tinubu there by 9,848 votes, polling 582,454 against the president’s 572,606. That result remains a reminder that even a candidate’s home territory can become a battleground. Party loyalty, local grievances, urban voting patterns and the credibility of candidates can all upset expectations. The numbers also require caution. INEC’s register measures people registered to vote, not the number who will eventually cast ballots. Turnout, voter accreditation, election-day logistics and the distribution of votes among candidates will determine how much of that numerical advantage translates into electoral power. What elections since 1999 reveal Nigeria’s presidential elections have repeatedly shown that regional strength matters most when it forms part of a wider national coalition. Olusegun Obasanjo’s victories in 1999 and 2003 rested on support extending beyond his South-West origins. Umaru Musa Yar’Adua’s 2007 victory reflected the strength of the Peoples Democratic Party’s national machinery, while Goodluck Jonathan’s 2011 success drew on substantial support in the South and parts of the North. The 2015 election changed the political landscape. Muhammadu Buhari’s victory demonstrated that an opposition alliance could defeat an incumbent when it combined a formidable northern base with support in other parts of the country. The merger that produced the All Progressives Congress brought together political interests that had previously competed against one another. Buhari’s re-election in 2019 again showed the importance of maintaining a broad electoral coalition, even as the contest exposed persistent regional divisions. Tinubu’s 2023 victory followed another complex pattern. He won the presidency with 8,794,726 votes, ahead of Atiku’s 6,984,520 and Obi’s 6,101,533. The result was not the product of one region alone. It reflected a combination of Tinubu’s South-West support, votes from the North and the fragmentation of opposition support across several candidates. The lesson for 2027 is not that a candidate must reproduce one previous election formula. It is that regional dominance, without alliances and sufficient support elsewhere, can leave a candidate short of victory. The 2023 result that changed the game The last election exposed the risks of treating Nigeria’s regions as predictable voting blocs. Tinubu secured 2,542,979 votes in the South-West and 2,652,235 in the North-West, according to zonal breakdown. The figures showed that his northern performance was at least as important as his home-region strength. But the North-West did not vote as a single political unit. Atiku won Kaduna with 554,360 votes against Tinubu’s 399,293, while Rabiu Kwankwaso carried Kano for the New Nigeria Peoples Party. The split deprived the opposition of a unified northern vote while also limiting Tinubu’s ability to sweep the region. In the South-West, Obi’s narrow victory in Lagos demonstrated that Tinubu’s political base could be challenged. Obi’s strength in the South-East, meanwhile, did not translate into enough votes across the country to secure the presidency. Atiku’s support in parts of the North also proved insufficient. The distribution of votes made the difference. Had opposition support been concentrated behind a single candidate, the contest could have looked very different. Instead, three major contenders divided the electorate, while Tinubu assembled enough votes across several regions to finish first. Simon Kolawole, veteran journalist and political analyst, captured the strategic calculation in his assessment of the 2023 presidential election result. “Tinubu did well in ‘two out of three’ – the South-West and the core North,” he surmised. Kolawole also noted that a winning candidate might need sizeable support from the North-Central or South-South, or both, in addition to strength in the South-West and core North. His point is central to the next contest: Commanding two major blocs may create a strong platform, but it does not remove the need to win elsewhere. The constitutional hurdle also remains. Under Section 134 of the Constitution, a presidential candidate must secure the highest number of votes cast and at least one-quarter of the votes in no fewer than two-thirds of the states and the Federal Capital Territory. Regional strength must therefore translate into both a national plurality and geographically distributed support. The road to Aso Rock runs through alliances Tinubu enters the race with the advantages of incumbency, an established party structure and a political network built over decades. But those advantages will be tested by the electorate’s assessment of his administration, particularly over the economy, living costs, jobs and insecurity. The North-West could become a referendum on the government’s handling of insecurity and economic hardship. In the South-West, the president will need to defend his political base against discontent and opposition efforts to make inroads in urban centres and states where local dynamics favour challengers. Atiku faces the challenge of converting northern support into a broader national coalition, while Obi must demonstrate that his strong following in parts of the South and among younger voters can expand into regions where he was less competitive in 2023. Both will also have to confront the consequences of opposition fragmentation, party defections and competing presidential ambitions. The choice of running mates, the strength of state party organisations and agreements with influential political figures could prove decisive. So could turnout: A candidate with a smaller but highly mobilised support base may outperform a rival whose larger pool of registered supporters stays away from polling units. The North-West and South-West will undoubtedly shape the arithmetic of 2027. But neither region can deliver the presidency by itself, and neither should be treated as a guaranteed bloc for any candidate. The contest will be decided by who can turn voter numbers into actual ballots, withstand local political surprises and build alliances beyond familiar strongholds. For Tinubu, the challenge is to defend the coalition that brought him to power. For his challengers, it is to break that coalition without splitting their own support. items.title: Au Brésil, la victoire de Flávio Bolsonaro relancerait la déforestation de l’Amazonie
items.description: Selon les derniers chiffres publiés par l’Institut national de recherches spatiales brésilien, qui surveille dans le cadre de son programme PRODES la déforestation en Amazonie, celle-ci a chuté de 42 % entre août 2025 et juillet 2026 par rapport à l’année précédente. La déforestation en Amazonie se trouve ainsi à son niveau le plus faible depuis le début des relevés PRODES, en 1988. Lula, le président brésilien qui fera face aujourd’hui, dimanche 25 octobre, à Flávio Bolsonaro au second tour de l’élection présidentielle, est largement crédité de la chute de la déforestation. Au cours de ses deux premiers mandats, entre 2003 et 2010, la superficie de forêt amazonienne rasée chaque année est passée de 27 800 km² (en 2004) à 7 000 km². Après l’arrivée au pouvoir de Jair Bolsonaro, en 2019, ce chiffre a nettement augmenté, dépassant les 10 000 km² pour la première fois depuis 2008. En 2022, dernière année de la présidence Bolsonaro, 11 600 km² de forêt ont été rasés. Le gouvernement Bolsonaro avait été caractérisé par un démantèlement des politiques environnementales mises en place par ses prédécesseurs. Son premier ministre de l’Environnement, Ricardo Salles, appelait notamment, lors d’une réunion ministérielle en avril 2020, au début de la pandémie, à profiter du fait que les médias étaient focalisés sur cette question pour « faire passer le troupeau » (« passar a boiada »), c’est-à-dire modifier et assouplir toutes les normes environnementales. Durant la campagne présidentielle, Lula a continué de défendre les thèmes qui l’ont porté au pouvoir par le passé : le développement économique, la lutte contre la faim et la pauvreté, et la lutte contre la déforestation. Il a placé au cœur de son discours la défense d’une politique étrangère indépendante et souveraine. Flávio Bolsonaro s’est, pour sa part, inscrit dans la même ligne que son père : son programme prévoit notamment d’assouplir les licences environnementales, d’accélérer les projets miniers et d’autoriser le fracking, tout en affaiblissant les organes chargés de la protection et de la surveillance des écosystèmes brésiliens. Flávio Bolsonaro a promis de mettre fin à la déforestation illégale d’ici 2029 s’il était élu. De l’avis de plusieurs experts, cet engagement pourrait toutefois se traduire par l’autorisation de l’abattage légal d’un plus grand nombre d’arbres Why the Future of the Amazon Could Depend on Brazil’s Election », The New York Times , 18 octobre 2026.'> 1 . Il est notamment favorable à l’ouverture de terres protégées à l’exploitation minière et agricole. L’article Au Brésil, la victoire de Flávio Bolsonaro relancerait la déforestation de l’Amazonie est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: First infant battling mpox dies in Karachi hospital
items.description: KARACHI: An infant boy battling mpox for more than a week at a hospital died early on Saturday morning — the first mortality of a baby from the contagious viral infection in Karachi. Sources told Dawn that the 52-day-old baby boy had reportedly contracted the infection during circumcision performed at an “illegal” hospital located in Malir. He remained under treatment at the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital & Research Centre (SIDH&RC) for at least 10 days. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, a senior doctor at the hospital said that another infant patient with mpox was still in critical condition. “His key health indicators are not good. The information gathered from his parents indicates that he too underwent circumcision at the Malir hospital that has been officially sealed recently over concerns related to lack of infection control measures,” he said. Death takes Sindh’s tally to 12, with 98 cases reported so far this year According to the sources, at least seven patients, including a SIDH&RC worker who is believed to have contracted the infection from the hospital, are currently under treatment for mpox at the healthcare facility. They all are residents of Karachi. These cases include two workers employed at the fruit and vegetable market on Superhighway and a female patient, who reportedly contracted the infection from her husband. First infant’s death in city The sources said the latest death is the first death of an infant in Karachi. Earlier, two patients with chronic lung and kidney diseases were admitted to the SIDH&RC with mpox. They died during treatment but their chronic illnesses were recorded as the cause of their deaths. With the latest death, the total number of mpox deaths recorded this year in Sindh has risen to 12 with 98 cases reported so far. The sources said nearly all victims were either infants or newborns who contracted the infection from hospital/clinic settings lacking infection control protocols. In April, an outbreak of mpox, which was earlier restricted to patients with a history of foreign travel, was reported from Khairpur, claiming the lives of at least seven infants. The babies were under treatment in the intensive care units of two hospitals. Investigations showed that these facilities lacked infection control protocols. The district of Sukkur also saw two infants’ deaths from mpox. Sources of transmission According to experts, mpox transmission occurs through close contact with someone who has mpox, contaminated bedding, towels, medical instruments, surfaces or objects. “People with mpox can spread it to animals or vice versa through close contact. Vertical and perinatal transmission is possible as well. Some people are infectious 1-4 days before getting symptomatic,” said Dr Samreen Sarfaraz, consultant infectious diseases and the Chairperson of Infection Control Services at the Indus Hospital. Most patients, she said, recover fully within 2-4 weeks without treatment, while some develop complications. “A patient remains infectious till his or her rashes are completely healed (and a fresh layer of healthy intact skin has formed underneath),” she said. Prof Faisal Mahmood, senior infectious disease specialist at the Aga Khan University Hospital, said that mpox can spread through the air to a limited extent, but only when lesions or material from lesions are aerosolised. “This may happen when a sample is taken or when lesions are in or around the airway. Compared with chickenpox, mpox is much less contagious. Chickenpox can spread through the air over a considerable distance and does not require direct contact. The same applies to measles,” he said. He further added: “Mpox outbreaks can occur where infection prevention and control measures, such as environmental cleaning, are suboptimal, or where people are in close quarters or have significant body-to-body contact.” It might be recalled that the Sindh Health Care Commission has recently sealed Ibn-i-Hassan Hospital at Malir 15 following a laboratory report confirming an mpox case in an infant, after concerns were identified regarding infection prevention and control practices. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Poison for profit: Why fake drinks are killing Nigerians and what must change now, By Chukwuemerie Uduchukwu

items.title: Fasoranti’s Death: Why reconciliation in Afenifere will be difficult — Okurounmu, ex-Secretary
items.description: •Group’s future uncertain —Mogaji Adejumo By Dapo Akinrefon Tongues across the country are wagging over a possible leadership crisis within the once formidable pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, especially with the demise of its leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti . Fasoranti died on Tuesday at the age of 100 years. Before his death, the Yoruba group had been engulfed in leadership crisis. It is instructive to note that Afenifere hinges on a traditional, non-competitive succession process to choose its next leader. However, the body faces the critical task of unifying its historically fractured factions. While the old guards like Chief Olu Falae express hope that a new leader will emerge seamlessly through ancestral custom, key insiders paint a much bleaker picture of the group’s future. How division set in In 2023, its then Acting Leader, late Pa Ayo Adebanjo, rocked the boat by suspending two of its officials, the National Publicity Secretary, Jare Ajayi and National Organising Committee, Abagun Kole Omololu. The suspension, however, led to a split and worsened the crisis. Both officials were removed from office and subsequently suspended for alleged uncouth activities and issuance of unauthorised statements, as well as constant denigration of the organisation. Recall that in November 2022, the late Afenifere leader, Pa Fasoranti, insisted that he remained the leader of the group. This was after he had named his deputy, late Pa Ayo Adebanjo, as the leader of the organization. Pa Adebanjo, who was taken aback over Fasoranti’s suddenly change of mind, had alleged that there was an attempt to split the organisation. Observers of events in the polity were of the view that he was not far from the truth. The split, however became a reality. It was as a result of the fact that during the 2023 electioneering campaign, then candidate of the All Progressives Congress, APC, Asiwaju Bola Tinubu had visited Pa Fasoranti in Akure, where the former Lagos State governor was endorsed. The decision did not sit well with the Adebanjo group. How Fasoranti stepped down in 2021 It will be recalled that in March 2021, Pa Fasoranti stepped down as Afenifere leader, citing old age. While Adebanjo had endorsed Peter Obi, who was presidential candidate of the Labour Party, LP, the Fasoranti group, threw its weight behind Tinubu. Fasoranti had named the deputy leader, Chief Ayo Adebanjo, as the acting national leader of the group, while the former financial secretary, Oba Oladipo Olaitan, the Alaago of Kajola Ago in Atakumosa East Council Area, Ilesa, Osun State, was named the group’s deputy leader. Fasoranti had said: “The development became necessary as the group needs, more than ever before, to have an improved organisation with a more effective approach to combat the monstrous invasion of our culture and pride as a people. “Only a more alike and active leadership can achieve this. At 95 I am hardly able to provide such and so it is time for me to step aside. “At this junction, I am proud to announce Chief Ayo Adebanjo, a politician of the Awolowo school of thought, as Acting leader of Afenifere and Oba Oladipo Olaitan, the Alaago of Kajola Ago in Atakumosa East Local Government Area, as the Deputy Leader.” The late Afenifere leader, in a viral video had claimed: “I am still the leader of Afenifere. Afenifere has not endorsed Obi, we are endorsing Jagaban (Bola Tinubu) for the presidency. “You can see the trend, the approval and the acceptability. You could see what happened when Tinubu came to meet me in Akure. The media carried the whole thing. “Adebanjo cannot warn me not to welcome Tinubu. Can he do that successfully? “What happened was that Adebanjo took a stand and I took a stand. I didn’t call him and he didn’t call me. We never spoke about the visit. “As you can see, Jagaban is accepted and we approve of him. Obi has no stand in our mind at all.” Adebanjo counters Fasoranti But in a swift reaction, Ayo Adebanjo, known to be a staunch Awoist, faulted Tinubu’s visit to Pa Fasoranti, saying the comments trailing it were aimed at dividing the group. Adebanjo, who earlier endorsed Peter Obi, said: “Nothing is going on other than an attempt to split Afenifere to which I will not be a party. “It is a sort of conspiracy among those who want to see Afenifere divided. They have been on this plan for over a month ago and my members came to me to alert me about it and I said, ‘Don’t talk about it. It would be a diversion. All we want now is an election on issues.” He said Pa Fasoranti had called to inform him about Tinubu’s planned visit adding that the former Afenifere leader was initially not open to receiving the APC candidate but he persuaded him to do so. Adebanjo had said: “I will tell you the story and I won’t go further. Pa Fasoranti phoned me on Friday that Tinubu had phoned him and that he wanted to come and see him and he wanted to say no. I said no, don’t do that, you are an elder statesman. If he wanted to see you, why not? “As far as he is concerned, Obi’s endorsement is based on the principles of equity as the South-East has not produced a president since the return of democracy in 1999. Since the South-West and South-South have produced the president, he said it is the turn of the South-East. “South-South has had its own and I said it is remaining the South-East.” Adebanjo died and the once formidable Yoruba body became polarized. But with Fasoranti’s death, both camps are still laying claim to the leadership of the group. Falae speaks However, a former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, Chief Olu Falae, dismissed concerns about a possible succession struggle in Afenifere, saying the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation has a tradition of producing leaders without contests or internal fights. Falae, who is now a monarch, rules out the possible division within the Yoruba fold. He said Afenifere was a self-perpetuating and self-regulating organisation in which leadership emerged through an established process rather than through competition for positions. “Leadership chooses itself. A new leader will emerge without any struggle. “It is obvious who the next leader will be, and I hope and pray it will be so this time,” he said. Is reconciliation a tall order? Vanguard was reliably informed that before Fasoranti’s death, there was underground moves to bring all Afenifere member under one roof. For instance, it Chief Sola Ebiseni, who was the General Secretary of the Adebanjo camp, had crossed over the Fasoranti camp. A senior Afenifere leader had confided in Vanguard that the reconciliation was to be unveiled immediately after the 2027 general elections. However, with Fasoranti’s demise, this may be turn out to be difficult to achieve. ‘No light at the end of tunnel’ Providing his perspective on the crisis and possible reconciliation, a former National Secretary of the Yoruba body, Senator Femi Okurounmu, said he does not see light at the end of the tunnel as far as reconciliation in Afenifere is concerned. Okurounmu, a former Senator from 1999-2003, said though it was too early to talk or reuniting the group, the two factions cannot be reconciled. In a chat with Vanguard, the former lawmaker said: “You see, it is difficult. Things are difficult. It is very difficult to unite the two groups. The Akure group supports Tinubu. You cannot criticise Tinubu in the presence of the Akure group.” Speaking further, he said: “Everything Tinubu does must be supported. That is the philosophy of the Akure group. “The Adebanjo group is very critical of Tinubu. That is an irreconcilable difference, and that is why the two groups cannot be reconciled.” Origin of crisis – Adejumo Giving his perspective on the crisis in Afenifere, Mogaji Gboyega Adejumo, a former Public Relations Officer of the body, traces the origin of the crisis. Adejumo, who is also the Gbonka Aare-Ona Kakanfo, said Afenifere’s future remains uncertain. Tracing the origin of the crisis within the fold, he said: “What happens to Afenifere after the departure of Pa Fasoranti? All I can say is that Afenifere lost its glory some time back. Perhaps it is as long ago as 2008, and I will explain. The momentum of the Afenifere as at the moment that the June 12 episode became a national movement, which Afenifere spearheaded by forming NADECO, the ascendancy of Afenifere was assured. “So it wasn’t in any way surprised that in 1999 Afenifere formed the Alliance for Democracy, AD, and the AD was able to sweep at least, all the southwest states. But that momentum faltered in 2003 due to so many reasons. “However, in 2008, when Pa Abraham Adesanya, who was not only Afenifere leader, but the leader of the Yoruba, that was proclaimed by every Yoruba group, apart from the fact that Afenifere leaders have always been known as Yoruba leaders, but Pa Adesanya enjoyed that, which was the spoken word of every other group appointing him as Yoruba leader. “So Pa Adesanya had suffered a stroke, and he felt it was time to anoint a new leader. As at that time, the foremost leaders were Pa Ayo Adebanjo, who actually started with them in 1951, and then there was Sir Olaniyun Ajayi, and the whole idea was Pa Adesanya asking the two of them to choose one among themselves. “So that he can then proclaim the choice of the two of them as the new leader. But Pa Adebanjo felt that, as at that time, Pa Adesanya, who was an Ijebu kan, who took over from Pa Adekunle Ajasin, who was from Owo in Ondo “And it just happened, there was nothing like Ijebu mafia, it just happened that Pa Ajasin and Pa Adesanya, and the mightier than the image of just a knighted man, somebody that was well loved, that is Sir Olaniyun Ajayi, they were all Ijebu; at least to that effect we could say that Pa Olaniyun Ajayi too, from Remo, is Ijebu.” How Fasoranti took over from Adesanya Mogaji Adejumo also spoke on how Fasoranti emerged of Afenifere and how the late Adebanjo convinced Adesanya to make him (Fasoranti) the leader of the group. He said: “So Pa Adesanya felt another Ijebu man to succeed Pa Adesanya might look like a reality, perhaps an accentuation of the idea that there was an Ijebu mafia. So he now suggested that Papa Fasoranti should be the new leader. Pa Adesanya didn’t quite even remember who Papa Fasoranti was. “Papa Fasoranti was the Commissioner for Finance during the time of Papa Ajasin as Governor of Ondo State, but he was not a member of the caucus of the Afenifere, and neither was he a participant in the struggle that followed after the June 12 1993 election, in which case Papa Fasoranti was not part of the Afenifere that fought for this democracy. He had more or less like retired from politics. So it was hard for Papa Adesanya to even remember him, let alone see him as the right kind of person. “But Papa Adebanjo went on to convince him that he is a very cool-headed man, and after all that happened between 2003 and 2008, quite a lot happened, because the Governor of Ondo State then, who campaigned on the platform of the AD in 2023, broke away and the Afenifere went into some serious crisis. It started from 2001 when Uncle Bola Ige died, mysteriously and unexpectedly. So what Papa Adesanya felt was that we needed a user-friendly leader, very cool and unassuming, somebody who will be able to pull everybody together, and they will support him. “And besides, he was older, joined the Afenifere in 1953 as what they called the Action Group Mosquito. As at that time, he was a student in the university, so he was recruited by Papa Adesanya himself. Anyway, that was how Papa Fasoranti was made the leader of the Afenifere, which eked Asiwaju Bola Tinubu, who was not even part of the Afenifere at that time, but had some influence here and there. There was even this Afenifere Renewal that had his signature all over it, but yet he was still interested in the leadership of the Afenifere. So, he went ahead and announced the late Senator Ayo Fasanmi as the leader, as against Papa Fasoranti. “And all of that happened. Papa Fasoranti, for about a year or more, was not even holding the Afenifere meeting at Akure. “In the tradition of the Afenifere, the leader becomes the rallying point, and meetings would be held in the leader’s house, and which means everybody should go to Akure. “Well, they started even at Ijebu Igbo for a while, and moved to the home of Sir Olaniyun Ajayi. “So it was, I should think, I should think, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi, who even suggested that, look, the leader is Papa Fashononji, and his home is Akure, why should we be having the meeting here? So somehow, that sank in, and then the meetings now moved to Akure. But in the true sense of it, Afenifere leadership has always been very energetic, very eloquent, and ready to engage anyone intellectually and forcefully to work on principles. And Papa Ajayi too was like that. “He gave late Sani Abacha some serious trouble, and even when he died, Abacha wouldn’t just have someone to come and preach. So it was Papa Ajayi who formed NADECO. And then Papa Adesanya, oh, well, a lawyer of note, he represented Papa Obafemi Awolowo everywhere. “And then, of course, he was a Senator in the Second Republic. He was yet in the same mould of the kind of leaders Afenifere have been able to produce. So he was just like Obafemi Awolowo and Papa Ajayi. “But by nature, his passion was not that kind of a Afenifere ready to fight, ready to carry the placard, ready to engage any one kind of leader. So that, again, would make the Afenifer to be a bit vulnerable and not to be as forceful, as pushful as Afenifere has been known to be. And sometime in 2015, Papa Ajayi actually wrote a letter and said he was resigning. “He didn’t want to carry on again as the leader of Afenifere. He was overwhelmed, really. The opposition came from everywhere and just couldn’t handle it. “And you won’t blame him because some are made very strong, some are mild-mannered. And he’s one of those mild-mannered, never-really-wanting-to-cause-any-trouble kind of gentlemen. So, but it was Pa Ayo Adebanjo again who said, no, you can’t just leave. “You won’t just succumb to pressure. Those who want Afenifere to die will really be happy if you suddenly just up and left. So he convinced him to stay on.” Afenifere’s rebirth under Fasoranti “And, yes, Afenifere went through some rebirth under Papa Fasoranti. He started to attract new members, too, and started to evolve as yet an offshoot of the original Action Group. They became involved in the 2019 elections. “From the 2015 elections, when Afenifere fully supported former President Goodluck Jonathan. Don’t forget that in 2014, there was the CONFAB organised by the Jonathan administration, which Afenifere had every signature of theirs in the preparation, the setting up, and even the exercise of having a conference of that nature happen. “Afenifere was there. It was well put together. That is, the framework was put together by Dr. Femi Okurounmu of Afenifere. “And co-chaired, well, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi was once a very active Afenifere member, was one of the co-chairs. So Afenifere rebirth, or let me say renewal and renaissance took place even at that time. Because when Afenifere had all the governors, yes, Afenifere was very solid. “But from 2005 to 2013, those were very trying years for Afenifere. But Afenifere was good to come together again. And in 2017, Baba Adebanjo called everybody and said, everything we said would happen with Buhari have started to manifest. “So what do we do? So Afenifere, by our tradition and principles and all that, is seen as a national movement. But then national movement with a particular principle, the Awolowo principle, which is so difficult for just anyone to pick up. So we decided we’ll pull in other Yoruba groups. “And many groups showed up, maybe about 70 or so, but 42 were chosen. And then we launched the Yoruba Summit Group. And that was how we came by the Yoruba Declaration of 2017. “I was made the National Policy Secretary of the Yoruba Summit Group. And that was when we even invited every other group in the Middle Belt Forum from the Southeast, the Ohanaeze Ndigbo, and from the South-South, the PANDEF. And we came together and formed the Southern Middle Belt Leaders Forum, SMBLF. “So all of this happened during the time Baba Fasoranti himself was thinking of, well, resigning. But he was buoyed, he was kept on by Baba Adebanjo and a few others, Chief Supo Shonibare and the rest, that, no, you go on. We will continue to fight. So all of this happened during Baba Fasoranti’s time. And in 2021, that was when the, would I say it was just some kind of innuendo, some, well, I wouldn’t know where it came from, that Baba was going senile. “And he moved against those who wanted to take an advantage of what they felt would make Anthony Ferry’s leadership come their way. So that was when Baba Fasoranti now decided, look, it’s time for me to truly bow out. And he made Baba Adebanjo the acting leader. “I wouldn’t know what exactly that meant. And then see Oba Oladipo as the deputy leader.” Vanguard News The post Fasoranti’s Death: Why reconciliation in Afenifere will be difficult — Okurounmu, ex-Secretary appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Oil Spill in Delta: When environment is destroyed from within and without – black tide ‘swallows 216 communities’
items.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi The water at Odidi struggles to flow. It sits, thick, black, and dead. For seven months, the 28-inch Trans-Forcados Pipeline at the Kantu-Odidi axis, Warri South-West LGA has bled crude and associated gas into the creeks. What was sighted February 19, 2026 as a single rupture has become a black tide that has swallowed over 216 communities, according to their leaders. This is no longer just an oil spill. It is a war of narratives about who is destroying the Niger Delta — from within, or from without? On one side, the Joint Investigation Visit, JIV, of February 20-21, 2026, conducted by the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency, NOSDRA, officials and community representatives, gave a technical verdict: Corrosion and equipment failure. No sabotage. On the other side, voices from inside the Niger Delta say the truth is more uncomfortable. That Odidi has been a hub of illegal bunkering for 25 years and that hot-taps have turned the pipeline into Swiss cheese. Between those two truths, the environment dies. Seven months of nothing Odidi Federated Community is angry because containment has been a theatre. Comrade Justin Gbenekama, Chairman of the community, narrated: “This spill occurred on the 19th of February 2026, and up to this moment as we speak, the operator, Heritage Energy Operational Services, HEOSL, has not done anything properly to contain the spill. “As you can see within the environment, even their recovery activities is not effective.” He measured the scale of tidal spill: “And so six hours flow from this point, you get to Escravos area. And where we are standing is just five minutes drive to Forcados River, 10 minutes to the Escravos Bar. So the spill has spread very far.” For the people, the consequences are immediate. Drinking water is contaminated with hydrocarbons. Fishing and farming are dead. Cooking is a risk. Gbenekama added: “And most importantly, there is no medical attention to any of the affected communities. And even relief materials that were brought were not adequate.” He called the recovery method futile: “They will scoop, take it (spilled crude) back to their station in Isoko and inject it back to the same line, and the oil here will still come out in this point. That is an exercise in futility.” His demand: “There should be immediate shutdown of the Trans-Forcados Pipeline and carry out the complete repair before operation will commence.” It is a demand backed by law. Because the JIV ruled out third-party interference, HEOSL bears absolute liability under Nigerian environmental law. The operator must fund 100 percent of clean-up and compensation. And the Federal High Court in Port Harcourt, in Suit No. FHC/PH/CS/132/2026, HRM Udogri Isaac I v. Heritage Energy & NOSDRA, ordered a mandatory injunction to cease discharge and clean up all impacted ecosystems. No more business as usual Ijaw Youth Council, IYC, says it has had enough. Its President, Dr. Doubra Collins Okotete, led youths to threaten total shutdown of OML 42, OML 30 and the Forcados Terminal. “Today we are here not for jokes, but to shut down the operations of the Heritage Oil and Gas Services. This spill has been on for over seven months. The operators of Heritage are heartless, wicked,” Okotete declared. He dismissed the sabotage argument: “This is not sabotage. This is pure equipment failure. And we all know this oil activity has been going on for a very long time. “And this pipeline has been damaged for over six, seven months, yet no tangible has been done.” He alleged: “All they do is to employ contractors to come and curtail oil, yet the contractors they have employed could not contain this oil because, what as the community chairman said, they come here scoop the oil, take it back to their station, inject it back to the same Trans-Forcados Pipeline, and this oil keep popping out, destroying our ecosystem, creating health hazard for our people.” Okotete linked Odidi to the wider Niger Delta crisis, including Bille in Rivers State: “The same thing is happening to Alakiri, Rivers State, same thing that happening to Bille, Rivers State, and other communities across the Ijaw nation that are being threatened, that today life expectancy has dropped.” His message to Abuja was blunt: “President Tinubu, you are the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The Minister, Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, this is under your watch and today our river has been bastardized.” And to the companies: “If they are tired of exploiting our oil, they should leave our environment.” Uncomfortable truth from within But long-time environmental monitor and Coordinator, Niger Delta Peace Coalition (NDPC), Zik Gbemre, offers a counter-punch that many in the creeks do not want to hear. He said Odidi’s black tide is also self-inflicted. “The Odidi axis in OML 42 has served as an active hub for illegal bunkering for over 25 years. What is happening there today is not a new development”, Gbemre said. “The ongoing environmental degradation is largely artificial and directly tied to pipeline sabotage. “Even after comprehensive cleaning and proper remediation, fresh spills reoccur within days because the root cause remains unchecked.” According to him, the pipeline is being killed by repeated hot-taps: “What is unfolding across the Odidi and Egwa fields is the direct impact of illegal bunkering operations. “Repeatedly placing hot taps on the same pipeline segments severely compromises structural integrity over time. “Even when damaged points are clamped and repaired, the weakened metal around the hot taps continues to deteriorate, making future leaks inevitable.” Gbemre, who has flown with Shell’s spill team over Odidi, said complicity is local: “A total stranger cannot enter a community, transport heavy equipment, and place hot taps on high-pressure pipelines without the knowledge, authorization, or passive approval of host community leaders and influential actors.” He listed it clearly: “Illegal bunkerers: Physical installation of hot taps, line breaching, and crude siphoning. Host Community leaders: Granting access, and providing cover.” His warning is moral: “You cannot destroy infrastructure, profit from illegal trade, and present yourself purely as an innocent victim. “You cannot demand millions in cleanup funds while harboring the very individuals who will re-break the pipes tomorrow.” He also punctured the IYC claim that surveillance by Tantita and others has ended vandalism: “It’s funny to hear the IYC boss claiming ‘no more vandalism in the operations space because TANTITA and other surveillance contractors are securing the space. “That is joke of the year and media gymnastics to justify sustenance of the multi-thrillion naira surveillance contracts. Oil theft still thrives.” Both sides in order Media consultant and Coordinator, Journalists for Just Development of the Niger Delta, Austine Aghomi, says both narratives must be held together to understand the ticking bomb. “Yes, NOSDRA is bound to do its work without bias when there are eventualities, just as oil and gas operators need to take responsibility on routine maintenance of their assets, particularly ageing pipeline from failure,” Aghomi said. He added: “What is equally concerning, however, is the realisation that unrestrained assets vandalism, particularly tapping into oil wellheads, flowlines and pipelines to steal crude oil now helps to hasten the ageing of pipelines beyond manufacturers’ set lifespan. “The lines suffer repeated cuts from oil thieves. Over time, assets operators get overwhelmed by repeated repairs and ultimately forced replacement earlier than normal.” Heritage Energy, through its Community Relations Manager Jeremiah Oharisi, told protesting women: “Heritage is more than willing to do the right thing.” But trust is gone. The pipeline is 50, its life was 25 The hard fact remains. Most trunklines in the Niger Delta, including Trans-Forcados, were laid in the 1970s with a 20-25-year design life. They have done double that, battered by corrosion outside and hot-taps inside. Whether the cause is rust or bunkering, the effect is the same: Odidi is dying. And if Odidi is not clamped permanently, if Bille’s gas leaks are not stopped, if the Trans-Forcados is not replaced, the black tide will come to the next community. The environment is being destroyed from without by ageing assets and corporate negligence. And it is being destroyed from within by an illegal economy that feeds on the same pipes. Until both are stopped, no clean-up will be final. items.title: Ali Haroun : disparition de l’un des derniers grands témoins de l’histoire contemporaine de l’Algérie
items.description: Son nom est intimement lié au retour de Mohamed Boudiaf en Algérie, en janvier 1992, et à l’interruption du processus électoral qui avait vu le Front islamique du salut (FIS), parti dissous, arriver largement en tête du premier tour des législatives de décembre 1991. Ali Haroun , avocat, ancien responsable de la Fédération de France du FLN et membre du Haut Comité d’État (HCE), est décédé ce samedi à l’âge de 99 ans, a annoncé la Télévision algérienne. Ali Haroun, l’homme qui a traversé plusieurs des grandes péripéties de l’histoire algérienne Avec sa disparition s’éteint sans doute l’un des derniers grands témoins directs de cette séquence de l’histoire contemporaine et mouvementée du pays. Il faisait, en effet, partie de cette génération de responsables qu’une certaine opposition désignait sous le vocable de « janviéristes », en référence aux acteurs de l’interruption du premier processus électoral pluraliste du pays en janvier 1992. Une décision dont il a toujours défendu le bien-fondé, mais dont les conséquences politiques et humaines ont durablement marqué l’Algérie. Elles continuent même par certains aspects à imprégner la vie politique du pays. « L'État n'a pas communiqué et, de plus, l'Algérie communique mal. C'est pourquoi nous avons été très mal compris à l'étranger. Et surtout, ce qui ne nous a pas été pardonné, c'est l'arrêt du processus électoral début janvier 1992. Dans certains pays du Moyen-Orient – il faut le dire – qui soutenaient à l’époque les intégristes islamistes ; et en Europe, on refusait de comprendre qu'il était essentiel d'arrêter ce processus, même s'il était antidémocratique », disait-il un jour dans un entretien. Homme de droit au style raffiné, militant de la première heure de la guerre de Libération nationale, Ali Haroun aura traversé plusieurs des grandes péripéties de l’histoire algérienne, de la lutte contre le colonialisme français à l’interruption du processus électoral en passant par les crises politiques qui ont émaillé le lendemain de l’indépendance et le Hirak. Ali Haroun : de la guerre de Libération aux procès Né en 1927 à Bir Mourad Raïs, sur les hauteurs d’Alger, dans une famille originaire de Kalaâ des Beni Abbès, près d’Ighil Ali, dans la wilaya de Béjaïa, Mohamed Ali Haroun fait ses études primaires et secondaires dans la capitale avant de rejoindre la France, à la fin des années 1940, pour y étudier le droit. Il obtient sa licence à la Sorbonne, puis le certificat d’aptitude à la profession d’avocat et un doctorat d’État. De retour au pays, il s’engage au FLN dès le début de la révolution et collabore avec Abane Ramdane pour le lancement du journal « Résistance » qui deviendra « El Moudjahid ». À partir de la fin de 1957, il rejoint la France. En mars 1958, il est nommé responsable politique de la Fédération de France du FLN, où il s’occupe notamment de la défense des militants et de la collecte des aides au front. Devenu membre du Conseil national de la Révolution algérienne (CNRA), entre 1960 et 1962, Ali Haroun est élu député d’Alger à l’Assemblée constituante, où il siège de 1962 à 1963. Pas pour longtemps puisque la rupture intervient rapidement. Opposé à Ahmed Ben Bella, premier président de l’Algérie indépendante, et à la Constitution défendue par celui-ci, il figure parmi les 21 élus qui appellent à ne pas l’adopter. Il se retire alors de la vie politique et reprend son activité d’avocat. Durant les années 1960 et 1970, Ali Haroun se distingue ainsi dans plusieurs procès politiques. Parmi les affaires qui ont marqué son parcours figure notamment la défense du MDRA (mouvement démocratique pour le renouveau algérien), organisation fondée par Krim Belkacem et Slimane Amirat. Un jour, dans un entretien consacré notamment à son livre « L’Été de la discorde », Ali Haroun revenait sur la condamnation à mort par contumace de Krim Belkacem et sur la publication, dans le quotidien La République, d’un appel invitant les Algériens à exécuter la sentence. Il dénonçait une démarche qu’il considérait comme un véritable appel au meurtre, émanant d’un journal se faisant le porte-parole du parti unique, en l’occurrence le FLN. Cette affaire illustre aussi la distance qu’il avait prise avec ce parti. Pour lui, tout comme pour Boudiaf qui le dira plus tard, le Front de libération nationale historique avait cessé d’exister avec la scission de juin 1962. Il refusait que le parti au pouvoir s’approprie l’héritage du mouvement de libération, comme il le répétera sans cesse depuis. Malgré un riche passé militant et son expérience d’avocat, Ali Haroun demeure cependant longtemps loin des feux de la rampe. Est-ce peut-être à cause de sa réserve et la place qu’il occupait dans les équilibres politiques de l’époque, lui homme de dossiers et de convictions ? Son rôle dans le retour de Boudiaf en Algérie Il faut attendre en tous cas la fin des années 1980 et l’ouverture politique qui suit les événements du 5 octobre 1988 pour le voir revenir au premier plan. Après l’instauration du pluralisme politique en 1989, il participe à la création de la Ligue algérienne des droits de l’Homme (LADH), avant d’être nommé, en juin 1991, ministre délégué aux Droits de l’Homme dans le gouvernement de Sid Ahmed Ghozali. Cette fonction le place au cœur d’une période particulièrement tendue. Lui, homme de droit se doit de convaincre l’opinion de la légalité des mesures prises à l’encontre des militants islamistes arrêtés dans la foulée de l’insurrection et internés dans les campas du sud. Et si Ali Haroun a depuis été pris à partie par les militants islamistes, particulièrement depuis un moment sur les réseaux sociaux, c’est précisément à cause de cette séquence. Mais c’est la crise de janvier 1992 qui va durablement associer son nom à l’une des décisions les plus controversées de l’histoire politique algérienne : la suspension du second tour des législatives après que le FIS dissous ait remporté un nombre confortable de sièges au premier tour. Favorable à cette interruption, il est chargé de se rendre au Maroc pour tenter de convaincre Mohamed Boudiaf , dont il avait proposé le nom avec son ami Aboubakr Belkaid, d’accepter de rentrer en Algérie et de prendre la tête du Haut Comité d’État, mis en place le 14 janvier 1992, après la démission du président Chadli Benjedid. Boudiaf finit par accepter. Son retour en Algérie suscite un immense espoir chez les jeunes notamment, mais de la défiance aussi auprès de la mouvance islamiste. Six mois plus tard, il est assassiné à Annaba, au cours d’une conférence qu’il présidait. Une tragédie pour l’Algérie, mais aussi pour celui qui l’a convaincu de revenir au pays après un exil de plusieurs années. Une blessure dont il aura peine à se remettre. « Je me sens en quelque sorte responsable de sa mort en ce sens qu’il m’avait reçu pour discuter de l’éventualité de son retour… Pendant des jours, je perdais le sommeil me posant la question sans cesse si j’avais bien fait d’aller le voir à Kénitra », confesse-t-il un jour. Membre du HCE jusqu’en 1994, Ali Haroun restera ainsi associé à cette séquence. Jusqu’à la fin de sa vie. Il ne fera jamais amende honorable. Selon lui, la victoire du FIS risquait de conduire à l’instauration d’un État islamiste et à la remise en cause des libertés fondamentales en Algérie. « La démocratie ne se limite pas à déposer un bulletin dans l’urne et à appliquer aveuglément le résultat, quel qu’il soit », soutenait-il, estimant que l’accession démocratique au pouvoir ne garantissait pas nécessairement le maintien des libertés. En 1995, Ali Haroun participe, avec Redha Malek, à la fondation de l’Alliance nationale républicaine (ANR). Il ne retrouve cependant pas une place prépondérante dans la vie politique nationale. Il intervient par intermittence dans le débat public, notamment en 2002, lorsqu’il témoigne à Paris au procès en diffamation intenté par le général Khaled Nezzar contre Habib Souaïdia, auteur de « La Sale Guerre ». Un livre se referme Au fil des années, Ali Haroun se fait plus discret n’intervenant que rarement dans les médias ou de documentaires relatifs à la guerre de Libération et à l’histoire de la Fédération de France du FLN. S’il reconnaît la force et le caractère inédit du Hirak populaire en 2019, Ali Haroun demeure attaché au respect des institutions et de la légalité. Marqué par les traumatismes des années 1990, il privilégie une évolution institutionnelle qui éviterait, selon lui, un nouveau vide politique. Cette position le distingue de ceux qui réclamaient une rupture plus profonde avec le système politique. Elle traduit aussi, en creux, la prudence d’un homme dont les convictions se sont forgées au contact des crises successives de l’Algérie indépendante. Comme d’autres acteurs politiques, il participe par la suite aux consultations engagées autour de la révision constitutionnelle par le président Abdelmadjid Tebboune, au cours desquelles il formule des propositions. Parfait francophone, Ali Haroun laisse une œuvre prolifique centrée essentiellement sur l’histoire de la guerre de Libération. Il est notamment l’auteur de La Septième Wilaya. La guerre du FLN en France (1954-1962), publié en 1986, L’Été de la discorde (2000) ou encore Écrits et documents de la Fédération de France du FLN 1954-1962 (2021). Avec sa disparition se referme sans doute le livre des derniers grands témoins du HCE. L’article Ali Haroun : disparition de l’un des derniers grands témoins de l’histoire contemporaine de l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .
