items.title: L’incroyable histoire d’Ahmad Khan
items.description: Testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois Comment avez-vous découvert l’existence d'Ahmad Khan et de l’histoire de ce voyage qui le conduisit à la fin du XVIIIe siècle, du Gujarat jusqu’à Londres en passant par Paris ? J’ai découvert Ahmad Khan par hasard, en 2015, alors que je travaillais aux Archives du Ministère des Affaires étrangères, à La Courneuve. Je feuilletais, pour un autre projet, une liasse intitulée « Mémoires et documents Asie » – une sorte de pot-pourri contenant des documents du XVIIIe siècle sur l’Asie. Je suis alors tombé par hasard sur des papiers qui faisaient référence à la présence de deux voyageurs indiens à Lyon en 1794. J’ai été étonné par cette information dont je n’avais jamais entendu parler, et cela a donné le coup d’envoi de la recherche. Je me suis aperçu qu’il existait déjà quelques travaux sur ces individus, mais aucun ne prenait en compte l’ensemble de leur parcours. De l’Inde à Londres, puis leur retour, dans la perspective connectée que j’ai adoptée. C’est donc un bel exemple de sérendipité scientifique qui est à l’origine de mon enquête. Vous évoquez la trace archivistique de deux voyageurs indiens, et vous nous apprenez dans votre livre qu’ils étaient en réalité quatre à avoir quitté l’Inde pour l’Europe. Mais votre ouvrage se concentre surtout sur l’un d’entre eux, Ahmad Khan. Pourquoi ? Rahul Markovits, L’histoire d’Ahmad Khan , PUF, 2026. Le livre est centré sur un protagoniste principal, Ahmad Khan, car lorsqu’il arrive à Paris au printemps 1794, il raconte son histoire au Comité de Salut Public. Mais dans ce récit, il s’inclut dans un groupe plus large de voyageurs parti d’Inde quelques années auparavant. Ce groupe est composé des fils de Mu‘azzaz Khan, le dernier nawab (gouverneur exerçant l’autorité au nom de l’empereur moghol) de Baroche, une ville portuaire du Gujarat. Ahmad Khan se présente comme l’un d’entre eux. Il raconte être parti pour Londres avec trois autres frères, dans l’intention d’y plaider leur cause auprès de la Compagnie des Indes orientales britanniques. Ils l’accusent de les avoir spoliés une vingtaine d’années auparavant en faisant la conquête de leur ville. Quatre historiens sont particulièrement mobilisés dans votre introduction : Carlo Ginzburg et Carlo Poni, qui rattachent votre entreprise à la microhistoire, Sanjay Subrahmanyam qui l’oriente du côté de l’histoire connectée, et Dipesh Chakrabarty qui l’inscrit dans le sillage des études postcoloniales. Comment situez-vous votre travail relativement à ces héritages historiographiques ? C’est en effet l’un des enjeux du livre que de croiser ces approches. Mon livre est une enquête multisituée qui relève de ce qu’on appelle aujourd’hui souvent la « microhistoire globale » – expression à laquelle je préfère celle, moins ambiguë peut-être, de « microhistoire en mouvement ». Il s’agit de suivre un petit groupe d’individus au travers de leur pérégrination grâce aux traces archivistiques qu’ils ont laissées. Par le biais de ces quelques trajectoires individuelles, j’essaie de poser des questions d’ordre plus général, de comprendre comment elles font « cas » : c’est l’héritage de la microhistoire. L’histoire connectée a quant à elle pour ambition de suivre les acteurs et les phénomènes par-delà les frontières historiographiques. Elle cherche à rétablir des connexions artificiellement « débranchées » par les découpages en histoires nationales ou aires culturelles. À travers la trajectoire d’Ahmad Khan, il s’agit ainsi de faire dialoguer des historiographies qui trop souvent s'ignorent : l’histoire de l’Empire moghol, l’histoire de la conquête britannique en Inde, l’histoire ottomane, l’histoire des révolutions atlantiques. L’objectif est de prendre en compte la multiplicité des perspectives, en évitant le biais eurocentrique. La référence à Dipesh Chakrabarty et à son ouvrage Provincialiser l’Europe va dans le même sens. Plus spécifiquement, elle permet de faire ressortir l’enjeu fondamental que constituent la langue et la traduction dans ce type de recherche. Contre la fausse transparence qui naît de l’oubli de la pluralité des langues, il s’agit de restituer les opérations de traduction qui confèrent au langage son caractère « translucide ». Cela permet de saisir la singularité d’une expérience formulée en d’autres langues que les langues européennes – en l’occurrence en persan. L’« Âge des révolutions » dans le sous-titre de votre ouvrage renvoie autant à une époque qu’à une géographie : celle de l’histoire atlantique. Or votre étude porte sur le monde eurasiatique… La notion d’« âge des révolutions » est effectivement principalement mobilisée en histoire atlantique, mais mon idée était de faire un pas de côté en l'élargissant vers l’Asie. C’est en cela que je m’inspire des travaux de Christopher Bayly sur la « crise globale du XVIIIe siècle », où il connecte les révolutions atlantiques aux difficultés que rencontrent les empires safavide et moghol, à partir des années 1720. Pour moi, il s’agit aussi d’insister sur le basculement géopolitique que constitue la conquête du Bengale par l’East India Company, à partir de 1757. C’était une des provinces les plus riches de l’Empire moghol, peuplée de plus de 20 millions d’habitants. Ce changement de souveraineté d’une région peuplée et prospère a des répercussions bien au-delà de l’Asie. L’onde de choc fut considérable. Ce voyage vers l’Europe que retrace mon ouvrage est l’une d’entre elles. Vous avez donc découvert l’existence d’Ahmad Khan par le biais d’un document attestant de son passage par la France en 1794. Comment et pourquoi y est-il parvenu ? Nous pouvons retracer son itinéraire grâce au récit qu’il en a donné à son arrivée à Paris en 1794, dans cette supplique qu’il adresse au Comité de Salut Public. Tout commence en 1772, lorsque la Compagnie des Indes orientales britanniques, via sa présidence de Bombay, s’empare du port de Baroche, dans le Gujarat. C’était un port prospère, actif notamment dans le commerce du coton. Le nawab local, Mu‘azzaz Khan, est alors destitué, et meurt peu de temps après. James Forbes, Baroche vue depuis la rivière Narmada , gravure, 1813. © Smithsonian Institution Libraries Ses fils sont alors de jeunes enfants. Mais une fois arrivés à l’âge adulte, une quinzaine d’années plus tard, ils décident de se rendre à Londres pour faire valoir leurs droits auprès de la Cour des directeurs de la Compagnie des Indes orientales. Leur objectif n’était pas tant de se voir restituer le contrôle de Baroche que d’obtenir une compensation financière pour le préjudice subi. C’était une démarche pour le moins téméraire ! Cela peut effectivement sembler audacieux voire désespéré. Pourquoi aller à Londres se plaindre auprès de ceux-là mêmes qui vous ont spolié ? Mais, rétrospectivement, ce n’était pas si insensé qu’il y paraît. D’abord parce que dans la culture politique moghole, la possibilité de se plaindre auprès du souverain d’un préjudice que l’on estime avoir subi était très enracinée. C’était donc une réaction assez logique de la part de ces élites indiennes. Ensuite, Ahmad Khan et ses compagnons étaient sans doute au fait qu’au sein même de la Compagnie, il y avait de forts clivages – notamment entre les agents déployés sur le terrain indien et ceux restés dans l’administration centrale en métropole. L’opportunité de l’expansionnisme faisait débat. Certains à Londres estimaient que le coût des conquêtes, aussi bien sur le plan financier que moral, était néfaste aux intérêts commerciaux britanniques. Sans doute, Ahmad et ses compagnons étaient-ils aussi informés de l’impopularité de la Compagnie des Indes dans une partie de l’opinion publique britannique. Ils espéraient en tout cas jouer sur ces failles pour obtenir gain de cause. Concrètement, comment font-ils pour rejoindre l’Europe depuis le Gujarat ? La principale route pour rallier l’Europe depuis l’Inde au XVIIIe siècle est la route maritime via le Cap. C’est celle qu’empruntent les navires marchands des puissances européennes. Mais les fils de Mu‘azzaz Khan n’ont, semble-t-il, pas les moyens ou les réseaux pour pouvoir prendre place sur un navire européen. Ils choisissent donc d’emprunter la route terrestre : partis de Bombay, ils passent par Mascate, franchissent le détroit d’Ormuz pour arriver à Bassora, porte d’entrée de l’Empire ottoman qu’ils traversent via Bagdad et Diyarbakir, avant d’atteindre Constantinople. Puis, via Salonique, deux des fils arrivent à Marseille. Un voyage de plusieurs milliers de kilomètres effectué en bateau – pour traverser l’océan Indien ou remonter le Tigre – ou bien, en caravanes. Cette route était aussi utilisée par les Compagnies européennes car elle pouvait être plus rapide que la route maritime à certains moments de l’année. Mais c’était surtout la route des réseaux musulmans – c’est en grande partie grâce à l’aide des réseaux soufis que les fils de Mu‘azzaz Khan ont pu traverser l’Empire ottoman. Et finalement, sur la route de l’Angleterre, Ahmad Khan fait un passage beaucoup plus long que prévu par la France… Les voyageurs débarquent à Marseille au printemps 1793, ils décident ensuite de remonter la vallée du Rhône vers Paris. Le choix de couper par la France plutôt que de la contourner s’explique facilement : c’était la route la plus rapide et la plus directe en temps normal. Mais ce qui devait accélérer le voyage va au contraire l’enliser, car ils arrivent sans le savoir en pleine Révolution et en plein éclatement de la guerre entre la France et la Grande-Bretagne. Ce qui les arrête, toutefois, c’est d’abord la mort de l’un d’entre eux, près d’un an après être tombé malade à Lyon. Pour ainsi dire, Ahmad Khan tombe dès lors dans une « faille spatio-temporelle ». Alors qu’il pensait avoir fait le plus dur de son itinéraire pour rallier la Grande-Bretagne, il va rester coincé en France près de deux ans – d’abord à Lyon, puis à Versailles. Mais l’objectif d’Ahmad Khan ne varie pas : il veut continuer sa route et, pour cela, doit obtenir le soutien des autorités qu’il sollicite. À la différence des migrants actuels, c’est un visiteur de passage qui ne cherche pas à s’installer mais à rallier Londres, puis à rentrer chez lui après avoir, espère-t-il, obtenu gain de cause. Mais lorsqu’il finit par arriver à Paris au printemps 1794 et qu’il demande au Comité de Salut Public de lui fournir les moyens de continuer son voyage, il se voit offrir l’« hospitalité », ce qui interrompt son voyage. Il se trouve ainsi contraint de s’installer de longs mois à Versailles. Les traces archivistiques laissées par Ahmad Khan prennent principalement la forme de suppliques adressées aux autorités françaises et ottomanes. Ce sont des sources riches, mais problématiques. Car le requérant a tout intérêt à dire, ce qu’il pense que les autorités ont envie d’entendre, plutôt que la vérité. En effet, mon travail s’appuie principalement sur deux suppliques. Celle adressée par Ahmad Khan au Comité de Salut public en avril 1794. Et une deuxième qu’il adresse à la chancellerie ottomane au printemps 1796, alors qu’il est sur la route du retour en Inde. Ces suppliques se ressemblent, car, à chaque fois, c’est la même histoire qui y est racontée. Mais on repère de subtiles variations entre elles, en fonction des lieux, des interlocuteurs et de la langue dans laquelle elles sont écrites. Il m’a donc fallu mener un travail de type philologique pour comprendre ce que ces subtiles variations impliquent dans la position des suppliants. L’un des enjeux du livre a été de mesurer ce que l’on peut tirer d’un tel travail aussi fin sur les textes, en termes d’histoire sociale. Ce travail est compliqué, car ces suppliques ne sont pas adressées directement par Ahmad Khan aux autorités qu’il sollicite. Elles passent par le biais d’un intermédiaire – le plus souvent, Pierre-Marie Ruffin. C’est lui qui traduit en français, depuis le persan (langue administrative de l’Empire moghol, mais aussi langue de communication dans toute l’Eurasie), la supplique d’Ahmad Khan au Comité de Salut Public ; tandis qu’il prend sur lui de rédiger directement en persan, la supplique aux autorités ottomanes. Pierre-Marie Ruffin est l’autre héros de votre livre. Pouvez-vous nous en dire plus sur son parcours ? Ruffin est ce qu’on appelle un drogman – un mot dérivé du turc tercüman , lui-même dérivé de l’araméen via l’arabe. Ce terme a aussi donné le mot « truchement » en français. Et il servait à désigner les interprètes au Levant. Charles-François-Gabriel Le Vachez, Vue de l'intérieur du nouveau cirque du Palais-Royal et des ambassadeurs du Nabab-Tipou , gravure, 1788. © Gallica Né en 1742 à Salonique où son père exerçait lui-même la fonction de drogman, Ruffin a été formé à l’École des jeunes de langues de Paris, dans l’actuel Lycée Louis-le-Grand, mais aussi sur le terrain à Constantinople. En 1774, il est rappelé en France pour exercer la charge de secrétaire interprète du roi dans les langues orientales. À partir de cette position, il cumule les fonctions. Rattaché à la bibliothèque royale, il est aussi le « Monsieur Levant » du ministère de la Marine, en charge de la correspondance avec Constantinople et l’Afrique du Nord. En 1784 enfin, il est nommé professeur de langues turque et persane au Collège royal. Lorsque Ahmad Khan arrive à Paris en 1794, Ruffin était donc tout désigné pour lui servir d’intermédiaire et d’interprète. Mais il fait plus que cela : il héberge Ahmad Khan chez lui, à son domicile personnel, à Versailles. Il lui donne aussi des leçons de français – on conserve d’ailleurs une grande partie du matériel pédagogique élaboré par Ruffin à destination d’Ahmad Khan. La relation entre Ahmad Khan et Ruffin est au cœur de l’ouvrage. Elle est particulièrement riche, puisque la médiation strictement linguistique se double d’une relation d’hospitalité – d’accueillant à hôte –, et d’une relation pédagogique – de maître à élève. Ahmad Khan parvient finalement à atteindre Londres en 1795. Qu’obtient-il, une fois là-bas ? Quand Ahmad Khan arrive à Londres en janvier 1795, il s’aperçoit qu’un autre de ses frères, Ahid ud-din, perdu de vue à Constantinople, est arrivé avant lui. Il est passé par une autre route qui s’est avérée plus rapide. Via Smyrne, Livourne et Toulon – au moment où ce port était occupé par la flotte britannique. À Londres, il met la pression sur la Cour des directeurs de la Compagnie des Indes orientales et obtient d’elle un dédommagement pécuniaire. Cette décision semble surtout résulter de la volonté de se débarrasser de ces requérants indiens susceptibles de provoquer de l’agitation et des polémiques. Par leur pouvoir de nuisance, ils parviennent donc à obtenir quelque chose : une petite pension d’environ 200 roupies par mois pour chacun des quatre frères. Cette histoire est intéressante, car elle montre une capacité d’action insoupçonnée de la part d’individus qui, bien qu’issus des élites indiennes, peuvent aussi être considérés comme des subalternes, du fait de la situation coloniale dans laquelle ils évoluent. Les protagonistes de mon enquête sont les fils d’un nawab, donc ils sont issus de l’élite indienne. Notamment, le fait qu’ils maîtrisent la culture écrite en témoigne. Mais ce sont aussi et surtout des protagonistes qui ont été dépossédés de leur capacité d’action par la conquête britannique. Ils en sont réduits à quémander protection et réparations. C’est donc malgré une histoire « par le bas » que j’ai voulu écrire. Pour l’élite colonisée, accéder au centre décisionnaire s’avère crucial. Dans la culture politique moghole, c’était un aspect important : l’élite dialoguait en permanence avec le pouvoir central. Or ce lien de communication politique entre élites et pouvoir central est rompu avec la prise de pouvoir de la Compagnie des Indes orientales. Donc, c’est sans doute ce qui explique ce projet – se rendre à Londres pour faire valoir ses droits et continuer en quelque sorte cette tradition de dialogue avec le pouvoir central. La Compagnie des Indes orientales se présentait volontiers comme la continuatrice de l’Empire moghol, mais Londres est à des milliers de kilomètres de l’Inde. Dans son livre L’Empire de la supervision , Gildas Salmon a bien analysé les enjeux de cette gouvernance à distance . Gouverner à distance, pour la Compagnie des Indes orientales, consiste ainsi à tenir à distance : elle ne veut pas l’arrivée des élites indiennes en Grande-Bretagne et fait en sorte de les décourager d’entreprendre un tel voyage. Par là, on voit que la colonisation passe aussi par un contrôle des mobilités. Le fait qu’Ahmad Khan et ses frères aient obtenu le versement de réparations est surprenant à plusieurs titres. D’abord parce que le rapport de forces leur était a priori défavorable. Ensuite parce qu’il fait commencer le débat sur les réparations du colonialisme, non pas avec la décolonisation, mais au moment même de la conquête coloniale. Quand Ahid ud-din arrive à Londres, il demande une réparation pour le tort qu’il a subi et produit pour cela un plaidoyer particulièrement argumenté. Dans ce texte, sans doute rédigé avec l’aide d’un avocat londonien, il décrit de manière très imagée et frappante la spoliation dont sa famille a été victime. Selon lui, une « énorme dette née de l’avarice, poursuivie par la rapine et maintenue par la cruauté, la violence et l’injustice » était due à sa famille. C’est un document assez remarquable, qui résonne avec toute une production pamphlétaire hostile à l’expansion de la Compagnie publiée dans les années 1770 et 1780. Thomas Malton le Jeune, East India House , aquarelle sur contour gravé, 1799. © collection Paul Mellon, Yale Center for British Art, Université de Yale, New Haven, Connecticut. C’est effectivement un cas très intéressant d’un colonisé qui soulève, dès le XVIIIe siècle, la question très actuelle des réparations. Ahid ud-din demande d’être indemnisé pour les dommages que lui et les siens ont subi du fait de la spoliation coloniale. Et de la même manière, tout au long du XIXe siècle, malgré l’hostilité de la Compagnie, des membres de l’élite moghole se rendent à Londres pour plaider leur cause. Après le passage à Londres, vient le temps du retour en Inde. C’est par là que vous choisissez de commencer votre ouvrage en décrivant la rencontre d’Ahmad Khan avec le sultan ottoman Selim III. Pourquoi ce choix contraire à la chronologie ? Il m’a semblé que Constantinople était un peu le point de bascule de cette histoire car les voyageurs y passent à l’aller puis au retour. Mais aussi, parce que cela permet de décentrer le regard et de montrer que l’Empire ottoman était alors dans la continuité du monde de cette élite indienne. Ce n’est que par la suite, en arrivant à Marseille, qu’ils basculent dans un monde différent. Sur le plan narratif, cela donne à l’ouvrage la forme d’une « composition en anneau », pour reprendre le terme de Daniel Mendelsohn : un procédé qui s’appuie sur le flashback pour densifier la narration. On fait passer une deuxième fois le lecteur là où il avait commencé, mais enrichi de tout le savoir glané au fil de sa lecture. Ce passage à Constantinople est aussi un moment où des soupçons apparaissent quant au statut et au récit d’Ahmad Khan ? Lorsque Ahmad Khan repasse par Constantinople au retour, il est accueilli à l’ambassade de France, grâce encore une fois à Ruffin qui y avait été nommé entre-temps premier secrétaire. Il a donc la bonne fortune de le retrouver. L’envoyé français à la Porte l’exhibe au cœur du cortège qui l’emmène à son entrevue avec le sultan Sélim III au palais de Topkapi en avril 1796. Or cela éveille les soupçons du chargé d’affaires britannique à Constantinople, John Spencer Smith. Pour lui, cet Indien qui voyage sous la protection des Français est éminemment suspect. Un autre récit se met alors en place qui fait d’Ahmad Khan un espion à solde des Français chargé de faire parvenir des documents à Tipu Sultan, le sultan de Mysore, grand ennemi des Britanniques en Inde. De fait, comme je le révèle dans mon livre, Ahmad Kahn cache quelque chose, mais ce n’est pas ce que les Anglais pensent. Ahmad Khan est finalement arrêté et emprisonné par les Britanniques à son arrivée à Bombay en 1796. Il doit se soumettre à plusieurs interrogatoires. À la suite de quoi, on perd sa trace ? On a conservé le verbatim des interrogatoires, qui permettent d’envisager selon une perspective différente son récit. Cette fois, il n’en est plus tout à fait maître, comme dans les suppliques soumises au fil du parcours : il doit tenter de se défaire des soupçons qui pèsent sur lui. Par la suite, Ahmad Khan disparaît plus ou moins. On pourrait soutenir qu’il n’existe comme acteur historique que lorsqu’il entre dans des réseaux de circulation. Lorsqu’il en sort, il disparaît des radars historiographiques. Mais on ne perd pas totalement sa trace en vérité, comme je l’ai pourtant longtemps cru : il reste dans l’orbite de la Compagnie, et donc de ses archives. L’histoire, d’ailleurs, se prolonge jusqu’à l’époque contemporaine, car les descendants des nawabs de Baroche ont longtemps touché une pension – conséquence indirecte du périple d’Ahmad Khan, de la part du Raj britannique. L’article L’incroyable histoire d’Ahmad Khan est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Ebola in Nigeria: Fears contacts could test positive mount
items.description: •Prof Tomori asks authorities to prepare •Nigeria’s real test is inside its hospitals •Can health workers count on running water, sanitizer, protective equipment? By Chioma Obinna The tap is there. But is there water? The sanitiser dispenser is mounted on the wall. But is it filled? And if a patient walks into a hospital with symptoms that raise suspicion of a dangerous infection, will the health worker attending to that patient have the protective equipment needed to stay safe? These questions may sound routine. But as Nigeria confronts a confirmed case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, they go to the heart of a more difficult question: how prepared are the country’s hospitals to prevent another outbreak? Nigeria has been here before. The 2014 Ebola outbreak tested the country’s ability to detect an imported infection, trace contacts and prevent wider transmission. The COVID-19 pandemic later exposed the importance of hand hygiene, personal protective equipment and infection prevention and control in health facilities. Emergency measures were introduced. Isolation facilities were established, surveillance was strengthened and health workers were trained to respond to infectious threats. But what happens when the emergency passes? Do the taps still run? Are protective supplies replenished? Can hospitals still isolate suspected cases safely? And do health workers have the equipment and practical support to implement the precautions they have been trained to observe? For infectious disease experts, Nigeria’s latest Ebola alert is a reminder that preparedness cannot be measured by emergency announcements alone. It must be evident in the wards, consultation rooms and emergency units where patients first seek care. One confirmed case, a nationwide test Nigeria’s latest Ebola alert followed the confirmation of an imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory on October 20, 2026. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the patient, a woman with a recent travel history involving Uganda, developed symptoms on October 7 and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on October 11. Laboratory tests confirmed the infection on October 20. Authorities identified 44 contacts for monitoring, including people who might have been exposed during the patient’s healthcare visits and travel. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) activated its incident management system, while surveillance and infection-prevention measures were strengthened. By October 23, the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate, said the patient was showing signs of recovery. There was no evidence of community transmission in the information released at that point, although investigations and contact monitoring were continuing. Genomic analysis also found that the virus detected in Nigeria was genetically related to the strain identified in Kenya’s index case. Pate cautioned that this similarity did not, by itself, establish a direct epidemiological link between the two patients or explain precisely how the infection reached Nigeria. The response is therefore unfolding on two fronts. Authorities must establish whether anyone else has been infected, while ensuring that hospitals can recognise and safely manage any suspected cases that emerge. Second responsibility That second responsibility is particularly important. A patient with fever, headache, vomiting or diarrhoea may have any of several illnesses. But when the symptoms are accompanied by a relevant exposure history, health workers must know what questions to ask, whom to notify and how to protect themselves and others while the patient is assessed. An outbreak may be detected by a laboratory, but preventing further transmission also depends on what happens at the patient’s first point of contact with the health system. When the basics cannot be taken for granted Running water, soap, hand sanitisers, cleaning materials, protective equipment and safe waste disposal rarely command the attention given to emergency operations centres or laboratory testing. Yet these ordinary provisions underpin the safe delivery of healthcare. A tap without water cannot support handwashing. An empty sanitiser dispenser offers little protection. Personal protective equipment that is missing when needed can leave a health worker unable to follow the precautions required when caring for a suspected infectious case. The problem is not necessarily that every Nigerian hospital lacks these facilities. It is that their availability, functionality and reliability cannot be assumed. A UNICEF Nigeria WASH Gender Landscape Analysis published in January 2025 reported that only six per cent of healthcare facilities assessed had basic water, sanitation and hygiene services. The figure relates to the facilities covered by the assessment, rather than every hospital in the country, but it highlights a significant infrastructure challenge. For Ebola preparedness, the implications are immediate. Infection prevention is not simply a matter of displaying instructions on a hospital wall. It requires dependable water supplies, adequate consumables, appropriate protective equipment, trained staff and systems that ensure these resources are available where and when they are needed. Items to stop virus The Medical and Dental Consultants’ Association of Nigeria (MDCAN), through its leadership, has called on hospital managements to provide running water, hand sanitisers, infrared thermometers, adequate personal protective equipment, other essential consumables and suitable isolation facilities. The association has also advocated the reactivation of infection prevention and control committees and emergency drills to test the readiness of healthcare workers. Its warning is straightforward, doctors and other health workers should not attend to suspected Ebola patients without appropriate protective equipment or manage them in open wards where other patients and staff could be exposed. These are not special provisions to be considered only when Ebola appears. They are basic requirements for a health system expected to manage infectious diseases safely. Training is not enough The Federal Government had announced that it is strengthening detection, laboratory capacity, case management and public communication as part of the response. “All hospitals should be sensitised and health workers be aware and, when there are suspected cases, to notify public health authorities,” Pate said. The government has also announced plans to reinforce infection prevention and control protocols and train health workers to identify suspected cases, protect themselves and notify the relevant authorities promptly. But experts say training alone cannot make a hospital ready. A health worker may understand the correct procedure and still be unable to follow it if protective equipment is unavailable, water is unreliable or there is no appropriate space to isolate a suspected patient. In an interview with Sunday Vanguard, Professor Dimie Ogoina, a professor of medicine and infectious diseases at Bayelsa Medical University, stressed the need to equip health workers with both the knowledge and resources required to prevent transmission. He warned that an imported case could lead to further spread if contacts became infected and passed the virus to others before preventive measures were put in place. Transmission could also occur during hospital visits or care if appropriate infection prevention and control measures were not observed. “Supporting healthcare workers in adhering to IPC through training and the provision of IPC resources will help promote the adoption of these measures,” he said. For Ogoina, the priority is to ensure that the country’s emergency response translates into practical readiness at federal and state levels. He called for active case searches, effective contact tracing, prompt laboratory diagnosis, clear referral arrangements and suitable isolation facilities for suspected and confirmed cases. He also advocated the advance provision of infection-control supplies and the training and deployment of designated healthcare workers to manage such cases. The point is not merely to have a protocol. It is to make sure that staff can carry it out when the need arises. Finding the next case before it spreads Contact tracing is one of the most important parts of an outbreak response, but identifying contacts is only the beginning. Those identified must be followed up, symptoms monitored and any suspected infection investigated promptly. Laboratories must be able to process samples and return results in time to inform clinical decisions. Hospitals, in turn, need clear procedures for referral, isolation and communication with public health authorities. Ogoina said Nigeria had taken proactive steps following the imported case, including identifying contacts for follow-up and sequencing the virus. He stressed that stronger surveillance and contact tracing would help authorities detect additional infections early and take steps to prevent onward transmission. He also called for stronger risk communication and community engagement to address anxiety, correct misinformation and encourage cooperation with public health teams. The response depends on a chain of connected actions: surveillance identifies a possible case; laboratory testing helps establish the diagnosis; hospitals provide safe assessment and isolation; and public health teams trace contacts and communicate appropriate advice. If one part of that chain fails, the entire effort becomes more difficult. Ebola is not an airborne infection. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. This distinction matters because accurate information can help people understand the risks and follow appropriate precautions without unnecessary panic. For the public, cooperating with contact tracing, providing accurate exposure histories and seeking medical advice when directed are important parts of the response. Fear, stigma and misinformation can undermine these efforts by discouraging people from reporting symptoms or engaging with health authorities. Fears What if more cases emerge? Renowned virologist and chairman of the West African National Academy of Scientists, Professor Oyewale Tomori, has urged authorities to prepare for the possibility that contacts could test positive. That is not a prediction that further cases will occur. It is a reminder that emergency planning should not depend on the assumption that the response will remain limited to one patient. If more infections are identified, hospitals could face simultaneous demands for assessment, testing, isolation and treatment. That would place additional pressure on trained personnel, protective supplies, isolation space and laboratory services, even as contact tracing and surveillance continue. Tomori has also emphasised the importance of taking travel and exposure histories seriously when patients present with symptoms that could be consistent with Ebola. The objective is not to treat every fever as Ebola. It is to ensure that health workers consider relevant exposure risks, recognise warning signs and follow established procedures when a suspected case is identified. Preparedness means anticipating what the health system might need to do next, rather than waiting for additional cases to expose its limitations. The lessons of 2014 and COVID-19 Nigeria’s experience during the 2014 Ebola outbreak demonstrated the value of rapid detection, coordinated contact tracing and decisive infection-control measures. COVID-19 reinforced the need for reliable hygiene facilities, protective equipment and sustained investment in healthcare preparedness. But the challenge is preserving those gains after public attention moves elsewhere. Handwashing stations and sanitiser dispensers are useful only when they work and are replenished. Isolation rooms matter only when they are suitable and available. Guidelines are effective only when staff understand them, practise them and have the resources to follow them. NCDC Director-General, Dr Jide Idris, has called for renewed attention to environmental control, personal hygiene and handwashing, drawing lessons from Nigeria’s previous experience. “It’s a contact issue. So, we need to address the issue of environmental control, personal hygiene, hand washing,” Idris said. MDCAN has also called for stronger surveillance at airports, seaports and land borders, alongside the activation of emergency response arrangements and isolation facilities. It has urged authorities to strengthen laboratory capacity, contact tracing and collaboration across borders. The association’s emphasis on staff welfare is equally significant. Health workers need appropriate equipment, training and practical support, as well as adequate welfare provisions, to carry out their duties safely. Protecting them is inseparable from protecting patients. A health worker who lacks the means to follow infection-control procedures may face avoidable risks, while a facility unable to isolate a suspected case safely could expose others and complicate the wider response. The consequences extend beyond Ebola. The same infrastructure and workplace practices are relevant to the safe management of other infectious diseases. Public assurance How will Nigerians know containment is working? Public reassurance is important during an outbreak, but it must be accompanied by credible information about the progress of the response. Ogoina identified several encouraging indicators: recovery of the index patient, effective identification and follow-up of contacts, prompt investigation and isolation of suspected cases, and adherence to preventive measures by healthcare workers and the public. These indicators must be considered together. A patient’s recovery is encouraging, but it does not by itself establish that transmission has been interrupted. Authorities must also continue monitoring contacts, investigating symptoms promptly and communicating verified developments. Regular public updates can help Nigerians understand what is known, what remains under investigation and what steps are being taken. They can also counter rumours before misinformation spreads. The public, meanwhile, has a role to play by cooperating with health authorities, following official guidance and avoiding the stigmatisation of people who may have been exposed. The real measure of preparedness Nigeria has activated its public health response, identified contacts and strengthened surveillance following the confirmed case. The government has also announced measures to improve infection prevention and control and prepare health workers. But the larger test lies in whether these actions are backed by the everyday capacity of hospitals to recognise suspected cases, isolate patients safely and protect those providing care. That requires reliable water supplies, hygiene materials, adequate protective equipment, suitable isolation facilities, trained personnel, effective laboratory links and clear reporting procedures. It also requires sustained funding, supervision and accountability long after the immediate emergency has passed. The experience of 2014 and COVID-19 should have made the importance of these measures unmistakable. The challenge now is to ensure that the lessons have not faded with the crises that brought them into sharp focus. When a patient with symptoms and a relevant exposure history walks into a hospital, preparedness should not begin with a frantic search for gloves, a check for water or the discovery that an isolation room is unavailable. It should begin with a system that is ready. For the health worker facing that patient, the difference between knowing what to do and being able to do it may depend on the most basic things in the hospital: clean water, protective equipment, practical training and a safe place to provide care. For Nigeria, those basics could help determine whether the current Ebola alert remains a contained public health event or becomes a more difficult test of the health system. items.title: What’s left for Tinubu: A legacy to sustain, a name to behold
items.description: By Opeyemi Eniola President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has already forced Nigeria to confront a set of structural realities that successive administrations preferred to manage, postpone or obscure. On the afternoon of 29 May 2023, standing before the nation after taking the oath of office, he declared that the fuel subsidy was gone. The statement was delivered without elaborate preamble. It landed with the force of a policy rupture. In the weeks and months that followed he moved to unify the foreign-exchange market, clear a multi-billion-dollar backlog of unpaid obligations, end the Central Bank’s inflationary reliance on Ways and Means advances, and begin the long process of rebuilding external reserves and non-oil revenue. These were not cautious, incremental adjustments. They were deliberate breaks with a system that had rewarded opacity, subsidised inefficiency, and deferred hard choices for decades. More than three years later, the question that now confronts both the president and the country is no longer whether those decisions were necessary. The necessity is increasingly acknowledged even by critics who continue to dispute the sequencing, the communication or the human cost. The more consequential question is what remains to be done if the reforms are to become a durable foundation rather than a painful interlude, and whether the name Tinubu will ultimately be associated with courage that delivered lasting improvement or with boldness that stopped short of transformation. That is the subject of this editorial: the unfinished work, the legacy still to be secured, and the standard by which a political name is finally beheld. The inheritance To understand the scale of what has been attempted, it is necessary to recall the condition of the economy Tinubu inherited. By May 2023 Nigeria faced a combination of fiscal stress, external vulnerability and institutional distortion that had been building for years. The petrol subsidy had become an open-ended claim on public resources, consuming sums that could otherwise have supported infrastructure, education and health while simultaneously encouraging smuggling and rent-seeking. Multiple exchange-rate windows created opportunities for arbitrage that enriched a narrow circle and starved legitimate producers of foreign exchange. The debt-service-to-revenue ratio had climbed toward 97 percent and, on some measures, threatened to exceed 100 percent, leaving almost nothing for capital expenditure or social investment once interest obligations were met. External reserves were under pressure. The Central Bank’s Ways and Means advances to government had expanded to levels that fuelled inflation and undermined monetary credibility. Oil theft was estimated in the hundreds of thousands of barrels per day. Investor confidence was fragile. States struggled to meet salary obligations. The macroeconomic dashboard was, in the language of one later retrospective, blinking red. None of these problems was new. They had been diagnosed repeatedly by domestic analysts, the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and successive Nigerian finance ministers. What had been missing was the political willingness to confront them simultaneously and at the beginning of a presidential term, when political capital is theoretically highest and the incentive to defer pain is strongest. Tinubu chose confrontation. In doing so he accepted a degree of short-term unpopularity that many of his predecessors had calculated they could not afford. The reforms and their macroeconomic results The removal of petrol subsidy and the move toward a more market-determined exchange rate were the signature decisions. They were followed by tax and revenue reforms, efforts to improve the efficiency of collection, and a stated commitment to fiscal discipline. The results, measured by official and independent data available by late 2026, are substantial. Non-oil revenue has risen sharply. The administration reported that the 2025 non-oil revenue target was achieved by August of that year, with collections exceeding ₦20 trillion, and that September 2025 alone produced ₦3.65 trillion—more than four times the monthly figure recorded in May 2023. The debt-service-to-revenue ratio has been brought below 50 percent. The government has paid down a significant portion of the Ways and Means stock that had threatened fiscal and monetary stability. External reserves have climbed from approximately $35 billion at the start of the administration to levels above $54 billion by September 2026, the highest in nearly two decades. Gross reserves have provided a stronger buffer against external shocks and have supported greater confidence in the foreign-exchange market. Real GDP growth has accelerated. After years of weaker performance, growth reached 3.89 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 4.43 percent in the second quarter, with the first half of the year recording approximately 4.2 percent according to World Bank figures. Both oil and non-oil sectors contributed. The oil sector posted strong year-on-year growth in the second quarter of 2026, while non-oil activity continued to expand. Trade surpluses have been recorded for consecutive quarters. Non-oil exports exceeded $6 billion in 2025, a historic high, and the share of non-oil trade has risen relative to oil. The Nigerian stock market has reflected improved sentiment: market capitalisation expanded from roughly ₦30 trillion in 2023 to more than ₦160 trillion by 2026, with the All-Share Index rising from the low 50,000s to levels above 250,000 at points in the period. Inflation, which peaked above 30 percent and reached 34.8 percent in December 2024 on some measures, has declined toward the mid-teens by the second half of 2026. The decline has not been linear—geopolitical tensions and domestic supply constraints have produced interruptions—but the direction from the peak has been downward. The current account has moved into surplus. Foreign direct investment announcements have increased. Nigeria was removed from the Financial Action Task Force’s increased-monitoring list, reducing a layer of international compliance friction. The country joined BRICS as a partner and became an association country of the International Energy Agency, signalling a desire for broader economic diplomacy. These are not trivial outcomes. They represent a restoration of macroeconomic policy space that had been steadily eroded. International institutions have acknowledged the improvement in stability, external buffers and the functioning of the foreign-exchange market. The World Bank’s Nigeria Development Update in 2026 noted that the poverty rate had stabilised for the first time since 2019 and projected gradual declines if growth continued to outpace population increase. Debt-to-GDP ratios at the federal and state levels have shown improvement in a majority of states, and combined state capital expenditure rose significantly in real terms between 2023 and 2025. Social policy, infrastructure and sectoral shifts Beyond the headline macroeconomic numbers, the administration has advanced several social and infrastructural initiatives. The Nigerian Education Loan Fund, established early in the term, has processed applications from more than 1.6 million students and disbursed hundreds of billions of naira in tuition and upkeep support. It represents the first large-scale, interest-free student financing system in Nigeria’s history, with repayment structured around future employment. The national minimum wage was raised from ₦30,000 to ₦70,000, and minimum-wage earners were exempted from income tax. Targeted cash transfers have reached more than ten million households according to government figures. The Three Million Technical Talent programme and related digital skills initiatives aim to prepare young people for opportunities in software, data, cybersecurity and the creative economy. The Consumer Credit Corporation has begun to offer working Nigerians pathways to spread the cost of essential purchases. In infrastructure, the government reports that more than 2,700 kilometres of highways and major roads are under construction, reconstruction or rehabilitation. Flagship projects include the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano corridor and the East-West Road. These projects are designed to improve connectivity between agricultural belts, ports, industrial centres and regional markets. In the power sector, efforts have focused on clearing legacy debts, attracting investment and improving transmission and billing, while the broader energy strategy has emphasised gas utilisation. The Compressed Natural Gas initiative has established conversion centres and fuelling stations, with tens of thousands of vehicles converted and the potential to lower transport costs over time. In oil and gas, reduced theft, higher production and the progressive shift toward domestic refining—supported by the operations of the Dangote refinery and other capacity—have begun to alter the balance between product imports and exports. Seaborne petroleum-product exports have risen substantially while imports have fallen. Housing programmes under the Renewed Hope initiative and the Federal Housing Authority have delivered thousands of units and associated construction jobs. Health sector efforts have included the commissioning of cancer treatment centres and attempts to revitalise primary healthcare. Pension reforms and more regular payment of salaries and pensions at the federal level have been cited as improvements in public financial management. Taken together, these measures constitute an ambitious attempt to pair stabilisation with investment in human capital and physical connectivity. They are the positive side of the ledger. The human cost and the incomplete translation The same period that produced these gains also imposed severe adjustment costs on households and firms. The removal of the subsidy and the exchange-rate realignment produced an immediate rise in transport and energy costs that fed into food prices and the general price level. Inflation, even as it has declined from its peak, has remained high enough to erode real incomes for large segments of the population. Food insecurity has persisted. Independent analyses, including those from the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, have noted that while macroeconomic stability has been restored and a deeper crisis averted, the benefits have not yet translated into significant improvements in living conditions for most citizens. World Bank and domestic data continue to show high levels of poverty. The absolute number of people living below the national poverty line remains elevated. For many families the statistical recovery is invisible; what is visible is the struggle to afford staples, transport and school-related costs. Businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises, have faced higher input costs, elevated interest rates and uneven access to credit even as larger corporates and the capital markets have recorded gains. Power supply remains unreliable for many users. Logistics bottlenecks continue to raise the cost of moving goods. Policy implementation at the sub-national level has been uneven, reflecting both capacity constraints and varying levels of commitment. The gap between the macroeconomic scorecard and the lived experience of the median citizen is the central political and economic vulnerability of the current moment. This gap is not unique to Nigeria or to this administration. Structural reforms that correct deep distortions almost always impose front-loaded costs while benefits accrue more slowly and unevenly. The political test is whether the administration can accelerate the transmission of gains to households and productive enterprises before public patience is exhausted or before political incentives shift toward reversal. Security: the binding constraint No discussion of what remains for Tinubu can avoid the question of security. Banditry, kidnapping and residual terrorist activity continue to exact a heavy human and economic toll. Farming communities in parts of the North-West and North-Central regions operate under persistent threat. The disruption of agricultural production feeds directly into food prices and rural livelihoods. Abductions for ransom have created a climate of fear that extends beyond the immediate victims to entire communities and to the investment decisions of households and firms. Urban centres are not immune to crime and the perception of insecurity. The administration has responded with increased budgetary allocations for defence and security, large-scale recruitment into the police and armed forces, improved equipment and logistics, the declaration of a national security emergency in late 2025, and structural proposals including the advancement of state police legislation, the deployment of forest guards, the withdrawal of police officers from non-essential VIP duties, and the creation of additional army divisions. Military pay has been increased. Intelligence-led and joint operations have been emphasised. Cooperation with regional and international partners has been pursued. These measures are necessary. They are not yet sufficient. The data on terrorism-related deaths and abductions in 2025 and into 2026 indicate that the security situation remains below the standard Nigerians have a right to expect. Progress has been reported in certain theatres, yet the overall sense of safety required for normal economic and social life has not been restored across large parts of the country. Security is not merely one policy area among others; it is a binding constraint on agricultural recovery, on internal trade, on investor confidence outside the financial markets, and on the legitimacy of the broader reform project. Without a sustained reduction in violence and the restoration of state presence in contested rural spaces, the macroeconomic gains will remain fragile and the political narrative of prosperity will ring hollow for millions of citizens. What remains: the agenda of delivery The unfinished work can be organised under several headings. First, the transmission of macroeconomic stability into lower living costs and higher real incomes. This requires continued disinflation, targeted measures to improve food supply through security and agricultural productivity, reduction in transport costs through the CNG transition and better roads, and policies that support job creation in labour-intensive sectors. Growth that does not produce employment and income gains for a broad base of the population will not be politically sustainable. Second, the completion and maintenance of critical infrastructure. Highways must move from construction sites to functional corridors. Power sector reforms must yield more reliable electricity. Ports, railways and digital infrastructure must support lower transaction costs for businesses. The fiscal space created by subsidy removal and revenue reforms must be protected from waste and directed toward high-multiplier investments. Third, the deepening of human capital interventions. Student financing must continue to expand access while developing robust repayment systems. Skills programmes must connect to actual labour market demand. Health investments must improve primary care and specialised treatment capacity. Social protection must be better targeted and more efficiently delivered. Fourth, the overhaul of security architecture and outcomes. Recruitment, equipment and legal frameworks must be matched by operational effectiveness, accountability and community trust. State policing, if implemented, must include safeguards against abuse. Forest guards and local security initiatives must be properly regulated and coordinated. The metric of success is not the number of personnel recruited or the size of the budget; it is the decline in attacks, abductions and the restoration of safe economic activity in previously contested areas. Fifth, the quality of governance and institutions. Increased revenue creates both opportunity and temptation. Transparency in the management of public resources, reduction of leakage, strengthening of procurement systems, and clearer accountability at federal and sub-national levels will determine whether the gains of reform are converted into public value. Tax reforms that raise the tax-to-GDP ratio must be accompanied by visible improvements in service delivery if compliance and legitimacy are to be sustained. The rule of law, the independence of key institutions, and the predictability of policy will influence both domestic and foreign investment decisions. Sixth, the management of the political economy of reform. Vested interests that benefited from the previous distortions have not disappeared. Pressures to reverse or dilute key policies will intensify as the 2027 elections approach. Maintaining the core of the reform programme while demonstrating flexibility on sequencing and mitigation measures will require political skill and clarity of purpose. The political horizon Tinubu is seeking a second term in the presidential election scheduled for January 2027. The contest will take place against a backdrop of incomplete transmission of gains, persistent security challenges and a fragmented opposition landscape. Continuity of the reform agenda is not automatic. It must be earned through results that a sufficient share of the electorate can recognise as improvement. A second term would offer the opportunity to complete major infrastructure projects, entrench institutional changes, deepen the social interventions and demonstrate that the adjustment costs of the first term were the price of a more durable foundation. It would also test whether the administration can shift from the politics of crisis management to the politics of broad-based delivery. The alternative—a loss of momentum, a dilution of reforms, or a change in administration less committed to structural discipline—would risk squandering the policy space that has been created. Nigeria has experienced cycles of partial reform followed by reversal or drift. Breaking that cycle is part of the legacy that remains available. Legacy and the name Political names are not fixed by the intentions of those who bear them. They are fixed by the consequences of decisions and by the collective memory of citizens. Tinubu’s name already carries weight in Nigerian political history. As governor of Lagos State between 1999 and 2007 he was associated with the expansion of internally generated revenue, urban transformation projects and a style of political organisation that reshaped the commercial capital and influenced national politics. As a central figure in the creation and consolidation of the All Progressives Congress he demonstrated strategic capacity in the arena of competitive party politics. As president he has added the identity of a reformer prepared to confront long-standing fiscal and monetary distortions at the cost of short-term popularity. That identity is real. It is also incomplete. History tends to reserve its more lasting judgments for leaders who not only initiate difficult change but also steward its consequences to the point where ordinary people experience improvement. The name that endures is the one attached to safer communities, more productive farms, functional infrastructure, expanded opportunity for the young, and a broader sense that the state is capable of delivering public value. Courage in diagnosis and decision is necessary. Delivery in implementation and results is decisive. Nigeria has seen bold policy announcements before. It has seen temporary stabilisations and subsequent drifts. What it requires in this moment is sustained execution that converts cleaner public accounts into better lives for a critical mass of citizens. The remaining period of this term, and any mandate that the electorate may grant in 2027, will determine whether the reforms of 2023–2026 are remembered as a successful foundation or as an unfinished experiment. The macroeconomic indicators provide grounds for cautious confidence. The lived experience of millions of Nigerians provides grounds for urgency. The security situation provides grounds for prioritisation. The political calendar provides a deadline of sorts. What is left for Tinubu is therefore not another dramatic announcement but the patient, visible work of transmission, completion, protection and accountability. It is the work of ensuring that the fiscal space created by reform is not dissipated, that the infrastructure corridors reach completion, that the student who receives a loan can find productive work, that the farmer can cultivate without fear, that the household can afford food and transport, and that the young person can see a pathway into the formal economy. It is the work of making the age of prosperity more than a rhetorical successor to the age of reform. That is the legacy still available to be sustained. That is the standard by which the name will be beheld—by the citizens who live with the consequences today, and by the historians and ordinary Nigerians who will assess the record tomorrow. The opportunity has not closed. The responsibility remains clear. The test is delivery. The time to meet it is now. Vanguard News The post What’s left for Tinubu: A legacy to sustain, a name to behold appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Viaje a la zona cero de la revuelta en Francia
items.description: Moktar, 21 años, se sube la braga, se ajusta la capucha del plumón negro brillante y pone un pie fuera de casa a media tarde. Detrás del bigotito y las gafas de grueso cristal y patilla dorada, sonríe un estudiante de tercer curso de facultad de una familia muy humilde de origen tunecino. Simpático, listo, con un sentido político raro a su edad y la piel curtida por el ambiente. Moktar creció en uno de los edificios más pobres del barrio de L’Abreuvoir, en Bobigny (48.873 habitantes) , justo delante de uno de los puntos de venta de droga donde todas las horas del día hay trasiego de camellos, policía, clientes, toxicómanos. “ Ballon aquí”, reza una pintada en la pared, promocionando el óxido nitroso gaseoso que se despacha para inhalar.
