items.title: #EndSARS: Cry of justice for victims louder six years after
items.description: By Gabriel Ewepu As Nigerians commemorated the sixth anniversary of the #EndSARS protests on Wednesday, October 20, civil society organisations (CSOs) and lawyers said the issues that triggered the protests remain unaddressed. They noted that while the core demands of the protesters remain largely unmet, commitments made by the government have also not been realised. There was a consensus that sacrifices made by those affected in various ways during the protests have not translated into improved policing in the country. Sunday Vanguard recalls that the #EndSARS protests were a series of nationwide demonstrations that erupted in Nigeria in October 2020 against police brutality, extortion, torture, unlawful arrests and extrajudicial killings allegedly committed by the Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS), a unit of the Nigeria Police Force established to combat armed robbery and other violent crimes. SARS Although concerns about alleged SARS abuses had persisted for years, the protests gained momentum following the circulation of a video in early October 2020 showing a police officer allegedly shooting a young man in Ughelli, Delta State. Young Nigerians mobilised through social media, particularly Twitter, using the hashtag #EndSARS to demand the disbandment of the unit, justice for victims of police brutality and comprehensive police reforms. The demonstrations spread to Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Ibadan and other cities, attracting thousands of young people who also called for better governance, accountability and respect for human rights. On October 11, 2020, the police announced the dissolution of SARS, but protesters continued their demonstrations, insisting on concrete reforms, accountability for alleged abuses and compensation for victims. Tragic The movement reached a tragic turning point on October 20, when soldiers opened fire on protesters gathered at the Lekki Toll Gate in Lagos, an incident that attracted international condemnation and became a defining moment in Nigeria’s recent history. Amnesty International reported that at least 12 protesters were killed at Lekki and Alausa in Lagos that day. Widely referred to as the Lekki massacre, the incident intensified public outrage and renewed demands for justice. Although judicial panels of inquiry were established in several states to investigate allegations of police brutality, concerns over accountability and the implementation of their recommendations have persisted. To date, the protests remain a significant expression of youth activism and the struggle for police accountability and good governance in Nigeria. Six years after, some stakeholders, including civil society groups, told Sunday Vanguard that key recommendations by the judicial panels of inquiry were yet to be fulfilled, while the immediate and underlying issues that led to the protests persisted. Nigerians deserve evidence of transformation — CISLAC Speaking with Sunday Vanguard, Executive Director of the Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC), Auwal Rafsanjani, said Nigerians deserved evidence of transformation, not another anniversary of unfulfilled commitments. He said: “Certainly, we cannot describe a relationship built on fear, suspicion, intimidation and widespread allegations of extortion as a healthy police-civilian relationship. Six years after #EndSARS, many Nigerians, particularly young people, still see police encounters as potential threats rather than assurances of protection. “The reported use of tear gas against citizens commemorating #EndSARS at Lekki today raises further concerns about respect for peaceful assembly. “CISLAC maintains that the greatest tragedy of October 20, 2020, is not only the lives lost and injuries suffered, but also the continued failure to establish full accountability and restore public confidence. “A police institution that citizens fear more than criminals has a serious legitimacy and accountability problem. “Government must implement outstanding judicial panel recommendations, ensure justice for victims and end the culture of impunity.” Torture “There have been reform announcements and institutional adjustments, but Nigerians are entitled to ask: what has fundamentally changed on the streets? “SARS was disbanded, judicial panels were established, police regulations were revised and training initiatives introduced. “Yet allegations of unlawful detention, torture, extortion, excessive force and extrajudicial killings continue. “CISLAC insists that changing the name of a police unit without changing its conduct is not reform. “Reform must produce measurable results: fewer abuses, independent investigations, prosecution of offending officers, compensation for victims and improved police welfare. “Six years is more than enough time for promises to become results. “Nigerians deserve evidence of transformation, not another anniversary of unfulfilled commitments.” Coercion However, he noted that Nigeria had dedicated and courageous police officers, but institutional weaknesses and persistent allegations of misconduct continued to undermine public confidence. “Poor welfare, inadequate equipment, political interference, weak supervision and insufficient accountability have complicated effective policing. “However, none of these challenges excuses brutality or corruption. “CISLAC is particularly concerned about allegations of indiscriminate arrests, unlawful payments at checkpoints, police involvement in civil disputes and intimidation of innocent citizens. “Policing must move from coercion to service, from intimidation to public cooperation and from impunity to accountability. “The police must stop treating citizens as subjects to be controlled and start treating them as rights-bearing people to be protected. “We demand independent civilian complaints oversight, stronger internal discipline, improved personnel welfare and enforceable sanctions against abuse.” State police Speaking on the need for state police, considering the current policing challenges in Nigeria, Rafsanjani, who is also Head of Transparency International Nigeria, said: “State police is relevant, but decentralising police powers without decentralising accountability could create 36 additional centres of political intimidation. “Nigeria’s security challenges require more effective local intelligence, community participation and faster responses to crime. “However, state police must never become private security organisations for governors or weapons against political opponents, journalists, protesters and vulnerable communities. “CISLAC supports a properly regulated state policing framework with independent recruitment and oversight commissions, constitutional human rights safeguards, transparent funding and clear restrictions against political interference. “State policing must also be subject to independent investigations and judicial accountability. “Nigeria needs policing closer to the people, not armed institutions closer to political power. “Without these safeguards, state police could reproduce the very abuses that triggered #EndSARS. “Six years after #EndSARS, Nigeria must choose between accountable democratic policing and the continued misuse of security institutions. “The sacrifices associated with #EndSARS must not be forgotten, and the 2027 elections must not become another opportunity for security agencies to violate the rights they are sworn to protect.” 2020 demands largely unmet — Global Rights On his part, Executive Director of Global Rights, Abiodun Baiyewu, lamented that the demands of the protesters remained largely unmet. He said: “As we commemorate the sixth anniversary of #EndSARS, we invite the Nigerian people, government, especially the Presidency, and security forces to pause and reflect on this tragic incident in which at least 135 protesters were extrajudicially killed across the country during the #EndSARS protest. “It is worrisome that six years after this tragic event, accountability that is commensurate with the gravity of the atrocities committed is still elusive. “The demands that brought Nigerians to the streets in 2020 remain largely unmet, and the pattern of impunity has persisted. “In the more recent incident of the August 2024 #EndBadGovernance protests, Global Rights documented the killing of at least 31 protesters by police across several states and the arbitrary arrest of 1,135 protesters, including children as young as 13 years old. “To date, there has been no accountability for these killings either. “Even more worrisome is the fact that this trend is unrelenting. “Since that incident, Global Rights has recorded at least 545 extrajudicial killings by security forces across the country. “The repression and continued use of excessive force against protesters, the killing of citizens exercising their constitutional and fundamental human rights, and the continued brazen impunity for security personnel responsible for such violations further expose the hollowness of claims that the grievances that gave rise to #EndSARS have been adequately addressed. ECOWAS judgment “The #EndSARS protests were a nationwide demand for an end to police brutality, unlawful arrests, extortion, torture, and the impunity enjoyed by security personnel. “Wearied by colonial brutality against citizens and having endured decades of the savagery of military juntas, Nigerians were hopeful that under a democratically elected government, their rights would be respected and that they would be treated with dignity by the security force that is funded by their taxes to protect them. “After two decades, realising that change was not forthcoming, they took to the streets to demand a transparent police force that respects the rights of citizens and is not a continuum of the colonial regime or military dictatorship. “As we soberly reflect on the Lekki Toll Gate incident, we are reminded that these acts of impunity are a stark demonstration of Nigeria’s failure to value and protect the lives of its citizens. “Nigeria’s perennial insecurity is fast eroding the bonds that bind its people together. “Its intractable hydra-headed extremism is driven and sustained by this trust deficit. “In order to extricate the nation from this vicious cycle, the government of Nigeria must urgently do the following: immediately implement the ECOWAS Court judgment on the Lekki massacre. “We further demand that the Lagos State Government publicly account for its response to the Judicial Panel of Inquiry’s recommendations, specifying what has been implemented, what remains outstanding, and the steps required to give effect to the recommendations it accepted. “Six years ago, we promised to stand with the victims and their families, however long it takes for the arc of the moral universe to bend towards justice for them, and indeed every citizen of Nigeria. “Global Rights has not reneged on this promise. “We remain standing in solidarity with all those who continue to demand an end to police brutality and the right of citizens to protest. “We honour the courage of those who stood up and keep standing for their rights and reaffirm that no state institution is above the law.” Citizens-police relationship deeply affected by mistrust — ActionAid Reviewing the matter, Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria (AAN), Dr Andrew Mamedu, said the relationship between the police and the people remained highly unfriendly. His words: “Six years after #EndSARS, the relationship between the Nigerian Police and citizens remains deeply challenged by mistrust, fear and unresolved questions of accountability. “The Lekki Toll Gate incident remains a painful reminder of what happens when institutions established to protect citizens are accused of turning their weapons against them. “The reported use of tear gas against citizens commemorating the anniversary today raises further concerns about how the police respond to peaceful civic expression. “Public relations campaigns alone cannot restore trust. “They must earn it through respect for human rights, professionalism, and accountability. “The Nigerian Police must understand that citizens are not enemies of the state, and demanding accountability is not a crime.” Reforms Mamedu, however, noted that some reforms had been implemented in the police force since the #EndSARS protests. “The police have undergone some institutional and policy reforms, including disbanding SARS, introducing new operational regulations, and efforts to strengthen police professionalism”, he said. “However, the real question is whether these reforms have translated into meaningful changes in everyday experiences. “Reports of extortion, arbitrary arrests, excessive use of force and other forms of police misconduct continue to raise concerns. “We must move beyond reforms that exist only on paper. “We must measure police reform by citizens’ safety and dignity, not by the number of policies announced. “Six years after #EndSARS, Nigerians deserve clear evidence of accountability, justice for victims and a policing culture that prioritises human rights. Officers “The Nigeria Police operate under difficult conditions, including inadequate resources, operational pressures and serious security challenges. “Many officers continue to serve professionally and make enormous sacrifices to protect communities. “However, these challenges cannot justify misconduct or violations of citizens’ fundamental rights. “The recurring complaints of harassment, extortion, brutality and abuse of power require urgent institutional attention. “We need to shift from a culture of force and intimidation to one of service, community partnership, and accountability. “A police officer should represent safety, not fear. “The true measure of effective policing is not how much power officers exercise over citizens, but how effectively they protect their lives, rights and dignity.” State-controlled On the issue of state police, the AAN boss asserted: “The conversation around state police is both relevant and necessary, particularly given Nigeria’s complex security challenges and the limitations of centralised policing. “Decentralised policing could strengthen local intelligence, improve response times and bring security institutions closer to communities. “However, there are legitimate concerns about the possibility of governors and political actors using state-controlled police formations to intimidate opponents or suppress dissent. “The ongoing constitution amendment process presents an opportunity to address these concerns through proper institutional safeguards. “We must not decentralise police power without decentralising accountability. “Any state police framework must guarantee operational independence, transparent recruitment, independent oversight and strong protection against political interference. “Otherwise, we risk reproducing at the state level the same abuses Nigerians have been demanding an end to at the federal level.” Weed out bad eggs from police — Faro Lending his voice, human rights lawyer Idris Faro said: “There are bad eggs in every organisation. “The police must continue to weed out the bad eggs and discipline them appropriately. “The Nigeria Police has improved in the way they relate with the people since the violent #EndSARS protest, which led to the loss of lives on both sides. “Evidently, there have been reforms since the nationwide protest, which turned bloody in some states. “The police have retrained their officers to be respectful in their relations with the people and be professional while suppressing public disorder. “The use of firearms is for self-defence and the arrest of violent armed criminals. They shouldn’t fire tear gas at peaceful protesters. “This was reported to have happened at the toll gate at the sixth anniversary. It is wrong. “As the elections approach, law enforcement officers must work to ensure that we have free and fair elections by providing security for all before, during and after the elections. “They must bring the full weight of the law to bear against persons and politicians who resort to violence to further their goals. Law enforcers, as the term connotes, work for the law only.” Six years after, we demand evaluation of policing — Odheke Similarly, another human rights lawyer, Toluwa Odheke, called for a thorough evaluation of the Nigerian policing system six years after the #EndSARS protests. Odheke said: “Nigeria’s policing system must be evaluated against a simple constitutional proposition: The police exist to protect the public, enforce the law and safeguard the rights of every person, not merely to maintain the authority of the state. “The events at the Lekki Toll Gate remain a reminder of the grave consequences that may follow when the use of force, public accountability and the protection of fundamental rights become matters of institutional controversy. “The continuing importance of that incident lies not only in the question of what happened on 20 October 2020, but also in the lessons that must be learned to prevent comparable failures in the future. “Nigeria has introduced relevant reforms, including the Police Act 2020 and the 2025–2026 police regulations. “Nevertheless, legislation and administrative directives must be accompanied by effective implementation, independent oversight, transparent investigations and appropriate consequences for proven misconduct.” Power On state police, he argued: “State police may offer advantages in local responsiveness and community engagement, but it must be designed to prevent political capture, discrimination and competing centres of unaccountable coercive power. “Decentralisation without accountability would merely relocate existing problems. “As the country prepares for the 2027 general elections, the responsibility of security agencies is particularly clear. “They must protect voters, candidates, electoral officials, journalists and observers impartially before, during and after polling. “They must not intimidate citizens, obstruct lawful political activity or become instruments for manipulating electoral outcomes. “Government should therefore make police accountability a measurable institutional priority, not simply a political commitment. “The relevant test is whether citizens can report abuse safely, whether complaints receive impartial investigation, whether victims obtain effective remedies and whether officers who commit offences are held accountable under the law. “The ultimate measure of police reform is not the number of policies announced, units renamed or regulations issued. “It is the extent to which the Nigerian people can trust that the law protects them equally, that the police will respect their rights and that no person is above the law. “That is the standard by which the legacy of #EndSARS should be assessed, state police should be designed and the conduct of security agencies during the 2027 general elections should be judged.” Nigerians don’t trust Nigerian police — Onoja Human rights activist Patrick Onoja asserted that six years after the #EndSARS protests, the relationship between the Nigeria Police Force and Nigerians remained strained. He said: “Six years after the events of 20th October 2020, I would describe the relationship as one still burdened by mistrust, apprehension and an unresolved demand for appropriate sanctions for proven violations and effective remedies for victims. “The #EndSARS protests did not emerge in a vacuum. “They reflected years of public frustration over allegations of brutality, extortion, arbitrary arrests and abuse of police powers. “The Lekki Toll Gate incident became a defining moment in that crisis. “Under Chapter IV of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, as amended, citizens enjoy fundamental rights to life, dignity and personal liberty. “The police are not above these guarantees. Their responsibility to enforce the law must be exercised within the law. “A police institution cannot effectively protect a population that is afraid of it. Trust cannot be restored through official statements or commemorative events alone. It must be earned through consistent professional conduct, transparent investigations and accountability”. Visible Onoja said the Nigeria Police Force remained one of the country’s most visible and important security institutions, with officers operating in difficult circumstances and often confronting serious crimes with inadequate resources. He said: “Nigeria Police Force remains one of the country’s most visible and important security institutions. “Officers operate in difficult circumstances, often confronting serious crimes with inadequate resources. “I acknowledge and commend officers who perform their duties professionally and courageously, sometimes at considerable personal risk. “However, acknowledging their sacrifices must not prevent us from confronting institutional shortcomings in funding, training, accommodation, equipment, welfare and internal discipline. “There are also persistent public concerns about alleged extortion and abuse of authority, which must be investigated fairly and thoroughly. “The police-civilian relationship must be built around policing by consent, the understanding that legitimate law enforcement depends not only on legal authority but also on public confidence and cooperation. “Years after #EndSARS, Nigeria must move beyond commemoration to addressing the institutional problems that made it a turning point. “The loyalty of every police officer must be to the constitution and the law, not to the personal interests of any politician. “We need a police force that is adequately equipped, professionally trained and properly supervised, and an accountability system that protects citizens from abuse. “The enduring lesson of #EndSARS is that security without accountability threatens freedom, while accountability without effective security undermines public safety. Nigeria must pursue both.” Vanguard News The post #EndSARS: Cry of justice for victims louder six years after appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: El acertijo de cada día en Madrid: ¿dónde le toca trabajar hoy a Ayuso?

La presidenta de Madrid es seguramente la política española más expuesta a la opinión pública por su ejercicio diario de acaparar la atención. No hay charco al que no se lance, ningún tema que le resulte ajeno. Sus explosivas declaraciones contra sus rivales impactan como golpes secos. Un lector medio informado puede desayunar, almorzar y cenar Ayuso. Sin embargo, adivinar en qué espacio opera a día de hoy no resulta sencillo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: No está tan enfadado Milei para insultar tanto. Vosotros tampoco
items.description: Un 15 de abril de 1970, Indro Montanelli tomó la estupenda decisión de enfadarse con el responsable de Il Gazzettino , Lauro Bergamo. Bergamo le había dedicado un editorial a Montanelli, y Montanelli escribió en sus diarios: “Voy a contestarle en su propio periódico y todos creerán que nos estamos peleando. Pero qué va, nos hemos puesto de acuerdo para discutir, y la pelea será fingida”. El caso es que los dos, movidos por la atención que se les prestaba, empezaron a endurecer su réplica. Hasta que Bergamo descolgó el teléfono iracundo: “Te publico porque ese era nuestro pacto. ¡Pero tú muerdes!”. “Tú también muerdes”, contestó Montanelli. “Sí”, reconoció humilde Bergamo: “Pero tú haces daño”. Escribe Montanelli en sus diarios, Cuentas conmigo mismo (La Esfera, 2011), que, efectivamente, Bergamo daño no hacía. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Judeline: “Voy a volver a España para votar”
items.description: Son las nueve en punto de la mañana en Los Ángeles, California. Judeline , Lara Fernández Castrelo en el DNI, se acaba de levantar y está despeluchada y con cara de sueño. Por eso, aunque la rutilante foto que ilustra esta entrevista se hizo en Madrid, en vísperas de su viaje, prefiere no activar la cámara en la llamada telefónica que hemos acordado a esa hora y que inicia ella misma como un clavo. La cantante, gaditana de Barbate, se marchó hace una semana a Los Ángeles sin billete de vuelta y pasa los días probando en el estudio sus nuevas canciones mientras, en la misma ciudad, los Javis y parte del reparto de La bola negra , promocionan a destajo la película en su carrera a los Oscar. La versión de Judeline del clásico pasodoble Soldadito español para la banda sonora del filme se ha convertido en una de sus señas más reconocibles. Eso, junto a que la canción BbYWOW , en colaboración con Karol G. y Rusowsky, la convirtieron en septiembre en la cantante española más reproducida de la historia en Spotify, pueden hacer parecer mayor de lo que es a una chica que solo tiene 23 años. Por algún sitio hay que romper el hielo. Seguir leyendo VIDAS DE LARA Lara Fernández Castrelo eligió de jovencita llamarse Judeline, en recuerdo de Hey, Jude , la canción de los Beatles. De más jovencita, se entiende, porque Lara (Barbate, Cádiz) acaba de cumplir 23 años, aunque algunos no alcanzan sus hitos en toda una vida. Ella misma ha contado que salió de una depresión severa, causada por el acoso y el aislamiento escolar que sufrió de niña, gracias a la música. Hoy, quiere comerse el mundo.

items.title: Todo el poder para la derecha
items.description: Por primera vez en democracia, el principal partido de la derecha negocia con la extrema derecha antes de que los ciudadanos hayan votado. Y lo hace a la vista de todos, discutiendo provincia por provincia dónde conviene que uno de los dos se retire para no estorbar al otro. Cabría esperar que dos partidos que aspiran a gobernar juntos empezaran por ponerse de acuerdo en algo que cambie la vida de los ciudadanos, por ejemplo, una política de vivienda o una reforma fiscal. Pero resulta que el primer proyecto común que se proponen, sin que Feijóo se moleste en disimular, es alcanzar en el Senado la mayoría que les permita renovar el Constitucional sin contar con nadie más. Lo que cohesiona este bloque, pues, es la voluntad de hacerse con los contrapoderes, un patrón que hemos visto en las democracias que se han deslizado hacia el iliberalismo. Y no hace falta exagerar ni hablar de Hungría para señalar que el orden de prioridades es revelador. La Constitución exige una mayoría de tres quintos para que las Cámaras propongan a los magistrados del Constitucional. La razón es bastante sencilla, aunque hoy pueda parecer ingenua : que la mayoría que aprueba las leyes no pueda elegir por sí sola a quienes tienen el poder de anularlas. En diciembre del año pasado venció el mandato de cuatro magistrados cuya renovación corresponde al Senado, dos del sector progresista y dos del conservador, y lo que habría correspondido, como es costumbre, era un acuerdo por el que los dos grandes partidos pactaran los cuatro nombres, de manera que el tribunal conservara su equilibrio. El PP, que no habría cedido un solo puesto, ha preferido usar su mayoría en el Senado una y otra vez para ampliar el plazo de las candidaturas, y hoy se entiende mejor por qué. Si la derecha alcanza los tres quintos el 29 de noviembre, podrá nombrar a los cuatro. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Donde no haya poseedor ni poseída
items.description: Haga usted memoria. Piense en todas las películas o series que ha visto en su vida en las que aparecían prostitutas. Tal vez no reparó demasiado porque las prostitutas aparecían como un elemento más de la decoración de un club en el que los hombres hablaban de sus negocios o sus crímenes, que era el asunto crucial de la trama. Lo más habitual en esa lista que usted está haciendo es que las historias le vengan a la memoria asociadas a directores varones, porque los retratistas del mundo prostibulario han sido ellos. Prostitutas en comedias, analfabetas y graciosas, prostitutas que no cobran si se encuentran con un follador prodigioso, prostitutas que aparecen en fichas policiales, prostitutas que salen de una tarta, que se contonean en una barra, que se meten billetes entre las tetas, que son asesinadas junto al gobernador de turno, prostitutas de buen corazón, prostitutas que hacen su servicio junto a la cuna del bebé. Qué poco se nos contaba de ellas. Qué poco sabemos aun encabezando el ranking de más puteros de Europa. ¡Y el tercero a escala mundial! Seguir leyendo

items.title: La isla vaciada
items.description: 1. En el aeropuerto internacional José Martí de La Habana hay una línea aérea con destino a otros países cuya fila tiene una reveladora peculiaridad: entre los pasajeros que se disponen a chequear, siempre hay varias familias que incluyen niños. Todos los días. Durante muchos días. Un empleado de esa aerolínea me ha dicho: cada semana se va un aula escolar. Cada dos meses sale del país una escuela, concluye. El dato, absolutamente empírico es, sin embargo, tan real que provoca, cuando menos, preocupación. La nación pierde así parte de su futuro y esa es una coyuntura que provocará muchas consecuencias. Los Albertos , Alberto Cortina y Alberto Alcocer —financieros, primos, casados ambos con las hermanas Koplowitz, empresarias españolas—, también propiciaron durísimos reproches entre ambos órganos. items.title: La acampada de Sol ya dura más que la histórica protesta del 15-M
items.description: Las comparaciones, se dice, son odiosas. Pero cuando el sábado 26 de septiembre una treintena de personas decidió plantar una treintena de tiendas de campaña en la Puerta del Sol para protestar por la vivienda, los recuerdos del 15-M, del campamento de los indignados que hace 15 años ocupó también el kilómetro cero de la capital, fueron inevitables. Hay quienes participaron la primera vez y se sumaron a esta segunda ―impulsada por el Sindicato de Inquilinas― con el “por fin” en la cabeza. Así lo contaron los primeros días , en los que no pararon de llegar tiendas. En una semana ya eran más de 1.200. La ciudad de Sol quedó constituida y ya ha superado en duración a la de 2011. Entonces, los manifestantes estuvieron 28 días asentados frente a la sede de la presidencia madrileña, y este domingo, la acampada motivada por el desahucio de Maricarmen Abascal ha cumplido su noche número 29. Por ahora, no hay fecha de retirada. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘El País Semanal’: 50 años en portadas
items.description: Hay portadas sobre temas de los que todos hablan; otras, de asuntos de los que nadie se atreve a discutir. También están aquellas que dan que hablar, las que tratan cuestiones sobre las que jamás pensaste que podrías tener una opinión y las que dan voz a alguien para que cuente lo que nadie ha contado. Las 219 portadas aquí recopiladas contienen todas estas categorías. Desde el primer número, que abordaba el tema del aborto cuando pocos se atrevían a hacerlo, hasta el relato de aquellas horas que Antonio Muñoz Molina compartió con Salman Rushdie, a quien el integrismo quería silenciar para siempre. También están las portadas publicadas en plena pandemia de la covid, que aportaban contenido a la conversación que todos queríamos tener. Y luego está Millás y su biografía de una mosca. Jamás pensamos que su vida nos llegaría a interesar tanto. Así es El País Semanal , la parte del periódico que es revista y la revista que más se asemeja a un periódico. Seguir leyendo Textos Quino Petit Fotografía Carlos Rosillo Edición Xavi Sancho, Borja Hermoso, Javier Rodríguez Marcos, Tereixa Constenla y Pablo Ordaz Corrección Paloma Espino Fotomecánica Ernesto Orellana y Marta Carretero Diseño Ruth Benito Desarrollo Alejandro Gallardo

items.title: Un Aleph en sus manos
items.description: Toda portada es un salto al vacío, a ese espacio donde la revista se lo juega todo a un golpe, a conectar con el lector, a plasmar el espíritu del momento. No hay fórmulas para el éxito, aunque sí palancas. La emoción, el gusto y la oportunidad son tres de ellas. Su naturaleza difusa las vuelve esquivas, pero cuando se logra unirlas salta esa chispa en la que convergen la mirada del portadista y la del lector. Seguir leyendo El País Semanal 50 Aniversario Este artículo forma parte del especial aniversario de la revista que se publica en su edición impresa el domingo 25 de octubre.

items.title: Una caja de tesoros
items.description: Un día, allá por mi breve y atormentado paso como redactora jefa de El País Semanal (entre 1981 y 1982), estando en el despacho de Juan Luis Cebrián para recibir, supongo, alguna reprimenda, el entonces director del periódico me dijo que debíamos sacar reportajes y contenidos más lujosos, que tenía que ser una revista aspiracional, que la gente la leyera imaginando que alguna vez podría llevar ese tipo de vida. Bajé la cabeza y asentí, cómo no hacerlo ante la jerarquía, pero regresé a la Redacción llena de dudas. Entendía a la perfección lo que Cebrián decía, pero ese era el modelo de un Elle , por ejemplo, y para mí El País Semanal siempre había sido algo muy distinto. Algo imposible de definir, de abarcar, de apresar y alicortar dentro de un modelo. Así que me temo que no hice mucho caso. Seguir leyendo El País Semanal 50 Aniversario Este artículo forma parte del especial aniversario de la revista que se publica en su edición impresa el domingo 25 de octubre.

items.title: Aquello de lo que no se hablaba
items.description: Que la primera portada de El País Semanal se dedicara a las mujeres que viajaban a Londres para interrumpir un embarazo no deseado me llena de orgullo. Es la constatación de que el periódico nació con la intención de escuchar el clamor de la calle. Este era un clamor extraño: todo el mundo sabía algo del viaje de las jóvenes españolas a Londres, pero nadie hablaba de ello abiertamente. Fue una emigración silenciosa, un éxodo de mujeres que solo confiaban su secreto a alguna buena amiga; pero en esa red eficaz en la que se suele mover lo clandestino, una chica de barrio siempre encontraba algún contacto que, de manera altruista, la ayudaba a emprender su viaje. Esta portada, la de la chica sin nombre que ha acabado siendo cualquiera de las que se vieron inmersas en aquella experiencia, me causa una indescriptible emoción. Seguir leyendo El País Semanal 50 Aniversario Este artículo forma parte del especial aniversario de la revista que se publica en su edición impresa el domingo 25 de octubre.

items.title: Un reportaje autobiográfico
items.description: Mi infancia y las moscas … ¡Había tantas y todas gratis, sin importar su tamaño o su color! Estaban en las iglesias, en las peluquerías, en las carnicerías, en las lecherías, en las aulas. Estaban en la cocina, en el comedor, en el dormitorio, en el cuarto de baño, y hasta en un poema de Machado , que luego musicaría Serrat , llegaron a manifestarse. No estaban las moscas ahí y nosotros aquí, sino que las moscas y nosotros formábamos una rara sustancia vital difícil de entender desde la soledad o las soledades de ahora. Había moscas que te acompañaban al colegio y que te esperaban a la salida. Quizá, dirán algunos, no eran las mismas, pero cómo saberlo, quién se atrevería a jurarlo después de los sucesos insólitos a los que hemos asistido durante los siguientes años. Seguir leyendo El País Semanal 50 Aniversario Este artículo forma parte del especial aniversario de la revista que se publica en su edición impresa el domingo 25 de octubre.

items.title: Pilar Eyre, la cronista incómoda de la Familia Real: “Hacienda me hace inspecciones todos los años por hablar de los Borbones”
items.description: A comienzos de la década de 1980, Interviú mandó a Pilar Eyre a cubrir un acto de los Reyes en Barcelona. La periodista nunca había tratado con el monarca y su consorte y estaba un poco nerviosa. Antes del encuentro, una experta en protocolo del palacio le explicó cómo debía comportarse. Tenía que hacer una genuflexión ante el jefe del Estado y su esposa, no debía tocarles ni mirarles fijamente a los ojos y, sobre todo, no podía comentar ninguna incidencia en su crónica. Eyre hizo exactamente lo contrario. No se agachó, les dio la mano, los miró a la cara y en la pieza que publicó al día siguiente en la revista reveló que Juan Carlos I había pedido un whisky en pleno besamanos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Israel no es una democracia normal
items.description: En las elecciones generales de Hungría celebradas el pasado abril, el Gobierno populista de derechas del primer ministro Viktor Orbán fue desalojado del poder no por una oposición de izquierda, sino por un partido de centroderecha comprometido con la lucha contra la corrupción y la restauración de la democracia . Israel se dirige a las urnas este 27 de octubre y un cambio similar es, con diferencia, el mejor resultado que cabe razonablemente esperar: que el Gobierno extremista del primer ministro Benjamín Netanyahu sea sustituido por una Administración decente y respetuosa con la ley. Una política exterior radicalmente nueva seguirá estando fuera de alcance. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Decoding defence deals
items.description: SINCE September 2025, Pakistan has signed multilayered and multi-domain defence agreem­e­nts with several Arab and Muslim states. It has sig­­ned a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, the Makkah Joint Def­­ence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, and a defence pact with Kuwait. Pak­istan has recently signed another defence agree­ment — the Badr agreement . Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia are signatories to this pact. These defence deals have, in the past year, increased Pakistan’s strategic relevance in the Middle East. Interestingly, each accord carries the explicit provision for joint defence production and investment in the defence industry. This clause in every defence pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region. There are four primary strategic factors that have driven Islamabad’s emphasis on the joint defence production clause in each defence pact. The India factor remains the primary driver. New Delhi’s defence budget now exceeds $80 billion, and its rapid induction of advanced platforms has widened the qualitative gap. Joint production arrangements with middle powers are likely to allow Pakistan to accelerate defence modernisation without bearing the full research and development cost. By manufacturing components and subsystems domestically, Pakistan can sustain a higher operational tempo and maintain credible conventional deterrence. Islamabad believes that strategic parity in South Asia does not require numerical equivalence. It primarily requires the ability to absorb, adapt, and indigenise technology at a pace that may prevent New Delhi from achieving decisive superiority over Islamabad. These defence deals, therefore, function as a force-multiplier for Pakis­tan’s conventional and strategic capabilities. Pakistan’s defence pacts over the past year have increased its strategic relevance. Islamabad’s second strategic objective is the diversification of defence suppliers and reduced reliance of its defence supply chain on Western weapons. Historically, Islamabad has relied on Chinese weapons but the extent of dependency has increased significantly in the last two decades. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute has noted that this dependency is nearly 80 per cent. Although Pakistan and China enjoy unprecedented trust and depth in their all-weather strategic relationship, in theoretical terms, heavy reliance on any single external source worries Islamabad. Similarly, Islamabad is increasingly seeking to decouple its military procurement from Western-reliant supply chains. This approach is rooted in Pakistan’s historically bitter experiences with sudden embargoes and sanctions, alongside Islamabad’s broader resistance to the West’s tendency to use defence exports as political leverage over the Global South during geopolitical crises. Primarily, Islamabad is eager to cultivate robu­­st, non-Western defence partnerships to secure reliable and uninterrupted arms supplies free from the influence of foreign powers. By integrating affluent Saudi and Qatari capital with the technologically advanced Turkish weapons industry, Pakistan is building an insulated, collaborative defence network with the middle powers to achieve this strategic objective. Islamabad belie­ves that these defence deals, alongside its strategic alliance with China, may allow Islamabad to minimise its conventional vulnerabilities, help mod­­ernise its armed forces, and ultimately achieve a much higher degree of long-term strategic autonomy. Moreover, Islamabad is acutely aware that the intensifying US-China strategic competition will make it increasingly difficult to maintain a purely China-centric defence supply chain in the long run. Therefore, by building parallel defence production partnerships with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkiye, and Indonesia, Pakistan is creating a middle-power buffer to avoid unwanted political pressure from the US. Interestingly, these countries are not fully aligned with either Washington or Beijing, and provide Islamabad greater room for manoeuvre. Third, the economic factor equally occupies the strategic motivations of Islamabad. Pakistan wants to enhance its ability to modernise the defence production industry and increase defence exports. Pakistan’s official defence exports stood at approximately $280m in 2024. The recently concluded deals can significantly enhance defence exports to $650-700m by 2027, crossing the $1bn mark by 2030. The Gulf states, seeking to reduce their own dependence on Western suppliers, constitute the most immediate and lucrative market for Pakistani defence exports. Joint ventures under the Badr agreement, MJDA and SMDA are designed to produce systems that meet the Gulf’s operational requirements, while carrying Pakistani certification, and, crucially, a lower price tag. Successful penetration of these markets would generate much-needed foreign exchange for Pakistan, create skilled employment, and justify further capital investment in the domestic defence industry. Beyond the Gulf, there is also potential for niche exports to African and Central Asian countries that face similar budgetary constraints and seek cost-effective, reliable platforms. The fourth objective linked to the third is to attract foreign direct investment to Pakistan’s defence sector. The joint production clauses are structured to encourage equity participation rather than simple technology licensing. Early commitments already indicate potential inflows of $1.2-1.5bn over the next five years in manufacturing facilities, testing ranges, and human capital development. These investments will upgrade the physical infrastructure of Pakistan’s public-sector defence industry. These inflows can stimulate related industries, including electronics, metallurgy, and software, while creating thousands of high-skill jobs for individuals who would otherwise migrate overseas. Time will tell whether these defence deals can deliver a meaningful technology transfer. The most important question is whether such a multipronged approach can genuinely enhance Pakis­tan’s long-term strategic autonomy or will merely redistribute its dependencies. It is also unclear to what extent these defence deals can genuinely reduce Pakistan’s strategic vulnerabilities. However, despite these uncertainties, these defence deals will bring critical capital and technical know-how, while reducing vulnerability to external supply shocks. Yet Islamabad must calibrate its exposure with precision. Over-commitment in the complex security theatres of the Middle East can risk entangling Pakistan in conflicts whose political and military logic lies beyond Islamabad’s core interests. Therefore, Pakistan must pursue these opportunities with strategic clarity and within well-defined red lines. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own. X: @itskhurramabbas Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Bestway launches Geely Auto in Pakistan
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Bestway Group on Saturday launched Chinese automaker Geely Auto in Pakistan, acquiring the Proton plant at Port Qasim, Karachi, for assembly. Bestway Automotive, Geely’s sole authorised distributor, will handle sales and after-sales service. The Group Managing Director, Irfan Sheikh, said the company would focus on localisation and build a charging network to support its long-term presence. The launch includes three models: the EX2 compact electric hatchback, the EX5 electric SUV, and the Starray EM-i with range-extended EV technology. Bestway said it has invested over $350 million in Pakistan and created 20,000 jobs in the last three years. Geely Auto Inter­national Corporation Vice President Evin Ye said Pakistan was Geely’s first market in South Asia, adding that it was the only automaker with a low-orbit satellite network. items.title: Pakistan export initiative
items.description: DOES any such initiative exist in our country, or is it a figment of my imagination? For sure, there is an initiative for remittances — but not for exports. One wonders about the presence of one and the strange absence of the other. Exports are stagnating, and remittances are rising . Are exports falling because of unwise policies or despite them? Are remittances rising because of good policy initiatives or despite them? The point here is not to denigrate the remittances initiative or its continually renewed push, but to emphasise that exports should be given greater policy priority than remittances — because, in some growth-promoting way, exports matter far more than remittances. Here we explore the reasons. This article focuses on increasing exports, not reducing remittances. In fact, remittances should continue to be promoted. Both exports and remittances matter to our economy. Both help contain the current account deficit. Exports are driven by agricultural, industrial, and services output — sectors that already provide a direct impetus to employment in the country. This impetus also has an indirect impact on the economy through spending by household members employed in export industries. Remittances follow increased output in foreign countries that employ Pakistani workers and pay them abroad. Part of their overseas earnings/ savings is sent home to their families. The economic impact of remittances is indirect and arises from spending by remittance-receiving families. Hence, both help fill the gap in the current account, but the growth impact of exports is both direct and indirect, while it is only indirect for remittances. Another, far more crucial point is that increasing exports to raise the economy’s productivity is paramount for growth. This is not true for rising remittances in Pakistan, although it is theoretically possible if a larger proportion of remittances goes towards export production. Our policymakers seem to have forgotten the importance of exports. A policy to increase exports is more likely to raise productivity than a policy to increase remittances. Increased productivity can fuel long-term sustainable growth. Exporting exposes domestic firms to international competition, better management practices, international quality standards, global supply chains, and new technologies. There is considerable empirical evidence that exporters tend to be more productive and that export expansion can generate productivity gains. For example, the World Bank reports that a 10 per cent increase in exports across its cross-country sample was associated with higher employment, earnings, and productivity. Another point to note is that exports are always preceded by the actual rise in production and employment (direct impact), as well as the indirect impact through consumption made possible by spending of wages by export-related employees. Contrast this with remittances, whose economic impact is not only indirect but also follows the receipt of remittances. This means that prioritising sustained export growth would create more employment in the country and reduce the desperation of unemployed people pushed abroad to find jobs, even at the risk of their lives. At the same time, increasing exports would have boosted the productivity our economy so badly needs. This is why remittances should not be seen as a substitute for exports. Exports should be promoted with more vigour than remittances. In terms of promoting growth, exports matter far more than remittances. Our analysts tend to blame high unemployment almost entirely on high population growth. The fact is that our unwise economic policies are at the root of frequent economic crises that cause growth and productivity to decline. The resulting rise in joblessness leads to greater migration abroad, which, in turn, drives remittances up. Of course, Pakistan’s remittance initiative has helped. But if we had implemented prudent policies that avoided various crises, exports as a proportion of GDP would have risen much faster than remittances. The export-to-GDP ratio peaked at 17.3pc in 1992 (according to World Bank data). It went down to only 10pc of GDP in 2025. The trajectory of the fall was not linear. Every onslaught of a balance-of-payments crisis precipitated a large decline. It fell to 9.6pc of GDP in 2000 in the wake of the 1998-99 crisis. With more prudent policies after the crisis, it recovered somewhat — only to decline again when imprudent policies followed, leading to other crises between 2000 and now. In contrast, our remittances have been rising almost consistently during this period as a proportion of GDP. Remittances dipped from 3.2pc of GDP in 1992 to 1.1pc of GDP in 2000, then rose to 9.9pc. The presence of a falling trend in exports and a rising trend in remittances indicates that exports always respond positively to prudent economic policies, while remittances largely show autonomous growth. Refinements in the banking infrastructure have indeed helped to increase remittances, but economic policies also played a role that pushed people into boats to find employment abroad. Subsequent remittance growth has largely occurred despite these economic policies. Pakistan’s export potential is much higher than its current level suggests. The simplest way to estimate what the level of exports could have been in 2026 is to assume the export-to-GDP ratio of 1992 (17.3pc). This translates to exports valued at $78bn, compared with the actual export value of $41bn (FY26 State Bank data). Frequent balance-of-payments crises in our country seem to have clouded the thinking of our policymakers. When they think about exports or remittances or even foreign investment, they only think in terms of foreign exchange earnings or inflows that fill a gap in the balance-of-payments. Constant firefighting and pressing short- and mid-term foreign financing needs have created a policy psyche that is obsessed with mobilising foreign exchange liquidity and has forgotten productivity and growth. Exports are badly in need of an initiative based on collective policy expertise in the country. The writer is a former deputy governor of the State Bank of Pakistan. rriazuddin@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Pakistan's trade gap with Gulf partners narrows
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s trade deficit with Gulf partner countries narrowed 26.35 per cent to $2.85bn in the first quarter of 2026-27 against $3.87bn a year earlier, largely due to lower imports and moderately higher exports. The steepest declines were 97.46pc and 72.51pc in import payments to Kuwait and Qatar. These two countries accounted for $947.923 million of the gross decline in import payments, partly offset by the substantial increase in imports from Oman. On the export side, the UAE accounted for approximately 66.21pc of Pakistan’s total exports to the seven countries in 1QFY27, followed by Saudi Arabia at 19.45pc. The remaining five countries collectively accounted for just 14.34pc, according to data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan. The Middle East conflict has disrupted Pakistan’s trade since March. Exports to most Gulf states are shrinking, while imports from them are surging—worsening Pakistan’s external vulnerability and dependence on Gulf energy and raw materials. Lower imports, higher exports cut gap by 26pc to $2.85bn in July-September September emerged as the sixth month after the March contraction, suggesting Pakistan’s import flows are highly sensitive to geopolitical developments, particularly in energy corridors. Pakistan remained heavily reliant on energy imports, particularly from the UAE and Saudi Arabia, which accounted for 90pc combined. Other countries, including Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan and Bahrain, remain secondary contributors despite their export capacity. Pakistan’s exports to the Middle East rose 10.96pc to $864.878m in 1QFY27, up from $779.425m in the same period last year. In FY26, exports to the region fell by over 2pc to $3.093bn from $3.152bn the previous year. In contrast, imports from the region fell 20.02pc to $3.717bn in 1QFY27, down from $4.648bn a year earlier. In FY26, imports posted negative growth of 4pc to $16.413bn from $17.097bn a year earlier. Country-wide data showed exports to Saudi Arabia grew by 4.92pc in 1QFY27 from a year ago. Imports, however, dipped by 18.52pc from Saudi Arabia, showing a clear dip in Pakistan’s imports of Saudi goods, especially oil. A positive trend was observed in export proceeds to the UAE, which increased by 16.35pc in 3MFY27, with notable gains in Abu Dhabi, Ajman, and Fujairah. Imports from the UAE fell by 6.15pc, mainly due to lower petroleum and commodity inflows. Exports to Qatar fell by nearly 22.79pc, while imports dipped by 72.51pc in 1QFY27 year on year. The import decline reflects a major reversal in energy-related purchases from the region. Exports to Kuwait dipped 2.24pc, but imports plunged 97.46pc in 1QFY27. This indicates Pakistan’s reliance on Kuwaiti imports, especially petroleum, compared to a year ago. Exports to Bahrain contracted 23.07pc, while imports also dipped 17.31pc in 1QFY27. Exports to Jordan rose by 4.70pc, while imports declined 29.27pc. Pakistan’s exports to Oman rose 10.73pc while imports surged 97.40pc during July-September. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Prudent warning
items.description: AS speculation grows regarding fresh US-Israeli aggression against Iran, major Muslim states of the wider Middle East, as well as European powers, have clearly expressed their lack of appetite for any such misadventure. Meeting in Istanbul on Friday under the ‘R4+E3’ umbrella, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkiye, the UK, Germany, and France discussed several global hotspots, including Iran and Ukraine. Italy also participated in the meeting. The Turkish foreign minister said that “no one supports” military intervention in Iran at this moment, while France’s top diplomat said any escalation “would only have losers”, besides increasing oil prices, which are already high. There is good reason for the international community to be worried. Strong signals are emerging from Tel Aviv and Washington that the US and Israel are planning a new assault on Iran, reportedly after the American midterms on Nov 3 — perhaps even earlier. US President Donald Trump has himself said that “we may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the name America gave to the aggression launched in February. While the US leader is known for his bluster and often non-serious threats, in this regard he may actually mean what he has said. The US has been sending more troops and military equipment to the Middle East, and American and Israeli forces have reportedly rehearsed attack plans. Tel Aviv is particularly enthused about going after Iran again. Doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results each time is equated with folly. But arrogance has blinded both the US and Israel to this reality. Israel had first attacked Iran in October 2024, while both the US and the Zionist state initiated two more aggressive operations against the Islamic Republic, in June 2025 and February 2026. These attacks, particularly the assault launched this year, inflicted huge damage on Iran, decimating its military, political, and religious leadership. But the country regrouped, defended itself, and fought back against the aggressors. The Iranians have reaffirmed that any new attack will be met with “offensive” measures. All of this is cause for alarm. The Gulf states that host American facilities will again be in the line of fire, which is why Muslim countries have warned against a new conflict. But will the war lobbies in Washington and Tel Aviv listen? Many governments and most people of the Middle East are tired of war, and want to rebuild their lives and economies. If conflict and bloodshed return, the shockwaves caused by disrupted energy and trade flows will leave few economies unscathed. Therefore, America should abandon its plans to further destabilise the region. Instead, it should rein in its ally Israel and its bloodthirsty leaders. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
items.description: Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said. After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux. But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France’s modern history. The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000. Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched. President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days. Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city’s Porte d’Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism. Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that “several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters”, the AFP news agency reported. In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France’s second-largest city. Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux. In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture. “There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street,” said one protester in France’s third-largest city. Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase. The minister also said two people had been “seriously injured”: one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were “really frustrated” and had been “suffering a lot” since Macron came to office. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything. Today we are in the streets because it’s been too long, it’s been too much,” the 26-year-old said. Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government. “I think looting is really not good,” one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday’s disorder. “But it’s because of poverty and the violence of the police.” He added that the protests would end “when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France”. Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully. Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday. In Albania’s capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium’s capital Brussels. In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

items.title: Mali: plus de 4.880 combattants neutralisés en près de six mois
items.description: Les Forces armées maliennes (FAMa) ont annoncé avoir neutralisé plus de 4.880 combattants de groupes armés et détruit 162 bases entre mai et le 20 octobre 2026, dans le cadre de leurs opérations de sécurisation du territoire, rapportent des médias locaux. Ce bilan, présenté vendredi par la Direction de l'information et des relations publiques des Armées (DIRPA), fait également état de la destruction de 315 véhicules de type pick-up et d'environ 1.300 motocyclettes, précisent les mêmes sources. Les opérations militaires ont notamment porté sur la consolidation des positions militaires dans la région de Kidal au nord du pays, et la sécurisation des corridors d'approvisionnement. Selon la DIRPA, l'armée a effectué 1.887 missions aériennes de surveillance et de suivi entre mai et septembre, ainsi que 791 frappes aériennes, ajoutant que soixante-cinq autres frappes ont été menées entre le 1er et le 20 octobre. Dans le nord du Mali, les opérations ont principalement concerné les régions de Gao, Ménaka et Kidal, où les forces gouvernementales ont repris position au début du mois d'octobre, à la suite d'une offensive lancée le 6 octobre. Une mission du chef d'État-major général des Armées, effectuée les 10 et 11 octobre, a notamment porté sur les conditions du retour progressif des populations, de l'administration et des services sociaux de base dans cette zone. Dans le centre du pays, les opérations récentes ont permis, selon le commandement militaire, de neutraliser plus de 200 combattants et de détruire dix véhicules et 95 motocyclettes. Par ailleurs, l'armée malienne a renforcé la sécurisation des axes routiers afin de faciliter l'acheminement des produits de première nécessité, notamment les hydrocarbures, vers les principaux centres urbains. Dans ce cadre, la DIRPA a fait état de l'escorte de 2.556 camions-citernes en septembre sur l'axe Kadiana-Bamako, contre 3.681 camions-citernes accompagnés sur différents axes en août. Les autorités militaires poursuivent également le renforcement des effectifs des FAMa, à travers l'intégration de nouvelles recrues et de jeunes issus du Service national des jeunes. Le Mali demeure confronté à l'activité de plusieurs groupes armés, notamment dans ses régions septentrionales et centrales, malgré la multiplication des opérations militaires et des dispositifs de sécurisation des axes d'approvisionnement. items.title: Tinubu blames opposition for hunger, poverty in Nigeria; Atiku kicks, says president delusional
items.description: President Bola Tinubu has accused opposition politicians of causing the hunger and poverty Nigerians are experiencing, insisting that his administration is working to address the problems as he formally launched his 2027 presidential campaign in Kaduna on Saturday. Mr Tinubu made the remarks at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign flag-off at Ranchers Bees Stadium (also known as Kaduna Township Stadium), ahead of the 2027 general elections. I have heard the opposition talking about hunger and poverty. Who caused them? They did! They caused hunger and poverty. We are trying to eliminate them,” the president said. He also urged his supporters to be wary of statements from the opposition, particularly criticism of his decision to remove the petrol subsidy, insisting that the country would not return to the previous system. “Be careful; watch them. Don’t let them lie to you. What is past is in the past. “Fuel subsidy is in our past: no more corruption, no more falsification of invoices, no more lies, no more smuggling of fuel,” Mr Tinubu told supporters at the rally. The president’s remarks come amid persistent public concerns over high food prices, inflation and declining purchasing power, issues expected to feature prominently in political debates ahead of the 2027 elections. In a swift reaction to the president’s remarks, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, described President Tinubu’s claim “as a delusional, shameless attempt to dodge responsibility for the misery his own government has inflicted on Nigerians.” He said a president cannot light the fire of hardship with his own policies, then blame the neighbours for the smoke. Tinubu defends petrol subsidy removal Since assuming office in May 2023, the Tinubu administration has implemented major economic reforms, including the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange regime. The government has defended the measures as necessary to reduce public expenditure, tackle alleged corruption associated with the subsidy system and establish the foundations for sustainable economic growth. While Mr Tinubu insists that the removal of the subsidy is irreversible, critics continue to demand evidence that the savings and additional revenue generated by the reforms are translating into improved living conditions for ordinary Nigerians. At the rally, the president also said salaries were being paid on time and praised APC governors for their development projects. Tinubu thanks Kaduna residents At the rally, Mr Tinubu thanked the people of Kaduna State for supporting him in the 2023 presidential election, saying their backing contributed to his victory. “You gave me the joy of remembering the victory you gave me to become president. I have returned to thank you once again,” he said. He urged Nigerians to give him another opportunity in 2027, promising to continue pursuing his agenda of prosperity, development and national growth. Tinubu has a long history of supporting the North – VP Shettima Vice President Kashim Shettima defended Mr Tinubu’s political relationship with northern Nigeria, saying the president had supported politicians from the region for years, including those who contested the presidency in previous elections. Mr Shettima cited Mr Tinubu’s political relationships with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the late President Muhammadu Buhari to argue that the president had consistently supported northern political figures. “President Bola Tinubu is one person who has fiercely identified with the North over the years. It is pertinent to mention that when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar was harassed and chased off the PDP with his tail between his legs, he ran to the Lion of Bourdillon, who gave him political succour, support and a platform to contest for the presidency of this country in 2007. “In 2011, Asiwaju supported another northerner, Nuhu Ribadu, and in 2015 and 2019, he supported our late President Muhammadu Buhari,” Mr Shettima said. The expression, “Lion of Bourdillon,” refers to Mr Tinubu, whose residence on Bourdillon Road in Lagos has become associated with his political influence. Atiku contested the presidency under the Action Congress (AC) in 2007 after leaving the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), with support from Mr Tinubu and other party leaders. In 2011, Mr Ribadu contested the presidency under the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN), a party led by Mr Tinubu. In 2015 and 2019, Mr Tinubu supported Mr Buhari’s presidential bids under the APC. However, Mr Tinubu and Atiku subsequently became political opponents, particularly during the 2019 and 2023 presidential elections, when the former vice president contested under the PDP while Mr Tinubu was in the APC. Mr Shettima’s remarks were part of the APC’s effort to highlight Mr Tinubu’s history of political alliances and support for politicians from Northern Nigeria as the party seeks another presidential term for him in 2027. Top government officials attend the rally The event attracted senior federal government officials, APC governors and party leaders from different parts of the country. Those in attendance included Vice President Kashim Shettima and Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, who received Mr Tinubu upon his arrival in the state. Secretary to the Government of the Federation George Akume was also among the senior officials at the event. Other attendees included ministers, senators, members of the House of Representatives, APC governors and prominent party figures. APC National Chairman Nentawe Yilwatda and Abdulaziz Yari, director-general of the party’s presidential campaign council, were among the party leaders involved in preparations for the rally and efforts to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s re-election. The event marked the official launch of the APC’s presidential campaign, as the party seeks to consolidate its support base ahead of the 2027 general elections.

items.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
items.description: Former President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections. “This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration’s immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters “we’re in the golden age of America”. The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump’s term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans. Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump. Speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, at one point mocking the president’s attempt to redecorate the White House. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘enough is enough,'” the former president said in Cleveland. Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy. “If you thought everything was too expensive before ‘you know who’,” he said, referring to Trump without using his name, “everything is more expensive now”. Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were “temporarily high” but said “our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down”. The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry “we’re taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs”, and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would “loot your wealth” and “annihilate your borders”. Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia – countries which he described as “terror-infested”. Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: “I said, ‘Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can’t we take people from, like, well… Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'”

items.title: ATC warns Imaan, husband of verdict sans testimony
items.description: • Couple refuses to record statements under Section 342 of CrPC; judge directs them to respond at next hearing on Monday • Defence seeks delay in verdict pending IHC ruling on transfer plea ISLAMABAD: While offering yet another opportunity to human rights lawyer Imaan Zainab Hazir-Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to record their statements in a security breach case, an anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday warned them that a verdict could come even without their testimony if they refused. ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra, who conducted the proceedings at Adiala jail, issued the warning after both accused declined to record their statements under Section 342 (power to examine the accused) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) during Saturday’s hearing. The judge directed the couple to record their statements at the next hearing and adjourned the case until Monday, Oct 26. During Saturday’s proceedings, Hadi requested the court, “Let the state counsel record the statement under Section 342 on our behalf.” However, the judge replied that recording statements under Section 342 was a matter between the court and the accused, adding that they would have to respond themselves. “We will not record the statement under Section 342,” Ms Mazari stated. The judge warned that if the accused did not comply, the court would mention in its order that no response had been submitted. Ms Mazari and Mr Chattha are facing a jail trial in a 2024 case pertaining to the alleged disruption of an international cricket team’s security route and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, was indicted on Oct 7. At the last hearing, a state-app­ointed counsel had cross-examined all prosecution witnesses. The court appointed Atif Mehmood as the state counsel to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses, replacing Taimoor Janjua, who was dismissed from the case over his past conduct. The court had ruled to appoint the state attorney after the defence counsel failed to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses. Separately, the defence filed an application requesting the trial court to refrain from delivering a final judgement until the Islamabad High Court decided a petition seeking the transfer of the case to another court. The application stated that the transfer petition was already pending before the IHC and requested that this development be made part of the trial court’s judicial record. The defence also pointed out that the appointment of the state counsel had been challenged before the IHC. The application urged the trial court to defer its final decision until the high court ruled on the transfer petition. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Wapda inks Rs133bn deal for Diamer-Bhasha Dam project
items.description: LAHORE: The Pakistan Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) signed an agreement on Saturday with the Power China-IKAN Joint Venture for the Rs133.18 billion hydro-mechanical (HM-1) contract for the Diamer-Bhasha Dam project. According to a Wapda spokesperson, the agreement was signed at Wapda House by Diamer-Bhasha Dam Project Chief Engineer and Project Director Arif Ali on behalf of the authority and Ling Jianke, the authorised representative of the joint venture. Wapda Chairman retired Lt Gen Muhammad Saeed, the authority’s members for finance, water and power, the chief executive officer of the Diamer-Bhasha Development Company, a delegation from the joint venture led by Power China International Group Limited chairman, and representatives of the consultants also attended the ceremony. The HM-1 contract covers the project’s hydro-mechanical equipment and hydraulic steel structures. The work includes the manufacture, supply and installation of gates and steel structures to control water flows at the dam. The equipment will be inst­alled at the flushing tunnels on both banks, the power intakes and the dam outlets. The contract also covers steel lining, hoisting and pumping systems, and related electrical works. The spokesperson said the Diamer-Bhasha Dam was a priority project of the federal government for ensuring the country’s water, food and energy security. The dam is being built across the Indus River, 40km downstream of Chilas. Upon completion, it will have a gross water storage capacity of 8.1 million acre-feet and an installed power generation capacity of 4,500 megawatts. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Indian Punjab CM wants to attend Lahore moot
items.description: • Bhagwant Mann says World Punjabi Conference organisers invited him; doubts BJP-led government will let him visit • Speaker Sandhwan jokes, ‘If you get permission, take us along as well’ INDIAN Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann expressed desire on Friday to attend the World Punjabi Conference in Lahore, claiming he had received an invitation, while taking a jab at the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) over whether it would allow him to visit Pakistan, according to a BBC report. The 4th International Punjabi Confer­e­nce is scheduled for Nov 27-29 in Lahore. Mann made the remarks while addressing the Indian Punjab assembly. “They do not even let me go to France or Japan. How will they let me go to Pakistan?” he said, in a jibe at the BJP-led government in Delhi. In a video posted on his official YouTube channel, Mann said many poets from Indian Punjab would travel to the conference. “I also want to go, because our roots are one, our problems are also similar,” he said. The CM mentioned the invitation after reciting verses by Pakistani Punjabi poet Tajammul Kaleem. He said he had spoken to Pakistani Punjabi poet, Baba Najmi and received the invitation, adding that people on both sides of the border shared a culture and should interact. Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan replied, “If you get permission, take us along as well.” At this, voices of some other members also rose from within the house, endorsing what the speaker said. Mann also demanded the reopening of the Kartarpur corridor, sacred to Sikhs. Ties between India and Pakistan have been extremely strained since a four-day battle last year, with limited trade and diplomatic contact. Social media users in both countries called Mann’s wish pleasant despite the chill, according to BBC . Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026
